#6126. JSX Adds New Route From NY

JSX is launching a new nonstop route between the New York metro area and North Texas.

Starting Feb. 17, the public charter service will connect Teterboro Airport in New Jersey with Dallas Love Field. Flights will operate daily.

The service will be available only to members of the carrier’s free loyalty program, Club JSX.

“New York City and Dallas are two of America’s most influential business and cultural centers, and we believe traveling between them should be as seamless as the opportunities that connect them,” JSX CEO Alex Wilcox said in a news release. “As we continue expanding our network, our focus remains on giving customers something increasingly rare in air travel: more of their time back. With this new daily service, we’re bringing the simplicity, comfort, and convenience of JSX to one of the country’s most important travel corridors.”

JSX added service to Teterboro, which it markets as New York City, in 2025. It also serves Westchester County Airport, located just north of New York.

#6125. Transfer Amex Points To Avianca Lifemiles With 10% Bonus: Worth It?

The Amex Membership Rewards program has just introduced a new bonus for points transfers to Avianca Lifemiles. While this is hardly the biggest bonus, something is better than nothing, and the program is useful for Star Alliance redemptions.

Between November 16 and December 16, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 10% bonus when moving points from Amex Membership Rewards to Avianca Lifemiles. This is being offered on Amex’s end, so when you go the points transfer page, make sure that you see this offer available.

Ordinarily points transfer between programs at a 1:1 ratio (in increments of 1,000 points), while through this promotion you’d get 1,100 Lifemiles for every 1,000 Amex Membership Rewards points transferred. Points transfers from Amex to Avianca are typically instant, and the bonus miles will post the same time as the standard miles.

We see transferable points currencies frequently offer bonuses on transfers to Lifemiles, and we’ve seen such promotions from most major transferable points currencies in the past year.

Avianca is in the Star Alliance, which means you can redeem Lifemiles on all Star Alliance airlines without any fuel surcharges. Really this is the core value proposition of the program, since this is a great way to book Star Alliance premium cabin seats at a huge discount. Check out my guide on how to redeem Lifemiles for ideas on how to use these miles.

With a specific use in mind, this could represent a great value, whether you’re looking at traveling first class on All Nippon Airways, or are looking at traveling in business class on a countless number of airlines. Everyone has to crunch the numbers for themselves and decide whether this makes sense or not.

Let me emphasize that in some cases, Lifemiles doesn’t have access to the same award availability as Star Alliance partners, for better or worse. Sometimes Lifemiles doesn’t have access to partner awards that other programs do have access to, and other times the inverse is true.

That’s why I always recommend doing some “dummy” award searches before buying miles, so you can get a sense of how award availability lines up with your needs.

Through December 16, 2026, the Amex Membership Rewards program is offering a 10% bonus on points transfers to Avianca Lifemiles. If you’re looking to redeem on Star Alliance partners, there’s definitely some value to be had here.

With the 10% bonus, you can potentially get a very reasonably priced award on Avianca or one of its Star Alliance partners. As always, the challenge is actually finding award availability. Admittedly I wouldn’t make a speculative points transfer, though, as we have seen some bigger transfer bonuses in the past.

One of the best reasons to apply for a travel rewards card is the welcome offer. By hitting certain minimum spending requirements, you can often earn tens or even hundreds of thousands of points or miles within the first few months of opening a card.

But welcome offers change frequently, and knowing when to apply can make a big difference. After all, you don't want to miss out on bonus points by applying too early or too late.

To help you determine whether an offer is worth pursuing, we've compiled the welcome offer histories of several popular American Express cards, along with our recommendations for when to apply.

Apply now for the American Express Platinum Card®: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

You can also check our frequently updated list of the best increased card offers currently available.

Here are some of the most popular Amex cards, with guidance on when you should apply for each.

While American Express offers several types of welcome bonuses, we’re only discussing publicly available welcome offers.

Public offers are generally available to eligible applicants, while targeted offers are extended to select individuals and may feature higher bonuses or different spending requirements.

Amex also uses personalized bonuses on certain cards, allowing applicants to see which welcome offer they're eligible for before deciding whether to accept the card. The advertised "as high as" amount represents the maximum potential bonus, not necessarily what every applicant will receive. Additionally, offers may change at any time, and some of the offers mentioned below may not be available.

Keep in mind that American Express only allows you to earn one bonus per lifetime on each of its cards, so make sure to wait for the best time to apply. In addition, you may not be eligible for a welcome offer if you've already held a higher-tier card in the same family.

For example, if you currently have or have previously held the American Express Platinum Card®, you may not be eligible for a welcome offer on the American Express® Gold Card.

Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

The Amex Platinum has long been one of the most popular premium cards on the market, despite its steep $895 annual fee (see rates and fees).

It offers a slew of luxury-skewing, value-added benefits that can save cardmembers money on everything from airline fees to hotel stays.

Here are the offers we have seen on the Amex Platinum:

(Offer no longer available; welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Generally, apply for this card only if you can secure a welcome offer of 150,000 points or more, whether through a targeted or limited-time offer.

The Amex Business Platinum often extends even more lucrative welcome offers than its personal counterpart and offers many of the same luxury perks, though some of its statement credits are focused on typical business expenditures.

Cardmembers pay the same $895 annual fee for the Business Platinum (see rates and fees) as the consumer Platinum.

Here are the offers we have seen on the Amex Business Platinum:

(Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.) If you receive an offer for the full 300,000 points, that's by far the best we've seen.

The Amex Gold is an excellent everyday choice for foodies since it earns 4 points per dollar spent at restaurants worldwide on up to $50,000 per calendar year (then 1 point per dollar spent thereafter) and on up to $25,000 per calendar year at U.S. supermarkets (then 1 point per dollar spent). These are solid earning rates for a card with a $325 annual fee (see rates and fees).

#6123. The Subtle Signs That Give 1st Time First Class Passengers Away, According To Cabin Crew

Most of us don't have the luxury of affording a first class or business class airfare, but we can still dream of turning left instead of turning right at the aircraft door. There is a huge difference between regular frequent premium class passengers and those who are upgraded or traveling in first class for the very first time, and cabin crew can spot the difference immediately.

There are the large signs and the more subtle signs that show a passenger is flying first class for the first time, but what are they? In this guide, we'll take a look in more detail. Usually, in just a few seconds, cabin crew will know. After all, they are well-used to assessing passengers during the boarding process.

Cabin crew assess passengers during the boarding process in order to spot any potential issues. This may be an unruly, entitled, or drunk passenger, or it may be that a passenger needs some extra assistance. They will also monitor the cabin through situational awareness to assess if someone has become sick or is a nervous flyer.

They also use emotional intelligence to understand passengers who are not in their usual environment; after all, the sky is home for many of us, and flying is an event for the passenger. It is easy to tell if someone is not used to being in a premium cabin such as first class. Those who are used to traveling in premium cabins will know exactly where to stow their personal items and be comfortable with the workings of the seat.

Passengers who are new to the first-class cabin may be overwhelmed and hesitant and may well be clutching their ticket, especially if they received an upgrade or paid with points or were gifted the seat. Regular premium passengers have a calm demeanor and just walk to their seat. Usually, cabin crew can tell from the passenger's body language and mood.

However, how they are dressed can also give clues. Their familiarity with the aircraft cabin may also be a factor. First class passengers are usually dressed quite formally but also comfortably and have less hand luggage, whereas passengers more used to economy class are likely to be more casual or alternatively dress too formally and have more hand luggage. This is due to the increased checked baggage allowances offered by premium cabins.

The cabin is usually extremely quiet and private, the very opposite of the main economy cabin, so new passengers may have to adjust how they behave to fit in. Today's first class seats can be quite complex, with various recline and massage functions. This could be intimidating to a first time passenger, and they might be hesitant to try to figure out where the usually familiar armrest and tray table are.

A frequent premium passenger will just move their tray table into the correct position without thought, once the seatbelt sign is off. For a first-timer, it can feel like a very expensive puzzle. Amenity kits are often prized and kept intact as souvenirs, or some passengers like to resell them to collectors, according to The Points Guy.

They are designed to be used inflight, mostly to help combat the dry air conditions, and are especially formulated with premium passengers in mind. However, more frequent premium passengers might only use one or two items and leave the rest behind.

Service in the first class cabin is on demand and tailored to each passenger. The cabin crew will address the passenger by their name and introduce themselves. They will ask the passenger if they wish to eat or sleep or if they prefer not to be disturbed, which is sometimes the case. They will also bring any amenity kits or requested items and note any special requirements unique to each passenger.

This could be their favorite drink or what time they would like to eat. Someone who is not used to first class may be overexcited and want to try everything on the menu and ask for everything that's free. Some passengers may be overly apologetic when asking for something as they feel uncomfortable. Many first-timers like to document their experience with photographs or videos.

On the other hand, more frequent first class travelers will barely glance at a menu or wine list and will choose decisively what they want and may ask focused questions. They won't just immediately go for the 'best' or the most expensive but may order more traditional items.

In general, they are less demanding than those who have been upgraded or paid with points. They are not scared of missing out on something as the flight is very routine for them, and they tend to prioritize sleep on long-haul flights.

Some passengers like to 'be seen' when seated in a premium cabin, especially if they have not paid in full for it. They will look to see who notices them. Very experienced first class passengers rarely check out the rest of the cabin and usually their presence doesn't need to be acknowledged by other passengers in the cabin, according to an article at Yahoo Travel.

Cabin crew are used to strange passenger behavior and observing the rules of passenger etiquette in each cabin. They are used to being closely observed by passengers who are in an unfamiliar environment. The fear of missing out on something can be noticeable to the crew, but in general, they don't mind as long as passengers are polite and not entitled. Being over apologetic? The crew don't mind: they are happy for a smile and a thank-you.

The cabin crew in premium cabins understand that regular passengers can get overwhelmed by an ultra-luxury experience, and they will understand it and explain things in detail to help out. The passengers tend to observe every detail: how the food is presented, how the wine is poured, and how they are spoken to, as it's all part of the luxury, and they become somewhat enthralled by everything that is going on.

First class is no longer a given on all airlines, and for a good reason. Let's dive into how the front of the aircraft has totally changed today.

First class cabins are becoming quite rare these days, although some legacy carriers still have them, whilst other airlines have switched to improvements in premium economy and business class. Premium economy has become the new business cabin in effect, and business is the new first class cabin. Upgrades to first class are very rare and are more likely to be a points purchase, if not a fully paid fare.

Most airlines would rather first class seats went empty on flights than to upgrade passengers. This is because it protects their revenue model, and keeping the product exclusive forces people to pay if they want luxury. Giving luxury seats to random economy passengers undercuts the value for high-paying and loyal customers who spent thousands of dollars to sit there.

Cabin crew treat all passengers the same, whatever class they are seated in, but it's how you interact with them that is the most important thing, and they notice it from the moment they first see you. Eye contact and a smile or a polite greeting are much appreciated. Politeness and please and thank you should not be an exception to the rule, and etiquette is expected.

A first-class seat comes with many privileges, like lie-flat beds in private suites, the best in fine wines and champagne, caviar service and a wide range of high-quality meals, plated in the galley and on demand. There may well be a designer amenity kit and pajamas to take home.

A passenger new to the luxuries of the cabin will probably want to try everything, take things home, and also take lots of photos or videos of their experience. Someone used to traveling first class will likely leave most of the amenities behind. They will either eat something immediately after take-off or avoid food entirely in order to sleep.

Everything is routine for them, and they know the ropes, so they are often quite undemanding and do not require much attention, whereas upgraded or points passengers tend to want everything available to them. Most crew members don't mind this unless it's too demanding and distracts them from their duties and other passengers.

The cabin crew working in the first class cabin have a higher crew-to-passenger ratio. This allows them to tailor the service to each passenger in the cabin, as it is also on demand. They also receive training in silver service and how to operate the seats.

Although most first class passengers are easy to please, they can also go the other way and assume the crew are their personal servant throughout the flight. It varies. Upgrades to first class are very rare and more likely to be a points purchase, loyalty upgrade, or for a special occasion.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6122. Transfer Capital One Miles To Qatar Airways Privilege Club With 15% Bonus: Worth It?

The Capital One mileage program has just introduced a new bonus for points transfers to Qatar Airways Privilege Club. While the percentage bonus amount isn’t huge, there’s potentially value to be had, especially given the flexibility these rewards offer.

Between November 15 and December 14, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 15% bonus when moving points from Capital One to Qatar Airways Privilege Club. This is being offered on Capital One’s end, so when you go the mileage transfer page, make sure that you see this offer available.

Ordinarily rewards transfer between programs at a 1:1 ratio (in increments of 1,000 miles), while through this promotion you’d get 1,150 Qatar Airways Privilege Club Avios for every 1,000 Capital One miles transferred. Points transfers from Capital One to Qatar Airways are typically instant, and the bonus rewards will post the same time as the standard rewards.

We see transferable points currencies frequently offer bonuses on transfers to a variety of Avios currencies, and you can of course move rewards between those various currencies. We’ve definitely seen bigger than 15% bonuses in the past, but there’s no guarantee we’ll see a higher offer return anytime soon.

I’d argue that the Qatar Airways Privilege Club program is pretty lucrative nowadays. For one, keep in mind that Qatar Airways uses Avios as its rewards currency, so it’s possible to transfer Avios at a 1:1 ratio between the various programs that earn Avios. That includes Aer Lingus AerClub, British Airways Club, Finnair Plus, and Iberia Plus.

This means that you could use this offer to indirectly convert Citi ThankYou points into British Airways Avios with a 15% bonus as well. That’s something that will no doubt interest some.

However, there’s also huge value directly with the Qatar Airways Privilege Club program. Privilege Club has decent award pricing on Qatar Airways flights, and also has access to more business class award availability than partner programs (though availability still isn’t great). Privilege Club also has several unique airline partners, ranging from JetBlue, to RwandAir, to Virgin Australia, opening up valuable redemption opportunities.

Through December 14, 2026, the Capital One program is offering a 15% bonus on points transfers to Qatar Airways Privilege Club. If you’re looking to acquire any “flavor” of Avios, this could be a great value, as this is also a way to get rewards with British Airways, Iberia, etc.

However, if you’re thinking of making a speculative transfer to earn Avios, I might wait for a bigger offer, as we do sometimes see 30%+ bonuses on transfers to some Avios currencies.

#6121. Legislative Branch bill would hold off on GAO cuts

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

It joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

Her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

The Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

The GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

The House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds important efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., said in a statement.

The Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

#6120. Hello, OMAAT Readers! How I Got Here And What’s Next

Isn’t this a little surreal? After years of reading OMAAT, here I am writing my very first post.

First of all, a huge thank you to Ben for such a lovely introduction, and for everyone who gave me such a warm welcome in the comments already. I’m really looking forward to getting to know the OMAAT community Ben has built over the years.

In the first of what will undoubtedly be a lot of posts for One Mile at a Time, I thought I’d share a bit about who I am and what you can expect from me going forward.

I’m literally asking myself that as I write this.

Funnily enough, it was never my dream to be a writer, journalist, blogger, or anything similar. The only thing I can ever remember wanting to be “when I grew up” was a pilot. Despite several applications and reaching the final stage of cadet schemes with Aer Lingus and British Airways, it didn’t work out for me.

Determined to work in the industry, I quit my soul-destroying city job in London to do a Master’s in Air Transport Management at the University of Loughborough in the U.K. I was then offered 2 very different jobs: a junior marketing role with Air Transat, or to be part of a small team starting up TPG’s U.K. office. As a natural risk-taker, I took the latter. After almost 8 years of writing for various publications and dabbling in some video content, I’ve realized that this is what I was meant to be doing all along — the job just didn’t exist when I wanted to be a pilot as a kid.

So why OMAAT? Why now? I spent the last 2 years traveling the world, working remotely, in search of somewhere I felt connected enough to call home. In my heart of hearts, I always knew that was going to be Rio, so I moved here in September this year. I’ve also been considering a more permanent home for my writing and my online presence, so when happenstance did its thing and Ben offered me a full-time online home at OMAAT, it was the perfect opportunity.

I’m honored to have been entrusted to write alongside Ben, whose expertise I’ve learned from over the years. While I don’t promise to be an expert on everything, my almost 8 years of experience in this industry should hopefully mean my expertise meets the standard expected here.

What started out as a passion for planes and aviation has turned into a love of all things travel, loyalty, and the miles and points that help make it happen. I’m really looking forward to sharing some of my learnings, experiences, and tips and tricks from the past couple of years that should complement Ben’s breadth of knowledge.

To start with, much of what you’ll see from me will be written. But as Ben said, the plan is to gradually bring in more video and social content, which I’m really looking forward to helping OMAAT with.

I’m also a self-proclaimed expert on Rio and Brazil (I’ve been coming here since 2009), so if there’s any specific Rio, Brazil, or wider South American travel advice, reviews, or insights you’d like, I’d be more than happy to help, even if it means I have to hop a plane for the research. 😝

I’ll leave it at that for now, as I need to get packing to fly across the Pond for an exciting aviation event this week. All will be revealed soon. 🤓✈️

I’m very excited and honored to be Ben’s first full-time writer in a very long time. Today is the first day of a new adventure for myself, Ben, and the OMAAT behind-the-scenes team, and I can’t wait to bring you, the readers, along for the ride.

The airport lounge wars aren't heating up only among premium credit card issuers. Airlines are stepping up their own lounge investments, too.

American Airlines has been on a tear of its own lately, including upgrades and a huge new Admirals Club at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) Terminal C, a massive (and much-needed) new lounge complex at its Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT) hub and the reopening of its Flagship Dining offering at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

Now, Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX) is the airline's next base scheduled for a glow-up.

Read more: 3 reasons why this is the best credit card for Admirals Club access

American Airlines currently fields three Admirals Clubs at PHX — two in Concourse A and one in Concourse B at Terminal 4 — all of which are being updated.

The first lounge where flyers will see changes is this diminutive lounge in Concourse A. Effective immediately, there will be a new food service area and expanded food and beverage offerings.

More importantly, though, the airline plans to nearly triple the combined lounge footprint of its Concourse A lounges, which include another Admirals Club near gates A7 and A9; it will increase seating capacity by around 150%, and add new furniture and finishes. Hopefully those will reflect the more sophisticated aesthetics American Airlines has been pivoting toward, starting with its Ronald Reagan National Airport (DCA) outpost.

Over in Concourse B, one of the airline's other Admirals Clubs will see a new self-service food and beverage area (aka a buffet and bar), a 20% increase in seating capacity and new interiors.

“Phoenix continues to be an important hub in our network, and these investments reflect our commitment to giving customers more space, comfort and convenience when they travel through PHX,” American’s chief customer officer Heather Garboden said in an online statement. “While we look forward to the development of the new West Terminal, these enhancements will help create an even more seamless travel experience for the millions of customers who pass through Phoenix each year.”

The updates make sense and are badly needed at an American Airlines hub where the Admirals Clubs frequently become overcrowded.

The airline carries over 20 million passengers through PHX each year and operates over 300 peak daily departures, so expanding and refreshing its lounges there is a priority to continue attracting premium passengers.

Read more: The ultimate guide to American Airlines Admirals Club access

Though details are still scant, American Airlines is updating its three Admirals Clubs at PHX. Passengers should see immediate changes at its Concourse A club near gates A19 and A21, but travelers will have to wait for the larger changes, which will include an expanded footprint and updated interiors. It remains to be seen what other amenities might be available.

#6118. Delta Reserve Credit Card Review: Benefits Worth It For Delta Loyalists?

American Express and Delta have had a close relationship for many years. As part of that, they issue seven co-branded Delta Amex cards. The Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card is the most premium of these cards, and in this post, I’d like to take an in-depth look at the product. The Delta Reserve Card is worth it if you’re a frequent flyer with Delta, or if you want to earn elite status through credit card spending. Let’s take a look at all the details of the card.

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card

Before I get into my Delta Reserve Card review, here are some of the card’s key details, from its current welcome bonus to its annual fee and the perks you get with Delta:

I also put together my list of top pros and cons for the Delta Reserve Card:

Let’s look at the Delta Reserve Card‘s welcome bonus offer, eligibility rules, and fees. All of these are probably top of mind if you’re considering applying for this card.

The Delta Reserve Card currently has the following welcome offer: You may be eligible for as high as 125,000 Bonus Miles after you spend $5,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Card Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Delta SkyMiles to be worth 1.1 cents each. That means to me, the 125,000-mile bonus is worth $1,375. While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have quite a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles.

The welcome bonus offer on the Delta Reserve Card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available to you if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past. However, eligibility for the Delta Reserve Card (including the welcome offer) is unrelated to whether you have any other personal card in the portfolio. You’re also eligible for the personal card if you already have the business card, and vice versa.

You can read more about Amex’s general application restrictions here.

The Delta Reserve Card has a $650 annual fee (Rates & Fees). Obviously that’s on the high side, though you also get quite a few perks. You can add authorized users for $175 each, and authorized users get some card benefits, including airport lounge access and inflight savings on Delta.

If you spend on the Delta Reserve Card, the good news is that there are no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can efficiently use the card abroad.

Beyond the welcome bonus, how does the Delta Reserve Card earn rewards on your spending, both in terms of miles earned and in terms of elite status qualification? Let’s look at the ongoing earning rates and Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs) you can earn through spending on the card.

The Delta Reserve Card has fairly limited bonus categories for spending. The Delta Reserve Card earns:

Ironically, other Delta cards with lower annual fees have more robust bonus categories. The logic is probably that this is the most rewarding card for spending counting toward elite status, and therefore Delta believes that’s enough of an incentive.

Nowadays, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status is earned exclusively based on how many Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs) you rack up. When it comes to earning MQDs through credit card spending, the Delta Reserve Credit Card is as good as it gets:

For context, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status has the following annual MQD requirements:

Therefore if you wanted to earn elite status exclusively through credit card spending, you’d need to spend the following amounts:

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles.

Delta One (business class) awards can be a great option, especially on roundtrip awards rather than one way itineraries. Using SkyMiles for shorter hops on Delta can be great, too. I’ve seen award flights between New York (LGA) and Orlando (MCO) for less than 20,000 miles roundtrip.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles.

You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air. You can also redeem SkyMiles on some airlines that aren’t part of SkyTeam but still partner with Delta, like LATAM and WestJet.

One of the primary things that sets the Delta Reserve Credit Card apart from other Delta Amex cards is the lounge access perks that it offers. The card offers Delta Sky Club® access, Centurion Lounge access, and even several Sky Club passes. How does that work?

The Delta Reserve Card offers 15 Delta Sky Club visits each Medallion year for the primary cardmember. Each visit is defined as all entries within a 24-hour period, including at different airports. In other words, if you have a connecting itinerary, you can visit multiple Sky Clubs at different airports while using only one visit allotment.

It’s possible to unlock unlimited Sky Club visits after spending $75,000 in purchases on your card in a calendar year. Once all 15 visits have been used, eligible cardmembers may purchase additional Sky Club visits at a per visit rate of $50 per person using the card.

In addition to the primary cardmember getting Sky Club access when flying Delta the same day, they also receive four Sky Club guest passes annually.

These can be used by the primary cardmember to guest others into the lounge, allowing you to skip the $50 guesting fee four times annually.

The Delta Reserve Card also offers complimentary Centurion Lounge access when traveling on a same-day Delta flight booked with the card. The primary cardmember is entitled to access, and bringing additional guests costs $50 each.

Centurion Lounges, for the most part, offer a significantly improved food and beverage offering compared to most domestic airline lounges in the United States, so this is a nice option to have.

The Delta Reserve Credit Card has a good bonus, though if I were just looking for the best welcome bonus offer, I would go for the Gold or Platinum version of the card, since the cards have significantly lower annual fees.

The reason you want to get the Reserve version of the card is because of the valuable long term perks that it offers. Above I’ve talked about how the Reserve Card can help you earn status and can help you access lounges, though there are lots of perks beyond that. Let’s take a look at some of those benefits.

Every year upon renewal of the Delta Reserve Card, you receive a roundtrip companion certificate valid within the United States (including Alaska and Hawaii), and to Mexico, the Caribbean, and Central America. This can be used for fares ranging from first class to economy, so the flexibility offered by that is pretty awesome, and for many will more than justify the annual fee.

You just have to pay the government-imposed taxes and fees for the companion. There are some things to be aware of when redeeming the Delta companion certificate, including:

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive a $200 Delta Stays credit annually. The way this works, you receive up to $200 in statement credits per calendar year when you use your card to pay for a new Delta Stays prepaid hotel or vacation rental booking on the Delta Stays platform.

While I’m not usually a fan of using airline portals to book hotel stays and vacation rentals, this could prove worthwhile, as you can use it for a hotel stay costing right around $200, if you wanted to. If used right, the value here is considerable.

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive up to $240 in Resy credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $20 in statement credits each month after using your card on eligible purchases at U.S. restaurants that offer reservations on Resy.com and the Resy app, purchases made directly on Resy.com or in the Resy app, and purchases made via Resy Pay.

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive up to $120 in rideshare credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $10 in statement credits each month after using your card on U.S. rideshare purchases with select providers, including Uber and Lyft.

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you get a first checked bag free. With the ever-increasing cost of a checked bag with Delta, this can really add up:

Depending on how many bags you’re checking, a few trips with a companion could pay for the card’s annual fee.

You can receive priority boarding just for having the Delta Reserve. This helps maximize your odds of finding space for your carry-on and getting to your seat sooner. To receive this benefit, you must ensure the primary cardmember’s SkyMiles number is linked to the reservation.

If you have the Delta Reserve Amex then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible pre-purchased meals, and in-flight purchases of food, alcoholic beverages, and audio headsets, on Delta flights. Allow 8-12 weeks for the statement credit to post.

Delta has a Pay With Miles feature, where if you have a Delta co-branded credit card you can redeem miles for one cent each toward a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles toward flights, and then they still earn MQDs for taking those flights.

With the TakeOff 15 perk (exclusively for those with select Delta Amex cards), you can save 15% on the cost of a SkyMiles award ticket when traveling exclusively on Delta. Delta SkyMiles award pricing is dynamic, and generally you’ll find that each mile gets you a bit over a cent toward the cost of a ticket.

Saving 15% on these awards is valuable, and means that you’ll generally get somewhere around 1.2-1.3 cents of value per mile (or sometimes even more). In many cases this will end up being a better value than using the Pay With Miles option, so it’s a real perk of the card.

Having the Delta Reserve Card gets you priority for complimentary upgrades, assuming you have Medallion status. That’s because the card acts as a tiebreaker.

If you have the Reserve Card you get upgrade priority over other Medallion members within the same Medallion level and fare class. Given how competitive upgrades are, this can make a material difference in terms of whether you clear or not.

The Delta Reserve Card offers complimentary Delta First and Delta Comfort upgrades on eligible flights for non-elite members. You will be toward the bottom of the upgrade list, but there are lots of situations where this could help you score a good extra legroom seat, or in some cases even a first class seat.

Those with the Delta Reserve Card receive a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit. This benefit applies once every four years. This can save you big time both at security and immigration, and is something I highly recommend signing up for if eligible.

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive Hertz President’s Circle elite status, which is Hertz’s top-tier status. Status is valid for as long as you’re a cardmember. This should take the pain out of renting cars, and offers the following perks:

The Delta Reserve Card comes with a handful of coverage benefits that can protect you and your belongings both at home and on the road, including:

The maximum benefit amount for Trip Cancellation and Interruption Insurance is $10,000 per Covered Trip and $20,000 per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Up to $500 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 6 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in holding multiple Amex cards so that you can get these offers on multiple cards and enjoy a variety of offers across cards.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page.

The Delta Reserve Credit Card has a steep annual fee, but the card also offers great benefits. The card offers perks ranging from lounge access, to a companion certificate, to up to two free checked bags, to upgrade priority, to all kinds of credits, to the ability to spend your way to elite status.

This card isn’t for the casual Delta flyer, but for someone who flies Delta moderately or often, I’d say this card is well worth considering.

If the Delta Reserve Amex sounds interesting to you but you are instead looking for a card for your small business, consider the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve Business American Express Card.

Most of the benefits of the card are the same. One significant difference is that the business card earns 1.5x miles on all purchases after spending $150,000 annually, which could be useful for big spenders. Furthermore, the business card offers a $250 annual Delta Stays credit, rather than a $200 annual credit.

Many people might be trying to decide between the American Express Platinum Card® (learn more) and the Delta Reserve Card. The cards have some overlapping benefits:

But that’s largely where the similarities end:

The Delta Reserve Credit Card is Delta’s most premium credit card, though is it worth it compared to the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card (learn more), which has a $350 annual fee (Rates & Fees)?

The Delta Reserve Card is Delta’s most premium credit card. While the card isn’t for everyone, I do think it’s well worth considering if you’re a frequent Delta flyer, and could benefit from lounge access, the companion ticket, improved upgrade priority, all of the credits, and the ability to earn status through credit card spending.

If you want to learn more about the Delta Reserve Amex Card, follow this link.

#6116. Allegiant, Sun Country Add New Destinations, 16 Routes

Allegiant and Sun Country are adding new destinations and a combined 16 routes ahead of the summer of 2027.

Allegiant said Tuesday that it will resume service to Minneapolis, while Sun Country will expand to Belleville, Illinois (via MidAmerica St. Louis Airport), Gulf Shores, Alabama, and Knoxville, Tennessee.

Notably, Minneapolis is Sun Country’s main operating base; renewed service from Allegiant is expected to bring their networks closer together.

Allegiant acquired Sun Country in May, though for the time being they are continuing to operate as separate airlines.

“Minnesota is an essential part of the future of our combined company, and today’s announcement is another step in delivering on that commitment,” Allegiant CEO Greg Anderson said in a news release. “MSP is our largest base of operations by a wide margin, and we see opportunities for continued growth there. Combining Sun Country’s strong foundation in the Twin Cities with Allegiant’s nationwide network of communities will provide Minnesota travelers with more convenient, affordable nonstop travel options.”

The new routes will come online in April and May.

Additionally, Allegiant said it will operate four routes currently flown by Sun Country:

Allegiant and Sun Country are expected to eventually merge operations, with the Sun Country brand phased out, though it is not clear exactly when this will happen. Allegiant said Tuesday that it will continue operating separately from Sun Country “until 2028 or later.”

#6114. Buy Hilton Honors Points With 120% Bonus By November 21: Worth It?

Through November 21, 2026, Hilton Honors is offering a buy points promotion, which is the program’s best-ever bonus on purchasing points! While Hilton Honors ordinarily offers up to a 100% bonus on purchased points, this time around the program is offering up to a 120% bonus, which is a cost of 0.45 cents per point. This could represent a great value for hotel redemptions, especially with an immediate use in mind, as members can purchase up to 528,000 points in one transaction.

As always, I only recommend buying points with a short term use in mind, and if you understand the mechanics of how award redemptions with a program work, including what redemption costs are like.

Link: Buy Hilton Honors points with this promotion with a 120% bonus

Between 12AM ET on October 7 and 11:59PM ET on November 21, 2026, Hilton Honors is offering a bonus on purchased points. Different Hilton Honors members may be targeted for different bonuses, so you’ll want to log into your account to see what you’re eligible for. It would appear that the best offer is for up to a 120% bonus, and that’s structured as follows:

Hilton Honors ordinarily charges one cent per purchased point, including all taxes and fees. That’s before any discounts or bonuses. If you’re eligible for the 120% bonus and maxed out the offer, you’d receive a total of 528,000 points at a cost of $2,400, which is a rate of 0.45 cents per Hilton Honors point.

Ordinarily, Hilton Honors lets members buy up to 160,000 points per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion, that cap has been increased by 50%, to 240,000 points. With a 120% bonus, that means you could purchase up to 528,000 points.

The purchase of Hilton Honors points is non-refundable, and points purchased don’t count toward elite status. Purchased points will post within 48 hours of finalizing the purchase (though in my experience, much faster than that).

While Hilton Honors has a strict limit on how many points you can buy, note that there are ways to acquire more points than that limit without violating the rules.

Hilton lets members combine points across accounts at no cost, so in reality you could acquire substantially more points by simply buying them across accounts and then consolidating them. Hilton Honors lets members transfer up to 500,000 points, and receive up to two million points, per calendar year. Each member can make up to six transfers to other members per calendar year, and new Hilton Honors members can only transfer or receive points a minimum of 30 days after enrollment.

Hilton also allows points pooling, whereby Hilton Honors members can combine points with up to 10 other members, with the same limitations.

When Hilton Honors offer a promotion on purchased points, it’s most common to see a 100% bonus (the equivalent of a 50% discount). So this 120% bonus is the best-ever promotion we’ve seen from the program, so that’s awesome.

Below is a chart with some of the recent buy points promotions we saw from the Hilton Honors program, before this one.

Hilton Honors point purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with a Hilton credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s Hilton spending.

I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

There’s potentially huge value to be had buying Hilton Honors points. Hilton Honors sells points at a reasonable cost, has lots of aspirational properties, has good redemptions with a fifth night free opportunity, and elite status is also easy to earn with the program. Hilton’s partnership with Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) is also awesome, and offers great redemption opportunities.

However, people shouldn’t blindly buy Hilton Honors points, as there are also lots of redemptions where you won’t come out ahead. As I see it, the biggest value with buying Hilton Honors is for aspirational redemptions at expensive properties. Let me give some examples, based on current redemption rates.

For example, take the Waldorf Astoria Maldives, which is bookable for 250,000 points per night for a standard room. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $1,125. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be $3,400, so that’s like two-thirds off. That’s pretty amazing!

As another example, take the Waldorf Astoria Los Cabos, which is bookable for 250,000 points per night for a standard room. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $1,125. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be close to $2,200, so that’s like half off.

Above I mentioned the Hilton Honors partnership with SLH, so let me give an example there. RiverView Ranch Retreat is located in Montana, and is bookable for 220,000 points per night for a standard room. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $990. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be over $3,800 (the screenshot below is for two nights, since that’s the minimum stay), so that’s close to three-fourths off.

Now, while the above are all examples of what a good deal it can be to buy Hilton Honors points, let me of course acknowledge that these are all top-end properties. Unfortunately I find that for your run of the mill Hilton properties, including many limited service hotels, the value just isn’t there in the same way.

For example, take the Hilton Garden Inn Tampa, which is bookable for 45,000 points per night. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $203. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be under $180, so there’s absolutely no reason to buy points, only to redeem them for less value than what you paid. You’ll find that to be pretty common, which is why I always recommend crunching the numbers before making a purchase.

Hilton Honors doesn’t have a published award chart, but rather the program has dynamic award pricing. This means that the cost of a standard free night award can vary depending on the day of the week, time of year, etc.

As a general rule of thumb, Hilton Honors free night awards start at 10,000 points per night, and go up to 250,000 points per night (which is a shame, because up until last year, properties maxed out at 150,000 points per night).

Sometimes you’ll see award costs that are way higher than these amounts. In those situations it’s because there’s not a standard room available, so higher pricing kicks in for premium rooms. That’s generally not nearly as good of a use of Hilton Honors points, and you’ll find that some awards even cost one million or more points per night. Obviously that’s a lousy value.

If you have Hilton Honors elite status (which is easy to earn, as I’ll outline below), you receive a fifth night free on award redemptions. This is a way to stretch your points even further, and whenever possible, I’d recommend making your Hilton Honors award stays in increments of five nights.

To take advantage of this, just log into your Hilton Honors elite account, and go through the process of making an award booking for five nights. When you get to the booking page, you should notice that the cost of the fifth night is automatically deducted.

Let me give an example how much value this can add. Say you want to book five nights at the Waldorf Astoria Seychelles Platte Island. At a rate of 150,000 points per night, you’d pay a total of 600,000 points for five nights, which averages out to 120,000 points per night. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, that’s like the equivalent of paying $540 per night. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be over $1,800 per night, so that represents absolutely massive savings.

One thing I love about the program is how easy it is to earn elite status with credit cards, including both Hilton Honors™ Gold Status and Hilton Honors™ Diamond Status. These tiers offer perks like room upgrades, complimentary breakfast, hotel credits, and more. For example:

Hilton Honors points don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 24 months. Eligible account activity includes earning or redeeming points, so buying points would even reset the expiration of your points.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Hilton Honors points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. As you can see, the pricing here is potentially better than what I value these points, and there are lots of ways to get outsized value with this promotion.

Hilton Honors doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, and all standard rooms are available for award redemptions. So this is about as good of a policy as you’ll find with any hotel group when it comes to award room availability.

There are lots of ways to earn Hilton Honors points, beyond just staying at Hilton properties or buying the points directly. You can easily earn points by using Hilton Honors’ co-branded credit cards, which also offer great welcome bonuses. These cards include the following:

You can also transfer points from Amex Membership Rewards to Hilton Honors (at a 1:2 ratio), and from Bilt Rewards to Hilton Honors (at a 1:1 ratio). I wouldn’t consider either of those redemptions to represent a good deal. That’s simply because I value Hilton Honors points at 0.5 cents each, while I value those points currencies at 1.7 cents each, so the math just doesn’t work out.

Hilton Honors is currently offering a best-ever bonus on purchased points, whereby members can receive up to a 120% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire points for 0.45 cents each. In the past we’ve generally seen bonuses of up to 100%, so this is a better offer than ever before. In fairness, Hilton Honors points have also been devalued a bit over time. With a short term use in mind, there are plenty of situations where this could represent a good deal.

The math only works against the real cash price for your dates though. Google Hotels makes that bit lazy, pop in the dates and it shows the cash rate next to the usual range for that hotel

Is this the new MO for the Hilton Honors program? Instead of outsized earning promotions for stays they will just sell you points with a huge bonus? 0.45 CPM is JUST about worth it for a top up, nothing else IMO. And I've valued the Hilton points at 0.4 CPM for a while now, 0.5 is pushing it.

Black Friday is no longer just one day; it's practically an entire month. Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday deals are coming from every direction, and it can be tough to keep up with them all.

If you're feeling overwhelmed, we're here to help. Whether you're looking to save on your next big trip, hoping to score some amazing travel gear or want to buy holiday gifts, there's a deal for everyone — and we're here to help you navigate this year's sea of Black Friday sales and maximize your savings.

Although many deals are already live, the official 2026 sale days are as follows:

Traditionally, Black Friday is best for in-store deals. However, we've seen an increasing number of online deals emerge each year, so we recommend checking both in-store and online pricing before making a purchase.

Cyber Monday (the Monday after Black Friday) is when most companies release deals online, but it’s not uncommon for deals to launch even earlier. A good example is Amazon, which is already offering numerous discounts in advance of the official Nov. 19 launch of its Black Friday Week.

Meanwhile, Travel Tuesday (the day after Cyber Monday) is when airlines, hotels, cruise operators and other travel companies typically release deals, though some sales have already begun. You can check out our top picks for hotel deals here and all-inclusive deals here.

To see all of our top deals in one place, check out TPG's Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals page.

You should always be looking for ways to double or triple dip on your purchases, and Black Friday is no exception. Here are our top tips for saving even more money and maximizing your rewards this season.

If your desired merchant is available on a shopping portal, you can earn bonus rewards, such as points, miles, or cash back, on your purchase.

For instance, Rakuten is currently offering 8% cash back (or 8 American Express Membership Rewards points or Bilt Rewards Points per dollar spent) on accommodations at Booking.com. If this earning rate stays the same through Booking.com's Black Friday sale, you could potentially get 8% back on top of the platform's up-to-40% discount on hotels.

Payouts often vary from day to day, so we recommend using a shopping portal aggregator like Cashback Monitor to find the best portal for your purchase.

Amex Offers and Chase Offers are among our favorite ways to save money on everyday purchases, and they're easy to stack with Black Friday sales. Check your offers on all your credit card accounts (each card may be different) before making a purchase, and if any apply to your merchant, be sure to activate them on your card and pay with the same card.

If you collect Amex Membership Rewards points, check your Amazon account to see if you're targeted for one of these offers to save up to 40% when you redeem at least 714 points at checkout.

Lastly, remember to use the correct card to maximize your rewards on Black Friday purchases. Our lists of the top travel cards and best cards for online shopping are good places to start.

When booking travel, be sure to use a card that comes with built-in trip protections. For other purchases, consider a card that offers extended warranties.

As Black Friday sales continue to proliferate, it's helpful to plan ahead. Consider what you'd like to purchase (or book), and mark your calendars accordingly.

Don't forget that many travel bookings are refundable within 24 hours of making your reservation (and sometimes longer). If you spot a can't-miss deal, consider booking right away and double-checking your dates afterward.

#6112. Transfer Chase Points To Virgin Atlantic Flying Club With 40% Bonus: Worth It?

The Chase Ultimate Rewards program is currently offering a bonus for points transfers to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. While I’d only transfer points with a specific use in mind, there’s huge value to be had here, as a 40% transfer bonus is massive.

Between November 16 and December 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when transferring Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

This promotion is being offered on Chase’s end (in the United States), and is hard coded into the transfer ratio, meaning you should see the bonus at the time that you make the transfer. You can take advantage of this offer an unlimited number of times. Transfers from Chase to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club are generally instant.

We see a bonus like this to Virgin Atlantic a few times per year. We last saw a transfer bonus over the summer, so it hasn’t been a long gap at all. Past transfer bonuses have been in the range of 25-40%, so this is at the very top end of that spectrum.

There are several great cards earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points, and it’s easy to combine points between the cards.

Virgin Atlantic is a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic (with steep carrier imposed surcharges), there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta, as well as more broadly on SkyTeam airlines.

Nowadays Flying Club has dynamic award pricing for travel on Virgin Atlantic. What’s exciting is that on the low end, redemption rates are very attractive, and it’s possible to fly Virgin Atlantic Upper Class between the United States and United Kingdom for under 30,000 points, in some situations. And that’s before a transfer bonus.

Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

Paying 45,000-47,500 Flying Club points for a one-way business class ticket between the United States and Japan is a phenomenal value to start with. Then when you consider the 40% transfer bonus, that means you could be paying significantly fewer Chase points. First class can also be a good deal.

All Nippon Airways’ new first & business class are amazing products as well. The major catch is that availability can be really tough to come by.

Through December 30, 2026, you can receive a 40% bonus when you transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. This is more of a niche program, but with a specific use in mind, there’s a lot of value to be had.

With the 40% bonus, you can potentially get some incredible redemption values for travel on Virgin Atlantic, including in Upper Class. There’s also significant value to be had if redeeming on partners, whether it’s on a SkyTeam partner, or on one of Virgin Atlantic’s non-SkyTeam partner airlines.

#6111. British Airways Launches Major New 24-Hour Route In 7 Weeks: See Map Now

British Airways will finally reintroduce service to Melbourne in early January. Melbourne is the capital of the Australian state of Victoria and is now the nation's second most populous city based on the significant urban area population. It is also Australia's fastest-growing state capital by people added.

The carrier last flew there more than 20 years ago, in March 2006. That was when the UK's largest long-haul operator deployed the now long-retired Boeing 747-400. Things will be very different this time.

OAG data shows that the oneworld member will take off from London Heathrow to Melbourne on January 9, 2027. 20 years ago, flights operated via Singapore, but they'll now do so via Kuala Lumpur. This may also help to shore up the performance of Heathrow-Kuala Lumpur flights. Covering 9,134 nautical miles (16,916 km) each way on a great circle, but not real-world, basis, the new route to Melbourne will be the airline's new second-longest offering.

BA will deploy the Boeing 787-9 to Victoria, with both the 215-seat and 216-seat configurations used. This might not seem like a big difference, but it perhaps is, especially on such a long trip. The 216-seater has the airline's older business seats, while the 215-seat alternative has the newer cabin.

Kuala Lumpur to Melbourne (fifth freedom rights)

Melbourne to Kuala Lumpur (fifth freedom rights)

The configuration with the better product is due to operate 57% of the time between January and October next year. This includes the inaugural service. The 215-seat so-called Dreamliner, to use the Boeing moniker, has eight seats in first class, 38 in business, 39 in premium economy, and 130 in economy. Despite not having the newest cabins, this layout is slightly less premium. 21% of capacity is in first/business, against 23% on the 216-seater.

In the 12 months to August 2026, booking data shows that 1.4 million round-trip passengers flew between Europe and Melbourne. Excluding seasonality, around 3,800 people did so daily. Nearly half of the market flew with Emirates, Etihad Airways, and Qatar Airways via the Gulf or with Singapore Airlines via Changi. The quartet collectively benefits from lots of flights to Melbourne, while the Middle Eastern operators, in particular, have big European networks. Their dominance may reduce slightly, at least in specific markets, as four carriers will now fly between Melbourne and Europe, with three being European.

Their dominance may reduce slightly, at least in specific markets, as four carriers will now fly between Melbourne and Europe, with three being European. They include Finnair, whose debut in Australia, as unusual as that might appear, was in late October 2026. The oneworld member runs daily (which is even more surprising) on the Airbus A350-900 via Bangkok, with fifth freedom rights.

In the northern winter, Finnair has three daily flights from Helsinki to the Thai capital. As such, extending one flight to Australia during the cold season in the north with greater aircraft availability is less dramatic than might otherwise be the case. Significantly, it is the only EU airline to fly to Australia.

Turkish Airlines, whose Istanbul Airport hub is on the European side of the Bosphorus, also operates. Despite having lots of unused traffic rights to Australia, the carrier's frequency remains unchanged compared to when the long route began. This could be a sign of insufficient performance or a lack of widebodies. BA's return rounds out the European side of the equation. All three operators fly via a different city in Southeast Asia to benefit from the local traffic.

The ultra-low-cost carrier has no flights on Christmas Day, but things aren't quite as they seem. Find out more here!

Qantas has a long history of flying from Melbourne to Europe. For example, the oneworld member — there's a trend here — flew to Heathrow via Singapore (QF9/QF10) or Hong Kong (QF29/QF30) for years on the 747-400 and later via Singapore on the A380. The Kangaroo Route then switched to flying via Dubai on the A380 in partnership with Emirates (QF9/QF10).

In 2018, when the 787-9 appeared, the routing changed again, flying via Perth on a same-plane basis (QF9/QF10). Late last month, Qantas reintroduced a one-stop, same-plane, same-flight-number operation from the UK's busiest airport to Melbourne via the capital of Western Australia.

Due to the ongoing war in Iran, the 787-9 does not currently begin in Melbourne on a same-flight-number basis. Avoiding Iranian airspace means that the aircraft does not fly nonstop from Perth to Heathrow, stopping in Singapore instead. The total operation is Perth-Singapore-Heathrow (as QF219, not QF9), and then Heathrow-Perth-Melbourne (QF10). While subject to change, starting and ending in Melbourne is due to return on March 28, 2027.

#6110. Atmos Rewards Upgrade Certificates: How Do They Work, Are They Worth It?

Atmos Rewards is the loyalty program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. The program has four elite tiers — Silver, Gold, Platinum, and Titanium — and somehow I’m actually going to end the year as a top tier member, it looks like, without having once stepped foot on an Alaska or Hawaiian flight.

As I’ve worked my way through the elite ranks, I’ve become eligible for the milestone perks program, whereby you can select perks when passing various elite thresholds. Along those lines, At the higher tiers, one of the choices becomes upgrade certificates, so I’d like to talk about those a bit, as I’m trying to decide whether or not I should select these.

I’m intrigued by Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates, given the increasingly global route network of Alaska and Hawaiian. At the same time, the execution of this upgrade program definitely leaves a lot to be desired, including the lack of confirmable upgrade availability.

I have to make a selection soon, so I’d like to talk through the Alaska and Hawaiian upgrade certificate program, and then get some feedback from Atmos Rewards loyalists. The last time I was focused on upgrade certificates at the airline was when Alaska Mileage Plan had Gold Guest Upgrades as the upgrade currency, and MVP Gold was the top tier status… those were the days!

Atmos Rewards issues upgrade certificates as part of the Atmos Rewards milestone perks program. This can be unlocked based on how many status points you earn over the course of a calendar year. Let me emphasize that these upgrade certificates are intended for confirming upgrades in advance, and they’re separate from the complimentary space available upgrades offered.

Specifically, Atmos Rewards members could earn upgrade certificates at the following thresholds:

Titanium status requires 135,000 status points, and I expect to end the year with roughly that many status points. That means I could select up to eight upgrade certificates. However, that would come at the opportunity cost of 70,000 bonus points, for example. Of course I could also mix and match, like selecting four upgrade certificates and 50,000 bonus points.

Now let’s talk a bit about the rules for redeeming Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates, at least on paper. Upgrades are valid across the Alaska and Hawaiian route networks, and fall into one of two categories:

Upgrade certificates can be shared with others, but of course can’t be bartered or sold. One other interesting quirk is that if you cancel or change an itinerary that was upgraded, the certificate will be forfeited. However, a replacement upgrade certificate code can be requested through customer care. Let’s cover the details of upgrades based on the region.

When it comes to upgrading within North America, an Atmos Rewards upgrade certificate can be confirmed at the time of booking, as long as the “U” fare class is available. If it’s not available, the upgrade will be waitlisted.

To cover the very basics, the upgrade certificate is valid for one-way travel (with no connections longer than four hours), for tickets issued by and flown on Alaska and Hawaiian. Tickets purchased in Y, B, H, K, M, L, V, S, or N fare classes, are eligible for upgrades using certificates, while tickets purchased in Q, O, G, or X fare classes, are not eligible.

To search if a flight is upgrade eligible, select “Upgrade Certificate” in the dropdown in the “Upgrade type” section, during the booking process.

Then on the search results page, you should be looking for two things:

When it comes to upgrading outside of North America, Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates have completely different rules, both for better and worse. First, it’s worth understanding that an upgrade requires either one or two upgrade certificates, depending on the route, per the below chart.

When it comes to using Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates on global (non-North America) flights, there are both pros and cons:

I have to say, the execution of this perk is odd. Keep in mind that Atmos Rewards has a one-of-a-kind upgrade perk for top tier Titanium members, whereby they receive space available upgrades globally on the day of departure. So what’s odd is that if you’re a Titanium member you’re eligible for a complimentary upgrade close to departure, but having applied an upgrade certificate previously gives you no priority. You’d think they’d prioritize members who requested an upgrade, but I suspect it’s a technology limitation of some sort.

I’d like to address the question of whether Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates are worth it both broadly, and more specifically to my situation.

I hear all the time from Atmos Rewards members who are frustrated by the lack of confirmable upgrade space. And indeed, compared to back in the day, upgrade space that can be confirmed is incredibly limited. At the same time, that’s true across airlines nowadays, given how much better airlines have become at actually selling their first class seats, rather than filling them with those upgrading.

For example, looking at the route between my home airport of Miami (MIA) and Seattle (SEA) as far out as the schedule opens, I don’t see a single date that has confirmable upgrade space. Now, you’ll sometimes find confirmable upgrade space up and down the West Coast, especially during off peak times, so I don’t want to suggest it’s impossible to find a confirmable upgrade.

But just broadly speaking, confirmable upgrades with “U” class available for transcontinental and Hawaii flights are exceedingly rare, and it’s like winning the lottery. So it’s really hard to get excited about that.

In theory, I of course love the idea of being able to upgrade a long haul flight with upgrade certificates. The catch is that an upgrade clearing at most 72 hours before departure really limits flexibility. I suppose you could always apply an upgrade, hope it clears, and then cancel your ticket if it doesn’t, but this would be a last minute scramble.

To me, that’s just too risky. It’s not that I’d be unwilling to fly economy on a long haul flight, but by strategically using points, it’s really not necessary in a vast majority of situations, at least based on my own travel patterns.

The thing is, it’s also important to view Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates in terms of the opportunity cost of selecting them.

For example, as I mentioned above, at 55,000 status points I can select two upgrade certificates or 5,000 bonus points. At an opportunity cost of 2,500 points per upgrade certificate, I think it might be worth selecting upgrade certificates. Based on my latest points valuations, I consider Atmos Rewards points to be worth 1.5 cents each, so the opportunity cost per upgrade is $37.50. That’s a rate at which I’d probably be happy to gamble, because if the upgrades expire, it’s not the end of the world.

Meanwhile at 95,000 status points, the opportunity cost becomes 7,500 bonus points per upgrade, so that’s a value of $112.50 per upgrade. Then at 125,000 status points, the opportunity cost becomes 12,500 bonus points per upgrade, so that’s a value of $187.50. That’s the point at which I’m definitely more inclined to take the “sure thing,” rather than take my chances with an upgrade.

Atmos Rewards lets members select upgrade certificates as part of the milestone perks program. This always comes at an opportunity cost, and is a better value at some tiers than others.

Upgrade certificates can be used on Alaska and Hawaiian flights globally, with most one-ways requiring one upgrade certificate, though some global routes requiring two upgrade certificates. While upgrades within North America can be confirmed at the time of booking (pending upgrade availability), global upgrades can only be confirmed at most 72 hours before departure.

The big issue with upgrades is the lack of availability. Alaska is just really bad about making confirmed upgrades available, and upgrades clearing at most 72 hours before departure on global flights is less than ideal.

What do you make of the value of Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates?
