#6109. Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

Sources said Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”

The post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He said the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

In 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

After Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

“The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker said. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this important position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Collins said in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

Situated halfway between San Francisco and the Oregon border, California's Mendocino Coast has managed to remain a relatively hidden gem, of sorts. While it's certainly not a secret, its remote location has kept it from getting overrun with tourists — but new direct flights and millions of dollars in roadwork funding are making it more accessible than ever. And that's just one reason the coastal town of Mendocino made our list of top destinations to visit in 2027.

Nestled between rugged cliffs, redwood forests and rich wine terroirs, Mendocino has it all. No matter what you get up to out here — and there’s more to do than you might expect — it’s virtually impossible not to feel your blood pressure drop. The area’s relaxed pace of life is infectious, and during a recent two-day trip, this type-A traveler found herself hopping on the slow travel train.

From how to get there and where to stay to the best things to do and eat, here’s how to spend a long weekend (or longer!) on the Mendocino Coast. I dare you not to fall in love.

Travelers have several airports to choose from when flying to Mendocino.

The closest, albeit smallest, option is Charles M. Schulz–Sonoma County Airport (STS), which puts you only a two-to-three-hour drive from Mendocino. Alaska Airlines, Delta and Southwest have all launched new routes to STS this year from Austin, Phoenix, Salt Lake City and more.

You’ll have more options if you fly into San Francisco International Airport (SFO), Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK) or Sacramento International Airport (SAC). All are roughly the same distance from Mendocino — three to four hours depending on traffic — and offer plenty of direct flights from around the country through various airlines. A local I spoke to recommended SAC, saying that the drive is less stressful because it doesn’t go through a city.

No matter where your flight lands, you’ll need to rent a car. The drive can be tiring, especially as the roads get windier approaching the coast. Thankfully, there are plenty of wineries and cideries along the way where you can stop for a restroom break (and maybe a drink or two, if you’re not the driver).

One of the many facets of Mendocino’s appeal is the charming, walkable downtown — complete with views of Mendocino Bay.

You’ll find no shortage of souvenirs here, from bookshops and toy stores to clothing and home decor. Art lovers will enjoy perusing the handful of galleries. Coffeeshops, bakeries and chocolate shops abound, so you needn't worry about finding caffeine or snacks to sustain you during your wanderings.

If you wear jewelry (or are in the market for a unique gift that will fit in your suitcase), you won’t want to miss Mendocino Sandpiper, which offers a wide variety of work by local artists.

And that’s just the town of Mendocino. Its slightly larger neighbor, Fort Bragg, located about a 15-minute drive north along the coast, has even more boutiques to browse.

Related: 9 tertiary cities in the US that are both charming and affordable

You will need a car to get around the Mendocino Coast area, but you won’t have to spend much time in the car once you arrive. That’s because the area’s best outdoors activities are within easy reach of Mendocino and Fort Bragg.

The expansive Mendocino Coast Botanical Gardens were a highlight for me, and would probably be stunning in the spring and summer when most of the flowers are in bloom.

Mendocino Headlands State Park is literally steps from downtown, and there are several other state parks under 20 minutes away, including Jug Handle State Natural Reserve and Russian Gulch State Park. To commune with the area’s famous redwoods, head to Otis R. Johnson Wilderness Park, a glorious corner of green tucked away on the edge of Fort Bragg. Or head to MacKerricher State Park for a stroll along a black-sand beach and views of the aptly named Seal Rocks.

February to March is peak whale-watching season due to the gray whale migration, but this area gets visits from various whale species year-round, so keep your eyes peeled. I didn’t spot any whales, but I did see some seals and sea lions bobbing in the waves, as well as flocks of pelicans and other waterbirds.

You may also hear about a place called Glass Beach, which served as a community garbage dump at the beginning of the 20th century; over several decades, the waves tumbled some of the debris into colorful sea glass. Locals warned me that most of the glass is gone now, snatched up by tourists over the years. You’re better off going to the International Sea Glass Museum in Fort Bragg — with over 3,000 pieces on display, it boasts the world’s largest permanent sea glass exhibit.

Related: 7 warm-weather expedition cruises that will wow nature and adventure lovers

Both Mendocino and Fort Bragg have surprisingly varied food scenes, from the casual organic Good Life Cafe & Bakery and elevated all-vegan Fog Eater to the Irish-inspired Patterson’s Pub and Asian fusion Gnar Bar. And foodies won’t want to miss the local farmers’ markets, held on summer Fridays in Mendocino and Wednesdays year-round in Fort Bragg.

However, the main draws for foodies are, of course, the seafood — I heard Fort Bragg’s Sea Pals described as “the best fish ‘n’ chips outside of the U.K.” — and the thriving beverage scene.

Oenophiles will want to take the Highway 128 Wine Road to sample the fruits of the nearby Anderson Valley and Yorkville Highlands wine regions. But you’ll get plenty of opportunities to sample local wines in town as well. My hotel even offered a lobby wine machine where you can get wine samples with the press a button and tap of a keycard.

If wine isn’t your thing, don’t worry, there are plenty more local beverages to try. Gowan’s Cider Garden, which brews both alcoholic and non-alcoholic varieties, bills itself as California's first-ever cider tasting orchard. Meanwhile, the zero-waste, solar-powered North Coast Brewing Co. has been brewing unique beers (and winning awards for them) since 1988.

Related: The best credit cards for dining

The Mendocino Coast is also home to some fascinating history, and it has an array of museums and other attractions where visitors can learn more.

Fort Bragg’s Guest House Museum is a great starting point to learn about local history, from the logging industry to the Great 1906 Earthquake. Or visit during Labor Day weekend to experience lumberjack games at the annual Paul Bunyan Days festival.

If you have young travelers in tow, check out Fort Bragg’s Noyo Center for Marine Science, which offers interactive exhibits like tide pools and a full orca skeleton. Or climb to the top of a lighthouse and see a real Fresnel lens at either Point Cabrillo Light Station State Historic Park or the 156-year-old Point Arena Lighthouse.

Train enthusiasts won’t want to miss the historic Skunk Train, which started carrying timber in the late 1800s and now carries passengers through scenic redwood forests. While the train’s traditional 35-mile route has a reputation for jaw-dropping scenery, a tunnel collapse in recent years has shortened the route to a sliver of its former glory. However, I still enjoyed the nostalgic vibes of the Redwood Presidential Class, which made me feel like I had been dropped into one of my favorite Agatha Christie murder mysteries.

Related: The world's most scenic train rides

The Mendocino Coast has been leaning into slow and wellness travel, and for obvious reasons. With ancient redwoods on one side and windswept cliffs on the other — and blessedly few tourists crowding the trails — the landscape itself is therapeutic.

If you want something more structured, there are plenty of wellness activities if you know where to look. Many are offered by locals hotels but open to the public.

A few examples include yoga classes at Stanford Inn by the Sea, redwood hot tub and sauna sessions at Sweet Water Inn & Spa, sound healing in a geodesic dome at Mendocino Grove, and guided shinrin-yoku (forest bathing) walks at Brewery Gulch Inn & Spa.

Related: 9 wellness trends and where to experience them

Summer is Mendocino’s most popular season. It will also be the most expensive and busiest time to go — though I don’t expect the area to get too packed at any time of year, given its remoteness.

For adventure seekers looking to make the most of the area’s hiking, water sports and more, it’s probably worth planning your trip in summer for longer days and maximum sunshine. And with average highs topping out in the mid-70s Fahrenheit, Mendo could make a nice coolcation spot.

However, you can save money and all but guarantee a quiet vacation by traveling in the shoulder seasons from mid-October to November and April to early June. During these times, you can still expect warm enough weather for outdoor exploits, though temperatures will drop at night and more frequent rains may wash out hiking trails occasionally.

The hotel scene in Mendocino is characterized by quiet luxury. Its neighbor, Fort Bragg, has more variety and more budget-friendly options.

I spent three nights in the new Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino, a half-century-old property that was recently renovated before joining the Trailborn nature lodge collection and Marriott Bonvoy program. Other points options include Holiday Inn Express Fort Bragg by IHG and Baymont by Wyndham Fort Bragg.

If, like me, you love a good independent or boutique hotel, Mendocino is full of them. For instance, you could book a seaside cottage at Agate Cove Inn through Amex Travel or Capital One Travel, earning 5 points per dollar with your or 10 miles per dollar with your Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, respectively.

Or consider staying at SCP Mendocino Inn and Farm, a 19th-century manor turned B&B where guests can enjoy complimentary breakfast sourced from the onsite farm. Even better, you can redeem your points for more than 1 cent apiece via Chase Points Boost.

Overall, one of the things I loved most about the Mendocino Coast was its manageable size. From the downtown areas to the state parks, everything I visited was small but high-quality.

So instead of running around a city trying to cram in as much as possible, you can spend a leisurely weekend (or longer) exploring charming boutiques, quirky museums, local dining or natural wonders. You won’t run out of things to do, but the close proximity between attractions and “island time” mentality will help you savor the activities you choose.

That’s what slow travel is all about, right?

#6107. Wow: Lufthansa Adds Premium Business Seats On Some Short Haul A320 Flights!

Lufthansa has just announced plans to introduce “real” business class seats on some of its narrow body planes, and that’s a really exciting development, given the typical business class standard on narrow body aircraft in Europe!

Interestingly, this is a concept that was initially trialed on Lufthansa Group low cost subsidiary Eurowings, and we knew at the time it was being used as a test for a more widespread implementation across the airline group. I’m delighted to see this become more widespread, and I hope this is just the start of a bigger trend.

Lufthansa has revealed that it will expand its premium offering on short and medium haul routes. With the introduction of the new Premium Business Seat, passengers will get more personal space than they’re used to on short haul aircraft.

Historically, business class on Airbus A320-family aircraft has consisted of standard economy seats with a blocked middle. So that means with the 3-3 layout, four seats were only sold per row. What’s happening is that the first three rows on some aircraft are being replaced with two rows of recliner seats, meaning the per-seat footprint is around 50% bigger than in standard business class.

At launch, the new Lufthansa Premium Business Seat will be available on six Airbus A320 aircraft (and these planes will also be equipped with Starlink). The seat will feature significantly more space, with nearly one meter of legroom, plus extra recline. This doesn’t replace the standard business class product, but instead, is an upsell option.

This new product is now available for sale for flights as of March 1, 2027, on routes between Frankfurt (FRA) and Athens (ATH), Cairo (CAI), and Nice (NCE). However, the first plane with the seats will already be in service as of December 16, 2026, and as of February 2027, it’ll be deployed on the above routes (but tickets are only on sale as of March as of now).

If a flight has this product available, you’ll see the “Premium Business Seat” designator during the booking process.

The process of actually booking a Premium Business Seat is essentially an upgrade cost on top of the standard business class fare. For example, looking at a Frankfurt to Athens route, I see an upgrade cost of €139, which frankly seems quite reasonable for a flight of this length.

Lufthansa is for the time being describing this as a commercial test, with the aim of examining demand for additional comfort on these routes, and the results will form the basis for deciding whether to expand the offering.

You’ll see many people refer to short haul business class in Europe as a “scam” (I don’t agree, but people say that), and they’re shocked to find economy seats with blocked middles. Admittedly product standards differ vastly around the globe.

The reason that airlines in Europe can get away with this product is threefold:

Keep in mind that most of the network carriers in Europe don’t make much money on short haul flights (or even lose a lot of money), given high costs and fierce competition from ultra low cost carriers.

With that in mind, I think Lufthansa is going about this exactly right:

I’d love to see more airlines introduce something similar. In particular, Air France, as Europe’s most premium airline, seems best positioned to do this, and could do it with very little opportunity cost. Why?

Honestly, if I were Air France, I’d just introduce this throughout the A220 fleet, and it would be a major point of differentiation, competitively. No airline could do it as efficiently as Air France, and every A220 flight has at least two rows of business class, so the opportunity cost is minimal.

Lufthansa will be introducing “real” business class seats on a subfleet of its Airbus A320s. As of the spring of 2027, expect these planes to be flying from Frankfurt to Athens, Cairo, and Nice. This Premium Business Seat concept will complement the existing business class, and will be available as a buy-up for business class passengers.

I’m very happy to finally see some more comfort on flights within Europe, and I imagine this will prove successful. If it doesn’t, I suspect it would be due to a lack of people knowing about this, rather than there not actually being demand.

What do you make of the Lufthansa Premium Business Seat concept?

#6106. Alaska Cuts Four Routes

Alaska Airlines will drop four destinations from its network in Portland, Oregon.

The carrier confirmed it will end service from Portland to Baltimore, St. Louis, New Orleans, and Jackson Hole, Wyoming.

Three of the connections launched only months ago. Portland-Jackson Hole came online in June, and service to Baltimore and St. Louis started in May.

“As we add new routes to our network, we constantly assess existing routes to ensure we’re using our aircraft in the markets our guests want most,” the carrier said in a statement provided to AirlineGeeks. “As part of that process, we’ve made the decision to discontinue service between Portland and Baltimore, Jackson Hole, St. Louis, and New Orleans. We remain committed to Portland and will continue to invest in opportunities that strengthen our network there, including adding service in markets where we see the greatest opportunities for our guests.”

Alaska serves over 60 destinations from Portland, and recently opened a new lounge there.

#6104. New Resy Rewards Program Offers 4x Bonus Amex Points For Dining Out

Resy has just launched the Resy Rewards program, which lets American Express card members in the United States earn an extra 4x points per dollar spent at participating Resy restaurants, on top of their credit card rewards. As you’d expect, it’s not quite that straightforward, but I’d still consider this to be pretty exciting!

American Express owns both Resy and Tock (which is now being integrated into Resy), as part of its larger “lifestyle” play for attracting card members. So along with that, Resy is leaning more into the rewards program side of things, with the new Resy Rewards program offering an extra 4x Amex points per dollar spent at eligible Resy restaurants.

Resy Rewards is first launching in New York City, where users will see a new “Rewards” tab within the Resy iOS app, where they can browse and book eligible restaurants. Restaurants participating in the Resy Rewards launch include Carne Mare, Le Crocodile, Hearth, Kiko, OPTO, Le Pavillon, and more. In 2027, Resy Rewards plans to expand to additional U.S. cities, and select Tock venues will become eligible to participate in the program.

So, how exactly does Resy Rewards work? Card members need to enroll a US-based Membership Rewards program eligible card in Resy Rewards, then book a Resy Rewards reservation through the “Rewards” tab in the Resy iOS app, and then pay the bill for the dining experience with the enrolled card. So this requires a little more jumping through hoops than just using an Amex card Resy credit, for example.

These rewards are in addition to whatever the standard rewards are on an Amex card. For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) ordinarily earns 4x points at restaurants globally, so if you dined at a restaurant eligible for Resy Rewards, you could be earning 8x points per dollar spent, which is pretty awesome.

Here’s how Pablo Rivero, CEO of Resy and SVP of American Express Global Dining, describes this:

“For the first time, we’re bringing American Express’s industry-leading Rewards program into the Resy iOS app and connecting two things our Card Members value deeply: great dining experiences and meaningful rewards. As we’ve seen with the success of the Resy Credit, rewarding diners while driving demand and revenue to Resy restaurants is a win on both sides of the table.”

I’m delighted to see Amex introduce an opportunity to earn points for dining out, beyond the bonus categories already offered on some of the issuer’s most popular cards. For the time being, this is rather niche, given that it’s limited to select restaurants in New York City, but the expectation is that it will expand more broadly in 2027 (though it remains to be seen how broadly).

Essentially think of this as being similar to a dining rewards program, as the idea is that restaurants have to opt-in to participate in this, with the hope being that this drums up business for them (and presumably they pay Amex and Resy something extra in exchange for that).

Furthermore, you do have to specifically reserve your reservation through Resy to qualify for this, so if you don’t have a reservation made through the “Rewards” tab on Resy, then you won’t earn bonus points.

I’m happy to see this, as earning 8x points on dining when paying with the Amex Gold Card is quite a great deal. Then again, so much of my dining out is through InKind, which is my favorite dining rewards program, given the excellent selection of restaurants the program has in Miami, and it’s tough to compete with the rewards offered by the program.

The new Resy Rewards program offers bonus Amex points when you make a reservation at an eligible restaurant and then pay with your eligible Amex card. The idea is that you can earn an extra 4x points per dollar spent on purchases at eligible restaurants, which is pretty awesome.

The catch is that this is initially launching in New York City, only “eligible” restaurants qualify, and you need to reserve through Resy and then pay with the same linked card in order to earn the bonus points. It’s nice to see this launch, and I look forward to it expanding to more markets.

#6103. Trump’s ‘invasion’ asylum ban to face justices

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

“The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition says.

Trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

The D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”

Last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

The case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

#6102. Delta SkyMiles & World Of Hyatt Partnership Live: Dual Earning, Milestone Rewards, & Linking Accounts

In September 2026, Delta SkyMiles and World of Hyatt unveiled plans to launch a new, long term strategic partnership. This announcement came just shortly after American AAdvantage and World of Hyatt announced that they will be ending their partnership.

At the time, we didn’t actually have any details as to what the partnership would entail, but that has now changed, as additional information has been revealed. Parts of the partnership are even now live, and members can already link their accounts.

Delta and Hyatt are launching a new loyalty program collaboration, which comes with a “shared ambition to create additional value, recognition and engagement opportunities across more of the travel journey.” This includes reciprocal opportunities to earn rewards, and also reciprocal opportunities to select perks with the partner brand.

Here’s how Laurie Blair, Hyatt’s SVP of Global Marketing and Loyalty, describes this:

“World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles were each built to make travel more meaningful and rewarding, which makes this collaboration feel meant to be. By connecting the Delta flight and Hyatt stay, we are helping members get more from the journeys they are already taking while opening the door to new experiences, destinations and memories. It is an exciting next step in our commitment to caring for members throughout the full travel journey, from takeoff to check out.”

Here’s how Dwight James, Delta’s SVP of Customer Engagement & Loyalty, describes this:

“At Delta, we know loyalty is something we earn by delivering meaningful value and experiences that make our Members want to keep choosing us. Our relationship with World of Hyatt gives us another way to do that by recognizing and rewarding Members across more of their travel, while creating new ways to earn, engage and experience both brands.”

Effective immediately (as of November 17, 2026), elite members of both loyalty programs can earn simultaneously with the new “Dual Earn” benefit. Members must link their accounts, and can then earn additional rewards.

World of Hyatt members can earn bonus points on eligible Delta flights (which includes Delta Comfort, Delta Premium Select, Delta First Class, and Delta One), as follows:

Delta SkyMiles members can earn bonus miles on eligible Hyatt stays (which includes qualifying room rates, qualifying incidental spend, and qualifying non-stay charges at participating Hyatt properties, eligible Mr & Mrs Smith spend booked through Hyatt, and eligible spend at The Venetian booked through Hyatt):

As of 2027, eligible elite members of both World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles will gain access to new milestone reward choices, giving people more ways to earn, and more flexibility in how they use their loyalty benefits. This would apply to World of Hyatt Milestone Rewards, and Delta SkyMiles Choice Benefits.

As of January 1, 2027, World of Hyatt members will be able to choose Delta awards as they reach qualifying Milestone Rewards thresholds. The first Delta award choice will become available at 20 qualifying nights or 35,000 base points, with additional choices as members progress through the program, including:

As of February 1, 2027, Delta SkyMiles members will be able to choose Hyatt awards as they reach qualifying Choice Benefits thresholds. Members will be able to select free night awards, as follows:

To celebrate the start of this partnership, Hyatt and Delta are offering limited time offers for members who link their accounts.

First, from November 17 through December 31, 2026, linked members can register to earn one additional World of Hyatt elite night after completing their first qualifying Hyatt stay during the offer period. Taking advantage of this should be a no-brainer.

Next, from January 4 through February 15, 2027, linked members can:

Basically, Hyatt has dumped American in favor of Delta. Admittedly the partnership between American and Hyatt had already been scaled back over time. The two programs used to offer a dual accrual opportunity as well, but that was eventually cut.

After all, companies only want to offer perks like that if they’re driving incremental business, and I imagine at some point it’s hard to justify that expense, when you feel like there’s not much upside left:

Now the Delta and Hyatt partnership is starting out in a similar way to how the American one did, with one major exception. On the dual accrual front, SkyMiles elite members are lucky, as they earn rewards on all qualifying Hyatt spending. Meanwhile World of Hyatt members only earn rewards when booking premium tickets, which is a bit disappointing. And here I was thinking that all seats on Delta aircraft are premium!!

I do have to say, as much as I’m a World of Hyatt loyalist, the program has certainly become less differentiated over time. While Delta can argue all it wants about how premium it is, SkyMiles simply isn’t as good of a loyalty program as AAdvantage. So perhaps this swap reflects the direction Hyatt is trying to head on loyalty… I dunno.

Delta and Hyatt have launched an exclusive new partnership, which explains why American and Hyatt cut ties. The partnership is now live, and it includes dual points accrual opportunities, reciprocal milestone perks, and some limited time opportunities.

At a minimum, it’s definitely worth linking accounts. And if you’re a World of Hyatt member with a stay planned before the end of the year, be sure to register for an extra elite night, as there’s no reason not to take advantage of that.

Yes, Serbia requires U.S. citizens to have a passport to enter.

Small tips are customary at restaurants and hotels.

Taxis are cheap and plentiful, but public transport within the city is free.

Yes, Serbia is generally considered safe for travelers. The U.S. State Department currently lists it as Level 2, so travelers should exercise increased caution, but no severe threats are present.

September-October offers long days with plentiful sunshine, while April-May is when the city starts to warm up before the full heat of summer.

You might have seen Serbia in the news lately. The country’s recent national elections enacted a political sea change spearheaded by student groups seeking greater freedoms and opportunities.

The jubilant energy unleashed, combined with the Serbian capital’s soon-to-shine spotlight as it prepares to host the 2027 World Expo make now the perfect time to plan your visit to Belgrade. That’s why the city made our list of top destinations for next year.

Sleepier than some other European capitals, yet vibrant and buzzing with a construction boom, Belgrade is coming into its own. It’s also easier than ever to get there, thanks to plentiful airline connections not only to other European hubs but also to the U.S. via the country’s national carrier, Air Serbia.

So start your points planning and make Belgrade a part of your next transatlantic trip.

The fastest way to get to Belgrade’s Nikola Tesla Airport (BEG) from the U.S. is aboard Air Serbia from Chicago’s O’Hare International Airport (ORD) or New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). The airline also recently announced that it will launch twice-weekly service to Miami International Airport (MIA) in May 2027.

Air Serbia’s main major airline partner is Etihad, so your best bet for booking award tickets is to use Etihad Guest miles. The program is a transfer partner of:

That said, award availability is hard to come by since these flights only operate a few times a week. Instead, you might want to consider redeeming Flying Blue miles for flights on Air France via Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG) or via Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS) on KLM.

For Star Alliance flyers, award availability between the U.S. and Belgrade is plentiful on carriers like LOT via Warsaw Chopin Airport (WAW) and Lufthansa via Frankfurt Airport (FRA) or Munich International Airport (MUC) and Swiss via Zurich Airport (ZRH), starting at 42,500 Aeroplan points each way in economy and 75,000 Aeroplan points each way in business class. Taxes and fees range from about $100 to $150 in each direction.

Belgrade is expecting to see its first Intercontinental open in early 2027, just in time for the World Expo. Until then, there are plenty of other hotels where your points will come in handy.

Located in the new riverside Belgrade Waterfront District, which is home to a sprawling luxury mall, a promenade with tons of bars, cafes and restaurants, and more than a few high-rise apartment buildings, the St. Regis Belgrade opened in November 2024 in a striking glass-and-steel tower. The hotel has just 119 spacious rooms and suites with floor-to-ceiling windows, a beautiful spa with an indoor pool, a cafe-patisserie, a continental restaurant and an outpost of the brand’s signature St. Regis Bar. Rates start at $290 or 43,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

The Hyatt Regency Belgrade is a comfortable, modern hotel in Novi Beograd, the city’s main business district, across the Sava River from the historic core, so it’s not the best for leisure travelers. That said, you can’t beat nightly rates that start at $148 or 6,000 World of Hyatt points per night.

The Hilton Belgrade is centrally located near Slavija Square, within walking distance of attractions like the Nikola Tesla Museum and the Church of Saint Sava. It has 242 rooms and suites and a restaurant that serves contemporary Serbian cuisine. Rates start at $170 or 50,000 Hilton Honors points per night.

You won’t find Uber in Serbia, but taxis are plentiful and can be hailed via apps like Yandex, Pink Taxi Nova and Car:Go. The apps make it easy to pay with a credit card. Just be sure to use a credit card that earns bonus points on ride-hailing services or on travel charges in general.

Sometimes drivers will not accept rides unless you are paying cash, though, which you can also book through the app and then take a metered ride. So be sure to pull some cash out at the ATM at the airport before heading into the city.

Once in Belgrade, it’s easy to get around by public trams and buses, which are free to use within the city center.

Related: The best credit cards for commuting expenses

For a city of its size, Belgrade’s restaurant scene is surprisingly diverse. Of course, you should make it a priority to try typical Serbian dishes like grilled cevapi sausages with fluffy bread and ajvar red pepper sauce, and sarma, which is pickled cabbage stuffed with spiced meat and rice, not to mention the plethora of cured meats and mountain cheeses. Bela Reka is a great place to try a smattering of Serbian specialties, many of them sourced from the restaurant’s own farm in the Homolje Mountains.

Perched on the riverbank, Suvenir serves traditional dishes like roasted lamb and bacon-wrapped prunes in a beautiful setting.

For a contemporary take on Balkan cuisine, Iva is a sophisticated hideaway tucked into a courtyard near Saint Sava church where age-old dishes are reinterpreted through a modern lens. The piping-hot burek pastries stuffed with cheese, baked peach, hot pepper and honey are not to miss ($12), as is the confit river pike-perch with gnocchi and charred Swiss chard in a white wine sauce ($20). A glass of crisp Deuric Severna Morava white wine from the Fruska Gora region is the perfect accompaniment ($7).

Be sure to book ahead for a table at S5 by Angie, a fine-dining bolthole hidden in an otherwise unremarkable apartment building in the city’s quiet Zemun district. Spend a while enjoying a cocktail in the living-room-like parlor, complete with a vinyl record collection, then settle in for a multicourse feast prepared by chef "Angie" Risimic that might include dishes like creamy labneh with tart tomatoes, fluffy ravioli with mild ricotta-style cheese doused in a green herb and blackberry sauce with trout roe, and tender pork in a rosehip demi-glace with end-of-summer morels. Prix-fixe menu prices vary but range from $75-$150, though a la carte ordering is also possible.

For something more casual, spend an evening strolling cobblestones of Skadarska Street in the bohemian neighborhood of Skadarlija, just a short walk from Republic Square, where you will find over a dozen traditional kafane, or taverns, serving similar menus of hearty dishes along with plenty of plum-flavored rakija spirits.

Tri Sesira, or the Three Hats, was a favorite of the Serbian Romantic poet and painter Dura Jaksic, a statue of whom sits outside his humble former house nearby.

Belgrade has a handful of worthwhile museums, but not so many as to commandeer your entire timeline.

The National Museum has exhibits ranging from prehistoric artifacts to medieval Balkan icons, Italian Renaissance and Flemish masters, French Impressionists and modern artists, including pieces by well-known Yugoslav painters like Sava Sumanovic. Entrance is $3 for adults.

It’s free to stroll the grounds of Belgrade Fortress and Kalemegdan Park, which overlook the confluence of the Danube and Sava Rivers and are popular places for sunset meetups.

Some of the museums at the fortress have their own entrance fees and operating hours. The citadel dates to the third century B.C.E., though it has seen hundreds of battles and been destroyed, rebuilt and expanded dozens of times in the ensuing millennia.

Even if churches aren’t your thing, no visit to Belgrade would be complete without a stop at the brilliant white, copper-domed Church of Saint Sava, which is one of the largest Eastern Orthodox churches in the world.

The interior mosaics gleam with gold and are utterly breathtaking. Entrance is free.

Nearby the Nikola Tesla Museum is a fun, interactive affair. It offers guided tours every 45 minutes, but they fill up fast, so get there at least half an hour before the next one to line up. Entrance costs $7.50 and includes a short film, then demonstrations using Tesla coils before a small exhibit spanning the inventor’s life and some of his personal effects.

Sitting in a small park of its own, the Museum of Yugoslavia is a memorial to the former country’s late strongman, Josip Broz Tito, who rose to prominence in the resistance to the Nazi occupation of World War II and eventually oversaw every aspect of life in Yugoslavia until his death in 1980.

The complex includes his mausoleum — the so-called “House of Flowers” — an older building with some of his personal belongings and displays about daily life in Yugoslavia and a larger wing with temporary exhibits including a recent one on themes of propaganda in wartime. Admission is $7.50 for adults.

The pedestrian shopping street of Knez Mihailova is also well worth a wander, if only for unique souvenirs produced by Serbian craftspeople at the Belgrade Window boutique.

It might not have been on your radar before, but Belgrade is well worth a visit, especially with all the events on the calendar for 2027, including hosting the World Expo. Along with some luxurious new hotels and a growing crop of exciting new restaurants, plus a small but impressive cadre of museums and galleries, it might just become one of your favorite European capitals.

#6100. Saudia's Surprising New 8-Hour UK Route On 110-Seat Jet: See Map Now

Saudia is the fourth-largest airline operating flights between the United Kingdom and the Middle East. The airline has been reviewing its UK network in recent years. In fact, earlier this year, it discontinued services to Birmingham and London Gatwick. With that being said, the SkyTeam member now appears to be considering a new UK destination.

This time, to the Scottish capital, Edinburgh. According to Airport Coordination Limited's (ACL) Edinburgh Summer 2027 Initial Coordination Report, Saudia has secured slots at Edinburgh Airport (EDI) for the upcoming summer season. If the airline proceeds with the planned service, it will become its third UK destination.

According to the ACL report, Saudia has requested slots for four weekly flights to Edinburgh, using its 110-seat Airbus A320 aircraft. However, securing slots does not necessarily mean that the airline will operate the flights as planned. The aircraft type could also change, as airlines can revise their planned equipment after slots have been allocated.

Given the distance involved and the range limitations of a typical A320, operating the route with this aircraft would be unusual. One possible alternative is the Airbus A321XLR, which airlines are increasingly using on long-haul routes with relatively limited passenger demand.

According to ch-aviation data, the Saudi flag carrier currently operates five A321XLRs and is awaiting deliveries of another ten aircraft. It could therefore consider deploying the extra-long-range narrowbody on the Edinburgh route instead of the A320. In fact, Saudia already uses the A321XLR on its service between Jeddah’s King Abdulaziz International Airport (JED) and Manchester Airport (MAN).

Interestingly, the 110-seat A320 is no stranger to the UK. Saudia previously deployed the aircraft on its service between Neom Bay Airport (NUM) and London Gatwick Airport (LGW). The airline currently has seven A320s in this configuration and regularly uses them on several European routes.

According to scheduled data from aviation analytics provider Cirium, Saudia will deploy the aircraft on nine of its European routes in December, most of which originate from Jeddah. These include services to Barcelona, Rome Fiumicino, Frankfurt, Geneva, Istanbul, Munich and Zurich.

The airline will also use the 110-seat A320 on its flights from Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport (RUH) to Rome Fiumicino and Geneva. Apart from this, the SkyTeam member also operates its 188-seat Airbus A321neo on some European routes and regularly deploys the A321XLR, which accommodates 144 passengers.

A new era of travel dawns as Saudia unveils plans for its cutting-edge fleet addition.

Nevertheless, it will be interesting to see whether Saudia goes ahead with its plans to serve Edinburgh. Currently, there are no nonstop flights between the Scottish capital and Saudi Arabia, meaning passengers have to travel via other airports, such as Doha, Dubai, Istanbul, or London Heathrow. Demand for travel between the UK and Saudi Arabia is strong. In 2025, more than 1.76 million passengers traveled between the two countries.

According to Cirium data, four airlines have scheduled flights between the two countries for 2027; Saudia is by far the largest operator in the market. The airline serves four routes, three of which connect London Heathrow Airport (LHR) with King Fahd International Airport (DMM) in Dammam, Riyadh, and Jeddah. The fourth connects Jeddah with MAN.

London Heathrow – Riyadh (Up to 3x daily)

London Heathrow – Jeddah (Up to 3x daily)

London Heathrow – Riyadh (Daily from Jan. 11)

London Heathrow – Red Sea International (3x weekly)**

**Depends on whether the carrier starts service in December 2026

Apart from Saudia, newcomer Riyadh Air offers flights from Riyadh to London Heathrow and Manchester. British Airways is also set to resume its Heathrow-Riyadh service in January 2027. In addition, the all-business-class carrier beOnd had planned to launch three weekly nonstop flights between Red Sea International Airport (RSI) and London Heathrow on December 15, 2026. However, it has recently paused its scheduled flights for December.

#6099. Earning World Of Hyatt Elite Nights & Status With Credit Cards: Worth It?

Chase and Hyatt have two co-branded credit cards — the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Card (learn more). I’d consider these to be among the more lucrative hotel credit cards out there, particularly the personal version of the card.

One of the awesome things about Hyatt’s two credit cards is that they can earn you elite nights, making it easier to qualify for status in the World of Hyatt program. In this post, I’d like to get into the nitty-gritty of how earning Hyatt elite status with credit cards works, and discuss whether it’s worth it.

Chase and Hyatt have both the World of Hyatt Credit Card (a personal card) and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (a business card). Both cards have valuable benefits, though I think the personal card is considerably more compelling than the business card. Let me start by just briefly recapping the perks of the two cards.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card has a $95 annual fee and offers:

This means that you’re getting five elite nights toward status and a Category 1-4 free night award every year just for having the card. To me that more than justifies the annual fee, by a long shot (I consistently get $250+ of value out of the free night certificate alone). That doesn’t even factor in the incremental perks you can get for spending on the card.

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card has a $199 annual fee and offers:

The business version of the card isn’t quite as rewarding as the personal version of the card, especially if you’re not a big spender. However, for businesses that spend quite a bit on credit cards, this can be the best card for earning elite status.

Both the World of Hyatt Credit Card and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offer the ability to earn elite nights. However, the ways in which you earn elite nights differ between the two cards, so let’s go over those details.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers qualifying nights toward Hyatt status in two ways. First of all, the World of Hyatt Card offers five elite nights annually just for having the card. There’s no spending required to earn these five elite nights, and you receive them for each calendar year in which you have the card, including the year in which you open the card.

Beyond that, the World of Hyatt Card offers two elite nights for every $5,000 spent on the card (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,500 of spending). There’s no limit to how many elite nights you can earn this way, and the elite nights earned through spending on this card aren’t in any way tied to the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $2,500 on the card in 2026 and then spend $2,500 on the card in 2027, you’d earn two elite nights at that point.

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offers five elite nights for every $10,000 spent on the card in a calendar year (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,000 of spending). On this card, the spending counter resets at the beginning of the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $8,000 on the card in 2026, you’d still have to spend a full $10,000 in 2027 to earn five elite nights.

As you can see, this card offers elite nights for spending at an accelerated rate, though unlike the personal card, it doesn’t offer the five elite nights annually just for having the card.

How soon do elite nights post from the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card?

While the above covers the basics, I’d like to now analyze the overall value proposition of earning World of Hyatt elite status by spending on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, including addressing some of the most common questions and scenarios that come up.

With Hyatt, not all elite perks are tied directly to having status, but rather some require earning a certain number of elite nights in a year, known as the Milestone Rewards program. The Milestone Rewards program is how you earn perks like suite upgrade awards, club access awards, Guest of Honor awards, and more.

Hyatt elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards would count toward Milestone Rewards the same as any hotel stays would, which adds further value to credit card spending.

One of the perks of both Hyatt credit cards is that you receive Discoverist status for as long as you have the card. Discoverist status ordinarily requires 10 elite qualifying nights or 25,000 base points per year. As a reminder, here are World of Hyatt’s elite thresholds:

One common point of confusion is that people assume these cards really come with up to 15 elite nights per year. They assume you already get Discoverist status, and that any elite nights are on top of that. Note that while these cards offer Discoverist status, you don’t get the elite nights that correspond to that.

This means that if you have a Hyatt credit card, you’ll receive Discoverist status on an ongoing basis (and five elite nights every year if you have the personal card), but you’ll still need to qualify for Explorist or Globalist status based on the full criteria.

Hyatt’s lifetime Globalist status is based on earning one million base points in the program. World of Hyatt members earn five base points per dollar spent on Hyatt stays, meaning you essentially have to spend $200,000 at Hyatts to earn lifetime Globalist status.

Credit card spending, and any elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards, won’t count toward lifetime Globalist status. That’s because the qualification criteria is based solely on base points, and not based on elite qualifying nights (in which case it would count).

World of Hyatt Globalist is my favorite top tier hotel status, and what I love is that Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards make it easier to earn that. Let’s look at the best strategy for earning Globalist status with the card. Hyatt Globalist status ordinarily requires earning 60 qualifying nights in a year. So how much would you have to spend on a Hyatt credit card to earn that status?

On the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you’d need to spend $140,000 to earn Globalist status:

Meanwhile on the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, you’d need to spend $120,000 to earn Globalist status:

As you can see, the personal credit card offers more elite nights upfront, while the business credit card offers elite nights at a faster pace for spending (assuming you can reach the thresholds).

When you’re analyzing the value of spending your way toward status, don’t forget that even beyond the general status perks, the Milestone Rewards perks could really add up. For example, if you make it to 60 elite nights, you could select five suite upgrade awards and four club access awards, and would also receive a Category 1-7 free night award, a Category 1-4 free night award, and three Guest of Honor awards.

Then on the personal version of the card, you also receive an additional Category 1-4 free night award when you spend $15,000 on the card in a year. The value of all of those perks really adds up.

Hyatt counts award nights toward status, and just for having the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you get a free night every year, plus the opportunity to earn a further three free nights for spending $15,000, earning Explorist status, and earning Globalist status.

On top of that, presumably you want to earn Globalist status because you actually intend to stay at Hyatts with some frequency. Hotel status is worthless if you don’t actually stay at that brand.

To be realistic, let’s assume that long term you’re earning 30 elite nights per year through actual stays. There are so many great Globalist benefits to use (like suite upgrade awards and free night awards), so if you’re staying at Hyatts less than that I question whether Globalist is worth it for you.

If you earned 30 of the required 60 elite nights through credit card spending, you’d need to spend the following:

Given all the incremental perks you’re picking up with Milestone Rewards, I’d say the math could really check out.

When deciding if it makes sense to spend money on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, consider the opportunity cost of the spending. For easy math purposes, I tend to consider the opportunity cost of credit card spending to be around 3.4%.

That’s because based on my valuation of miles & points, most transferable points currencies are worth 1.7 cents each, and you have some cards offering 2x points per dollar spent. Meanwhile I value World of Hyatt points at 1.4 cents each.

If we were to theoretically assume you’re spending $60,000 on a Hyatt credit card per year (give or take) in order to earn Globalist status, what’s the opportunity cost of that spending? By my math, you’re looking at an opportunity cost of up to 2% (the spread between a 3.4% return and 1.4% return). That’s around $1,200, if you value things the way that I do. But that’s not factoring in the value of all the other perks mentioned above:

For many, I think the above perks could more than justify the difference in return on spending otherwise.

There are many things to love about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, though the ability to get a fast track toward status is probably my favorite perk. I absolutely love Hyatt Globalist status, and credit cards have historically helped me requalify for status. If you’re a Hyatt loyalist and don’t yet have the hotel group’s co-branded credit cards, they’re seriously worth considering.

What has your experience been using World of Hyatt Credit Cards to earn elite status?

#6098. Conservative firebrand Lauren Boebert ousted in Colorado

Colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

The red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

A newcomer to electoral politics, she quickly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

In 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

Running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch announced he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

This year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

#6097. Mullin: Wave of Tech Failures May Be Linked to AI

Artificial intelligence could be playing a role in the cascade of high-profile technology failures seen over the last week, U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Monday.

Mullin told FOX News’ Sean Hannity that he spoke with someone in the tech industry, “one guy who is very smart with tech,” who identified AI as a possible culprit.

“He said, ‘I believe that it’s the SI, because the programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is,'” he said.

The individual suggested that the technology’s ability to move fast and fix itself created “ripple effects” that overwhelmed older conventional systems. The secretary said that theory “kind of makes sense to me.”

The Trump administration uses the term “super intelligence,” or SI, in place of AI.

Mullin said his source did not want to be identified but ruled out at least one famous personality from the tech sector.

Multiple large, U.S.-based networks have crashed over the past week, including the FAA’s air traffic control communications system, United’s internal applications, Microsoft’s business services, and software used by banks such as JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo.

Mullin said there is no indication from the intelligence and cybersecurity communities that the outages are part of a cyberattack.

The FAA has blamed Friday’s nationwide ground stop on a faulty or improperly installed router, which flooded other routers with data and ultimately crashed the system.

#6096. Tulum Is Losing Airlines Fast: Why The Hyped New Airport Is Failing

In late 2023, we saw the opening of the Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport (TQO), in Tulum, Mexico. For those not familiar, Tulum is located on the eastern coast of the Yucatan Peninsula, and for years, it was a growing tourist destination.

While it could previously be accessed via Cancun International Airport (CUN), the hope was that by opening a new international airport, visitor numbers would expand massively. Unfortunately what has actually happened is exactly the opposite, as airline after airline has pulled out. What exactly is going on here? I think it makes for an interesting story, and thanks to TravelinWilly for flagging this.

In 2023, we saw airline after airline announce flights to Tulum. Among US carriers, we saw American, Delta, JetBlue, and United, all launch flights to Tulum, while Spirit announced flights, but never launched them.

That was only a small part of the overall international service to the airport, as we also saw flights to Tulum on Air Canada, Air Transat, Avianca, Copa, Discover, and WestJet, along with flights on domestic carriers like Aeromexico, Mexicana de Aviacion, Viva, and Volaris.

Less than three years after the airport opened, where do things stand? When it comes to international year-round service, we’ve now gone from service to 12 airports, to service to four airports, which is an absolutely massive reduction:

Just to put this into numbers, in the first half of 2026, the airport saw a 33.2% reduction in passengers. June 2026 was the worst month to date, with a 44.8% drop, as there were just 47,600 passengers, compared to 86,200 passengers the year prior.

It goes without saying that for a newly built airport, this is rather catastrophic, and not what you hope to see.

In some ways, it feels like the whole concept behind Tulum Airport was sort of unnecessary. That’s also easily explained by the fact that the airport was well over a decade in the making, so while I can see how it might’ve seemed like a good idea at some point, tourism trends do evolve over time.

The reality is that there was a point where Tulum was cool, edgy, and a bit off the beaten path, compared to… whatever it is now. But when it comes to the struggles that airlines have had with flying to Tulum, it seems like the problems have been endless:

It’ll be interesting to see if Tulum can reverse any of these trends, and regain visitors…

A few years ago Tulum Airport opened to some fanfare, as a good number of airlines rushed to add service there. Unfortunately the excitement didn’t last long, as the airport has gone from a dozen year-round international routes, to just four.

This reduction in demand particularly evident from the United States, as soon there will just be nonstop service on American and Delta, and even that will be with reduced frequencies and routes.

Tulum Airport is facing endless challenges, not the least of which is a decline in visitors to Mexico from the United States, combined with increasing competition for those fewer visitors. Mexico just isn’t a value destination in the way that it used to be in places like Cancun, Tulum, Los Cabos, etc., and that’s understandably impacting demand.

I’m curious if Tulum can find a way to turn things around, but it’s not a good situation.

What do you make of the Tulum Airport demand problem?

#6095. Delta CEO: “Customers Are Not Choosing Airlines Based On Wi-Fi”

I’ve gotta be honest, I don’t envy the situation that Delta CEO Ed Bastian is in. Unlike most other carriers in the United States, Delta hasn’t opted for SpaceX Starlink Wi-Fi, and has instead gone with Amazon Leo.

In theory that’s fine, except Amazon Leo is years behind Starlink, and just faced a new setback, due to a rocket failure. Elon Musk has also repeatedly publicly ridiculed Bastian, regarding what Bastian reportedly said about Musk to employees.

There’s now an interesting update, as Bastian made some comments about the carrier’s Wi-Fi choice, and overall customer preferences. It sure is amazing how narratives can change, based on what’s convenient…

This week at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum 2026, Delta’s CEO was asked about the carrier’s decision not to choose Starlink, plus the public spat with Musk. Here’s what Bastian had to say about this:

“We’ve been the leader in Wi-Fi, and in free and fast Wi-Fi, and we’ve been at it for five years. I’ve got a long history with Elon on that. We’ve looked at Starlink, we actually helped them started in aviation, we gave them our planes to use during COVID, when we weren’t flying, and they tested the system out. We just couldn’t come to agreement on a business model.”

“We’ve been the leader in free, fast Wi-Fi. We are confident there will be more than one LEO product in the world other than Starlink, and I’m confident Amazon has the capability to do a great job. Customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi. We’ve been out with a great product from Viasat, which we’ve got two new satellites in the sky. It’s not Starlink caliber but it’s pretty darn close.”

“This is about the total experience, and customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.”At the #F500Innovation Forum, @Delta CEO Ed Bastian told @ajs that the airline helped Elon Musk’s satellite Wi-Fi “get started in aviation,” but the two sides “just couldn’t come to… pic.twitter.com/xmSERJNjjH

Look, before I get too deep into this, let me make several points that I think no one reasonable will disagree with (which is not to say some commenters won’t disagree!):

When Bastian formally unveiled plans for free Wi-Fi at CES 2023 in Las Vegas, he said the following:

“At work, at home and everywhere in between, connectivity is essential to daily life, and your journey on Delta should be no different. Our vision has long been to deliver an experience at 30,000 feet that feels similar to what our customers have available on the ground.”

“We didn’t just want free Wi-Fi to offer base-level service – we wanted it to be transformative for the entire onboard experience. It is imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home, and we’ve put this system through meticulous tests to make that possible.”

Earlier this year, when announcing plans to partner with Amazon Leo for connectivity, Bastian said that “we need to stay the leader” in inflight connectivity. Obviously that won’t be the case for a long time.

As I see it, Delta’s problem here is pretty simple. Customers absolutely notice a difference between Viasat and Starlink. The issue isn’t that people will stop flying Delta altogether. The issue is that Delta has built its entire brand on being the industry leader, and on being on the forefront of technology.

There’s no denying that this sentiment among the public changes over time, because inflight Wi-Fi is easily one of the top amenities that passengers notice nowadays. Seriously, I can’t count the number of people I’ve heard from or just overheard talking about their first Starlink experience, and how blown away they were.

I guess to look at it from another angle, there’s no airline that loves talking about how premium it is more than Delta. What makes Delta premium? If we’re going to believe that Delta is premium, it’s not based on any one single thing, but rather, it’s based on the sum of the experience. And I think anyone who thinks a major Wi-Fi disadvantage lasting for years isn’t part of what contributes to consumer sentiment is lying to themselves.

Delta CEO Ed Bastian is now downplaying the importance of inflight Wi-Fi. He’s arguing that “customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi,” which in isolation, is probably true. But he’s also arguing that Viasat is “pretty darn close” to Starlink, which is most definitely not true, as I see it.

I wouldn’t be so critical of these statements if it weren’t for Bastian spending years hyping up how it’s “imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home,” while also saying “we need to stay the leader.” And for that matter, Delta has of course also long hyped how premium it is — if that’s to be believed, it’s not about any one feature, but instead, it’s about the sum of the experience.

What do you make of Bastian’s inflight connectivity comments?
