#6094. 45-Minute Immigration Queues & $25 Airport Meals: My Experience Flying Through Vietnam's Overcrowded Airport

Vietnam's Ho Chi Minh International Airport (officially Tan Son Nhat International Airport) is the airport serving Ho Chi Minh City (Saigon) and southern Vietnam. Its passenger volume has grown to the point where it is considerably over capacity, and the international terminal is struggling.

I have lived in Vietnam (a few minutes' drive from the airport) for more than two years, and I regularly fly through it on both international and domestic flights. My gym offers a view of aircraft taking off and landing. For me, the convenient proximity of the airport is worth much more than the modernity of the soon-to-open Long Thanh International Airport located well outside the city.

However, the airport is over capacity and cannot accommodate future growth. The existing terminal was built to handle 8-10 million passengers a year and was expanded to 13 million a year in 2018. Currently, the terminal is handling 18+ million passengers annually. The new airport being constructed (expected to open at the end of 2026 or early 2027) is to complement, but not entirely replace, Tan Son Nhat International Airport.

Terminal 2 is the international terminal. Domestic services use Terminal 1 and Terminal 3 (more on them below). From my experience, Terminal 2 has enough boarding gates to serve its international flights, although the low-cost airline, VietJet, uses airport shuttle buses. Overall, the terminal is old, somewhat cramped, and run-down.

Meanwhile, many of its vendors feel more like ad hoc street vendors than modern international airport vendors. I have seen the check-in queues for VietJet wrap around much of the area with wait times of at least an hour. Sometimes VietJet's queues are modest, but they are highly variable. Those flying with VietJet should arrive at the airport sooner.

The check-in queues for other airlines are generally fine, with VietJet being a major outlier. Besides VietJet, the airport's major bottleneck is immigration (emigration). As a rule of thumb, the queues for checking in for Vietnam Airlines, AirAsia, and international flag carriers are modest or otherwise acceptable.

After immigration, the queues for security are relatively better, but it can still take another 15 minutes. Altogether, I consider the terminal to be old, prone to significant queues at immigration, strained, but also perfectly functional. Even under strain, with a single runway, the terminal operates smoothly, and flights are not normally delayed.

Once past immigration, prices are listed in US dollars, and everything feels overpriced relative to the state of the terminal and the presentation of the vendors. It is common to see the same Vietnamese noodle soup (Pho) that costs the equivalent of $3 outside the airport cost around $25 inside it.

I'm anticipating that the vendors will be one of the biggest changes at the upcoming Long Thanh International Airport. Most of the vendors sell Vietnamese souvenirs such as traditional conical hats, figurines, Vietnamese coffee, and Vietnamese chocolate. The airport does have a duty-free section, but it is relatively limited.

Capacity and forecasts of HCMC's twin airports (per Tuoi Tre News)

50 million (combined terminals, current, to be expanded)

44.5 million passengers (mostly international)

77.5 million passengers (mostly international)

Separately, when arriving, there is also a relatively modest duty-free section at the baggage reclaim area. The waiting area of the airport is functional, but dated and limited in options. There are dining options offering a selection of Western and Vietnamese food, some lounges, and cafes.

One upshot is that the terminal's windows and main dining area have excellent views of the runway and airplane operations. Many of the stock photos used by Simple Flying's articles are from Shutterstock, and a meaningful percentage of these were taken by plane spotters at Tan Son Nhat International Airport​​​​.

All of these routes are flown by just one airline.

Generally, all the immigration and emigration booths are manned all the time. I have never had any issues with immigration, nor have I seen other passengers having issues. That said, I did talk to one Azeri father of several children who said he shouted at the Vietnamese immigration officers until his voice was hoarse.

As I recall, his distress was due to immigration refusing entry to his daughter on account of a spelling error on her visa. They eventually let her through. I have passed through Vietnamese land and air checkpoints dozens of times with no issues. The queue for emigration is commonly 45 minutes. This can be less, but it can also be more, with queues lasting an hour.

There are some e-Gates, but generally no one, apart from flight crew, seems to use them. I understand there is a fee to use them, but I'm not exactly sure. Unlike most countries, Vietnamese immigration and emigration at this airport do not have separate lines for citizens and foreigners. Having dual nationality, I can choose to visit Vietnam on a British or New Zealand passport.

Vietnam is visa-free for British citizens and most of Europe. US, NZ, Australia, and most others can get a straightforward 90-day eVisa. As a note of caution, there are many third-party websites online offering Vietnamese eVisas. Sometimes these can be faster than going through the official site, but it is important to remember these are not official sites. Bring a printed copy of the eVisa.

Vietnam now requires visitors to fill out the online arrival card. The queues at immigration are around the same as those at emigration. It routinely takes around 45 minutes to get through immigration, with 20 minutes being impressive. An hour is common, depending on how many flights have arrived. All the booths are typically staffed. Arriving passengers can purchase a hassle-free local SIM card before immigration or after customs.

After immigration and collecting baggage is customs. As of the time of writing, Vietnam does not require a customs declaration form, and it's somewhat random as to whether arrivals need to go through the queue to scan baggage or just walk through the Nothing to Declare line. Plenty of taxis are waiting outside customs. Passengers can book a taxi, or go by e-hailing (Grab is popular).

There are also currency exchange booths for those wanting Vietnamese Dong. In my experience, Vietnam's ACB bank has the lowest cash withdrawal fees: for me, it's the only bank I've found that is free for international withdrawals. Taxis typically need to be paid in cash (or QR code for those with a Vietnamese bank). The e-hailing app Grab accepts international credit cards, but others may not.

VietJet commands over 40% of Vietnam's domestic market, making it more or less equal to Vietnam Airlines.

The airport has two domestic terminals. Vietnam's low-cost carrier, VietJet, uses the old Terminal 1, while the flag carrier, Vietnam Airlines, has moved operations to the recently opened Terminal 2 (along with Bamboo Airways, Pacific Airlines, Vasco, Sun PhuQuoc Airways). This has freed up capacity in Terminal 1.

When I've flown through Terminal 1, VietJet was not making use of the extra capacity and check-in counters, meaning queues were as long and frustrating as ever, with terminal capacity idle. Some of the terminal's security capacity was also not in use, resulting in more queues.

Terminal 3 is the opposite. It is a modern, gleaming new terminal with plenty of capacity, bright lighting, large windows, and modern vendors. Vietnam is considering plans to continue to expand and upgrade the terminal with more technology. The security check is rapid, and checking in is straightforward.

Getting between the three terminals is a short five-minute, mostly covered walk between Terminal 2 (the international terminal) and Terminal 1 (VietJet's domestic terminal). However, Terminal 3 is isolated and cannot be reached on foot or within the airport itself. There is a free airport shuttle connecting them, or passengers can take taxis.

The routes taken are through dense parts of the city and take around 10–15 minutes. Vietnam is currently considering building a tunnel to connect the two domestic terminals. Passengers flying with VietJet should plan for more time at check-in and security than those flying with Vietnam Airlines.

Ho Chi Minh City is soon to join other megacities in operating a two-airport system: Mumbai and Bangkok are other notable Asian examples of such cities. When the new airport, Long Thanh International Airport, opens, it will take over long-haul international operations. However, the old airport will continue operating as a domestic and regional international airport.

Vietnam Airlines has its new terminal for domestic flights, and there are renovation plans for VietJet's rundown domestic terminal. Proposals will see Terminal 1 demolished and rebuilt, as well as the international terminal upgraded and Terminal 3 progressively expanded. Several rail and road links are being built or expanded to connect the two Ho Chi Minh City airports.

Work is underway to build the Thu Thiem – Long Thanh Railway to the new airport. Construction started in July 2026. Thu Thiem is still a considerable distance across the densest parts of the city, so it will improve connectivity, but not directly connect the airports. Meanwhile, future metro lines are expected to reach the original airport in the future. Authorities are discussing a direct highway link, but that is in the early planning stages.

​​​​​​​Until then, the connection between the airports will likely be an issue. Tan Son Nhat is expected to remain a regional international airport, mostly for Southeast Asia destinations. Overall, its traffic is expected to increase to around 40 million annually by 2030, with domestic passengers accounting for around 75% of the total. By that time, Long Thanh should be handling around 45 million passengers annually.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

You'll need a valid passport to enter the Cayman Islands. U.S. citizens do not need a visa for stays of up to 30 days, though you'll receive a tourist entry stamp on arrival. Make sure your passport is valid for at least 6 months beyond your travel dates to be safe.

Yes, many restaurants automatically add a 15% gratuity to your bill, so check before tipping on top of that for exceptional service. Cash tips are fine, but many places also take cards.

English is the official language and is widely spoken everywhere you'll go as a visitor. You won't need a translation app.

Grand Cayman is compact and manageable by taxi, rental car, or ride-sharing services. Taxis are metered and reliable; rides typically start at  $8–15, depending on distance. If you rent a car, remember to drive on the left side of the road. Uber does not operate here, but other services are available.

The Cayman Islands are generally safe for tourists, with a strong police presence and low rates of violent crime. Standard travel precautions apply: don't leave valuables unattended, be aware of your surroundings at night, and keep a copy of your important documents separate from the originals.

November through April offers the best weather, warm and comfortable. In peak season, expect higher prices and more crowds. May through October is hurricane season, so be aware that even though direct hits are rare. If you're flexible, September and October can offer lower rates and fewer tourists, with the tradeoff of higher humidity and occasional afternoon storms.

Top-tier resorts, nature excursions and seven-mile stretches of clear water — there's much worth experiencing when visiting the Cayman Islands.

The Cayman Islands’ luxury boom in hotels, restaurants and experiences made it an easy pick for our 2027 Where to Go list. But building the right itinerary can be a challenge when there’s so much to enjoy — especially when you're trying to maximize your point earnings and fit everything into a long weekend.

What really makes the Cayman Islands work as a points destination is how every part of your trip, from flights and hotels to dining and activities, can help you earn.

That's why TPG and Chase are teaming up to bring travelers everything they need to know to make the most of their trip to the Cayman Islands. Planning and earning are easier with the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees), thanks to its recently refreshed benefits, including the annual $100 Chase Travel℠ Hotel Credit, a statement credit of up to $120 back every four years for a TSA PreCheck®, Global Entry or Nexus application fee charged to the card. Cardmembers also enjoy long-standing benefits, including no foreign transaction fees and a comprehensive suite of built-in travel protections.

Here's how I spent four unforgettable days on the islands, and how you can use your Chase Sapphire Preferred card to do the same.

Getting to the Cayman Islands is easy, as there are plenty of nonstop flight options to Owen Roberts International Airport (GCM) year-round from major U.S. hubs, including:

All three airlines are Chase transfer partners, meaning you can book through the Chase Travel or transfer points to any of these airline loyalty programs.

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Getting to and from the airport is one of my favorite ways to earn some extra points on a trip. With the Chase Sapphire Preferred, you can earn 5 points per dollar on Lyft* if you opt for a ride, or 3 points per dollar on gas station purchases and EV charging if you decide to drive yourself, as I did.

Either way, don't forget that your Chase Sapphire Preferred card offers a statement credit of up to $120 every four years toward a Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or Nexus application fee. If you choose Global Entry, membership also includes TSA PreCheck, making it easier to breeze through airport security.

Once you land in Grand Cayman, you will need to take a taxi or book private transportation to your resort. Hotels, resorts and condo properties are not permitted to offer complimentary or in-house airport shuttle services to arriving and departing guests to protect the local taxi and licensed public transit trade. When exiting the airport, simply locate the taxi stand directly outside the main arrivals greeting area for a ride to your hotel.

The best part of staying in Grand Cayman is that the island has no shortage of luxury hotel options in the Seven Mile Beach area, the ideal home base for island activities and excursions.

I stayed at the Kimpton Seafire Resort + Spa, which has three on-site restaurants and bars, a Forbes Five-Star spa (trust me, book the massage) and daily yoga and fitness classes overlooking the ocean. The sprawling pool connects directly to Seven Mile Beach, and the hotel regularly hosts events ranging from mixology classes to live Caribbean music, so there is always something to do.

Other TPG-recommended properties include:

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Cardmembers can book hotels through Chase Travel and receive up to $100 in statement credits each account anniversary year on eligible hotel stays. The cherry on top? After the first $100 in hotel purchases that qualify for the credit, you'll earn 5 points per dollar on additional hotel purchases made through Chase Travel with your Sapphire Preferred card.

All these recommended properties are part of a wave of luxury hotels elevating the Caribbean escape. Keep an eye out for additional resorts opening in 2027 and beyond, including the highly anticipated Grand Hyatt Grand Cayman Resort & Spa.

Once you check in and freshen up, head downstairs at Kimpton Seafire to dine at Ave. The Mediterranean-inspired menu has plenty to choose from, and I can say the local snapper ($38) and the Mediterranean orzo salad ($22) were excellent — and don’t skip the creamy mashed potatoes ($9).

The cocktails were as beautiful as the sunset you'll watch from their outdoor patio. I sipped a colorful mocktail called the Butterfly Lemonade ($12), made with butterfly pea flower, ginger, rosemary, orange, cinnamon, lemon and soda, while my husband enjoyed the Ponoma, which features Beefeater gin, Dolin dry, grapefruit and hibiscus cordial, lemon and ginger ale. It was a perfect ending to day one.

Spend day two on one of Cayman Island’s most popular and iconic excursions: a boat tour to Stingray City. The famous shallow sandbars on the North Sound sit in water that can only be described as Gatorade blue, where visitors can stand, swim and interact with dozens of friendly, wild southern stingrays. If you don’t feel like getting up close and personal with the rays, you are welcome to soak up the sun and enjoy the views from the boat.

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Activities and tours booked through Chase Travel, such as a boat excursion to Stingray City, earn 5 points per dollar when you pay with your Preferred Card.

For a rooftop sunset dinner, make a reservation at Pom Pom at the neighboring Hotel Indigo, where you can enjoy Caribbean small plates and cocktails with some of the best views Grand Cayman has to offer. Since Hotel Indigo and the Kimpton Seafire are IHG sister properties, you can just take a quick three-minute golf cart ride to get there, no taxi required.

After a long day in the sun, I sipped on the Raspberry & Chicha Tereré ($13), an alcohol-free refresher that blends yerba mate, raspberry, and purple corn. For food, our server recommended the Picanha ($39), a 10-oz. sirloin cap with a Brazilian vinaigrette and lava salt, and Pollo Anticuchos ($30), chicken skewers with Peruvian chilies puré and chimichurri that had a little kick without being too spicy. For dessert, do not skip the Quatro Leches ($15) cake; it was sweet, light and absolutely delicious. Needless to say, it was one of my favorite meals of the whole trip.

Wake up bright and early and take a taxi to Cayman Crystal Caves, an underground cave system that's part geology lesson, part adventure, and it’s safe for all ages. The caves are accessible through guided tours that last about an hour and a half, and take you through chambers filled with stalactites and stalagmites that formed over millennia.

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Transportation expenses such as taxi rides can earn 2 points per dollar with the Chase Sapphire Preferred card, helping you earn bonus points even when you're exploring beyond your hotel or resort.

If you have time, visit the Queen Elizabeth II Botanical Gardens before heading back to the resort. It has 65 acres of maintained grounds with orchid gardens and woodland trails. You'll wind through native plant collections, endemic species and tropical pathways, home to endangered Grand Cayman Blue Iguanas and other Caribbean-native animals. I’d budget about 90 minutes to wander.

For sunset dinner on the beach, head over to Bonny Moon Beach Club. It’s a two-minute walk from the Kimpton, and the restaurant offers seating under their outdoor canopy or directly on the sand. You can’t go wrong with anything on the menu either: flatbreads, ceviches and hummus will all make for delicious accompaniments to another perfect view of the sun setting over the water.

After a few days full of adventure and sightseeing, I prefer to slow it down on my last full day with a little R&R, and that, of course, includes a trip to the spa. Book a morning treatment at The Spa at Seafire, as I did, and enjoy the Artisan’s Touch massage ($250) or a facial that incorporates locally inspired ingredients and techniques to really lean into the Caribbean vibes. (Ask for Donna if she is available!)

And of course, take advantage of the included amenities, such as the spa garden, steam room, cold plunge and hot tub.

In the afternoon, take it easy with a poolside lunch, then head on over to the beach to unwind on a lounger and go for a calming swim in the Caribbean's clear waters.

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: One of my favorite multipliers on the card focuses on dining. You’ll earn 3 points per dollar on dining, whether it’s happy hour at Tillie's or breakfast at Ave.

For your final night, make your last dinner count at Cocoloba. The beachfront Mexican-inspired restaurant is elevated enough to feel like a celebration, but since it's located at the Kimpton Seafire, you can enjoy the meal and easily head back up to your room to pack and get proper rest before your flight home the next day.

After four days spent swimming with stingrays, exploring underground crystal caves and enjoying the Caribbean, leaving was definitely the hardest part. Thankfully, my Chase Sapphire Preferred card helped make the trip home easier. The card's application fee credit for Global Entry helped cover the cost of enrollment, and the program's expedited arrival process meant minimal wait times when we landed. Instead of standing in long lines, we had extra time to enjoy our layover before the final leg of our journey.

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Back home, my grocery delivery was waiting for me. The Chase Sapphire Preferred can earn 3 points per dollar on online grocery purchases to help make the reset from vacation a little easier.

The growing number of hotels bookable with points in the Cayman Islands means your points stretch further when you visit. Plus, when you're making the most of everything the islands have to offer, the Chase Sapphire Preferred card makes it easy to earn along the way so you can easily redeem when you’re ready to come back and visit again.

*Valid through Sept. 30, 2027; does not apply to Wait & Save, bike or scooter rides; activation required.

#6091. An Airline You’ve Never Heard Of Will Fly From Seoul Incheon To Los Angeles

A very small international airline plans to add long haul, international flights to the United States as of next spring, and I feel pretty confident in saying that 99% of people have never heard of this airline (I had to look it up after seeing one of their planes at an airport several weeks back, and I know a thing or two about identifying airplanes). 😉

As reported by AeroRoutes, as of May 1, 2027, Parata Air will launch daily nonstop flights between Seoul Incheon (ICN) and Los Angeles (LAX). The flight will operate with the following schedule:

WE301 Incheon to Los Angeles departing 12:00PM arriving 7:20AMWE302 Los Angeles to Incheon departing 9:50AM arriving 3:20PM (+1 days)

Parata Air will operate the route with an Airbus A330-200, featuring 260 seats, including 18 business class seats and 242 economy seats. The 5,944-mile flight is blocked at 11hr40min eastbound and 13hr30min westbound.

Tickets on the flight are now on sale, and I see fares starting at around $670 one-way in economy, and around $2,500 one-way in business class. Those aren’t exactly terribly attractive fares for a newcomer that appears to have a pretty lackluster onboard product.

For those not familiar with Parata Air, the airline launched operations back in 2019, but it has a fleet of just a handful of planes, including three Airbus A330s and two Airbus A320s. This will be the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. As I hinted at in the headline, I imagine this is a fully unknown player to most people, and I had never heard of the airline until a few weeks ago.

Random thought — can anyone think of a smaller international airline (in terms of fleet size) that added long haul flights to the United States? I know that’s very specific, but I can’t think of another one… it’s possible I’m missing something, though!

The airline acquired its three A330s secondhand from different sources, with the planes having flown for Garuda Indonesia, Hainan Airlines, and Thomas Cook (though that plane doesn’t have business class).

The Seoul Incheon to Los Angeles market is pretty well served in terms of capacity, but not so well served in terms of competition. That’s because no US carrier flies between Los Angeles and Seoul Incheon, and with Korean Air having acquired Asiana, there’s now only one South Korean flag carrier.

If you look at the market, you’ll see that Korean Air operates up to four daily flights, and Air Premia operates up to two daily flights. Now we’ll see a third airline from the country operating in the market, though with the lowest capacity, and arguably the worst product.

It’ll be interesting to see when we see some competition here on the US side. Delta might operate the route eventually, but that doesn’t actually increase competition, since the airline has a joint venture with Korean Air. American has (smartly, probably) given up on Los Angeles as a long haul hub. So that leaves United, and I could definitely see the airline eventually adding service in the market, as a competitive response against Delta and Korean Air, if nothing else.

As of May 2027, Parata Air will be launching a new nonstop route between Seoul Incheon and Los Angeles, representing the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. The airline will be operating daily in the market with Airbus A330s. With this, there will be three South Korean carriers flying this route, though no airlines from the United States.

What do you make of this new Parata Air service?

#6090. Delta SkyMiles Blue Amex Review: Is The No Annual Fee Card Worth It?

American Express and Delta have had a close relationship for many years, and as part of that, they issue seven co-branded Delta Amex cards. This is my in-depth Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card review, as this is the entry-level personal Delta credit card with no annual fee (Rates & Fees), and probably the least talked about card in the lineup. It’s far from the most rewarding Delta credit card, but if you want to earn Delta miles and only fly the airline occasionally, it could be worth a look.

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card

Before I get into the full Delta Blue Amex Card review, here’s an overview of the card’s main features, from its welcome bonus and earning rates, to other benefits:

Beyond that, here are my thoughts on the pros and cons of the Delta Blue Amex:

When applying for a credit card, the welcome bonus, eligibility rules, and fees, are obviously major factors that people consider. With that in mind, let’s take a look at those details for the Delta Blue Amex Card. As you’d expect for this card, the lack of fees largely comes at expense of a smaller welcome offer.

The Blue Delta SkyMiles Amex has a welcome offer of 10,000 bonus SkyMiles after spending $1,000 within the first six months of your card membership. Based on my latest points & miles valuations, Delta SkyMiles are worth 1.1 cents each, making this bonus worth $110. We’ve seen this card’s bonus go a bit higher, but not by a huge amount.

The bonuses on all other Delta Amex cards are significantly higher, which isn’t a surprise, since cards with annual fees often have better bonuses than cards without annual fees. It’s hard to get excited about that offer, but I guess something is better than nothing?

The welcome offer on the Delta Blue Amex Card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available to you if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past. The rules go beyond that, though.

You’re actually not eligible for the bonus on the card if you have or have had any of the more premium versions of the Delta Amex card portfolio, at least among the personal cards. This is true across the portfolio, and the idea is that you’re always eligible for the bonus on a more premium card, but not eligible for the bonus on a less premium card.

So if you do want to pick up multiple Delta Amex cards, you’ll want to first apply for the Delta Blue Amex, then the Delta Gold Amex, then the Delta Platinum Amex, and then the Delta Reserve Amex (or at least you’ll want to move in that general order).

Beyond that, Amex’s general card application restrictions apply, including that you can typically have at most five credit cards from Amex at a time (that doesn’t include hybrid cards).

Let me emphasize once again that the Blue Delta Amex has no annual fee. It’s great to see a trend whereby we’re seeing more airline credit cards with no annual fees, since it’s a nice option for someone who wants a co-branded credit card, but doesn’t want to pay an annual fee.

You can also add additional users to the card at no extra cost.

There’s no doubt that card issuers are moving toward offering more no annual fee cards with no foreign transaction fees, though it’s still not the standard. The Blue Delta Amex has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), which is awesome, since most Amex no annual fee cards do still have these fees.

When it comes to earning rewards, the Blue Delta SkyMiles Credit Card offers:

For a no annual fee product, it’s nice to see a card offering a bonus on dining. While some bonus categories are better than none, I don’t find the bonuses to be particularly compelling, as there are still better cards out there for airfare purchases and restaurant purchases.

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles. You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on Delta or on Delta’s SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles. I’ve also seen some good award prices for Delta One (business class) awards, specifically for booking roundtrip rather than one way.

The Delta Blue Amex is a decent no annual fee card in the sense that it offers 2x miles at restaurants and has no foreign transaction fees, but how are the perks on the card? Not surprisingly, this is an area where the card lags, and where the cards with annual fees offer significantly more value.

Nonetheless, there are some perks to the card that may prove valuable to the occasional Delta flyer.

If you have the Blue Delta Amex, then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible pre-purchased meals, and in-flight purchases of food or alcoholic beverages, on Delta flights. Allow 8-12 weeks for the statement credit to post.

Having the Blue Delta Amex makes you eligible for the Delta Pay With Miles program. What is that? This allows those with co-branded Delta Amex cards to redeem miles for one cent each towards a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles towards flights, and then they still earn elite miles for taking those flights.

In other words, the 10,000 miles available as part of the welcome offer can be redeemed for a minimum of $100 worth of travel on Delta. This is obviously the lowest cost option for unlocking that benefit.

The Delta Blue Amex includes access to dedicated entrance lanes and fast lanes at stadiums and arenas that participate in the Amex Venue Collection program. As part of this benefit, you can also get 10% back on qualifying concessions purchases, up to $250 back per calendar year. (Enrollment required)

Amex Offers is a program that offers discounts for purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards.

The ideal situation is to have a no annual fee card (like this one), so you can get access to these offers without paying an annual fee to get access to this.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page.

The Delta Blue Amex comes with some basic travel and purchase protection benefits:

There are some coverage limits and exclusions to be aware of, so you’ll want to review the full details in the card’s benefits guide before assuming you’re insured.

Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

Many people who like Delta as a brand may be tempted to pick up the Delta Blue Amex — it allows you to earn miles with Delta, it has no annual fee, and it offers some perks that could add value (20% off inflight purchases, Amex Offers, access to Delta Pay With Miles, etc.).

However, in general, I wouldn’t recommend outright applying for this card:

Let me address both of those points below.

If you’re considering the Delta SkyMiles Blue Amex, let me make the case for applying for the Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (learn more) instead, which currently has the limited-time offer:

You can always get the Gold Delta Amex, and then if you don’t find it to be worth the annual fee, you can downgrade it to the Blue Delta Amex after a year. That would allow you to maintain the card account, and you wouldn’t pay the annual fee when you downgrade (and you’d still get the elevated perks and bigger bonus for the first year).

At a minimum, it really is worth trying the Delta Gold Amex to see if you like it and to take advantage of the better bonus, and then you can downgrade at a later point if you find it’s not worthwhile.

If you are looking to earn Delta SkyMiles through credit card spending then consider using a card earning Amex Membership Rewards points. That’s because these points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles at a 1:1 ratio, and you can in many cases earn points at a much faster rate.

For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers 4x points at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year and then 1x) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25,000 in purchases per calendar year and then 1x), and 3x points on flights booked directly with airlines or at AmexTravel.com. That’s a much better return than you’ll get on this card, and it’s also quite easy to make the math on the card work.

If you’re absolutely committed to having a no annual fee card and want to maximize your return on spending, there are lots of excellent no annual fee cards to consider.

My favorite is the Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more). The card earns 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase (in the form of ThankYou points).

But it gets even better than that — rewards earned on this card can be converted into ThankYou points at a 1:1 ratio and can be moved to partner programs at the best possible ratio, assuming you have the card in conjunction with one earning premium ThankYou points, like the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more).

That means the card earns two ThankYou points per dollar, and I value those points at 1.7 cents each, so that’s like a 3.4% return on everyday spending.

I appreciate that American Express and Delta offer a no annual fee option with the Delta Blue Amex. For someone absolutely committed to getting a Delta Amex Card and not paying an annual fee, this is the best/only option.

The card has no foreign transaction fees, offers 2x miles on dining, and gives you access to Pay With Miles and 20% discounts on inflight purchases.

However, for most people, I think it’s worth applying for the Delta Gold Amex. The card has a lot more perks and a much better bonus, and you can always downgrade the card to the Delta Blue Amex after at least a year.

#6089. Former Washington Rep. Jim McDermott dies at 89

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family announced.

In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

“Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”

When McDermott announced his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”

Born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

He attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against new sanctions on Iran.

Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a new life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

“I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”

As he said, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

Then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

“The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he said in a statement at the time.

McDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

“Jim McDermott was as big as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”

#6088. 17 Aircraft Spotted In GTA 6’s Trailers, From Boeing 747s To Biplanes

13 years after the launch of its predecessor, Grand Theft Auto VI is launching on November 19, with the title going down in history as one of the most eagerly awaited video games of all time. Rockstar's open-world extravaganza is set in a fictionalized version of the US state of Florida, and, since the first trailers for the game dropped, eagle-eyed fans have been trying to find out whatever small details they can.

For an avgeek, one of the most interesting aspects of the trailers is the wide range of aircraft on show. Planes and helicopters have long played a key role in video games in the Grand Theft Auto series, with some even able to be flown by players: who could forget the near-impossible challenge of stealing a fighter jet in GTA V!? Across the trailers, there are 17 aircraft sightings (including some duplicates).

Based on what is seen in the trailers, GTA VI looks set to include an interesting range of fixed-wing jets. On the airliner side of things, GTA Base highlights the fact that a double-decker quadjet that is clearly based on the Boeing 747-400 and/or 747-8 can be seen. This is listed by the site as being simply known as 'Jet' in the game's files. A separate clip shows an unidentified large airliner or freighter during a heist.

Private jets, however, are more detailed and numerous. GTA Base notes that the game will feature three 'Buckingham' private jets: the Luxor, the Shamal (both based on the Learjet 45), and the Nimbus (based on the Cessna Citation X). Regardless of (or perhaps thanks to) its aviation diversity, GTA VI already tops Metacritic's 'best games of all time list' on a score of 99, with a Vice review saying that:

"Grand Theft Auto VI was worth waiting 13 years for, and will no doubt be one of the most influential games over the next decade."

There is also a considerable degree of diversity when it comes to the light aircraft and floatplanes that are visible in GTA VI's trailers. Once again, these are fictionalized versions of the aircraft rather than the real thing, but they draw inspiration from the kinds of aircraft that can be seen in Florida today. As seen above, one is a floatplane with similar proportions to the Cessna Caravan or De Havilland DHC-3 Otter.

Another trailer shows a floatplane that is reminiscent of the De Havilland DHC-2 Beaver. This is known in the game, per GTA Base, as the Mammoth Dodo. In terms of wheeled planes, a light aircraft that is reminiscent of the Cessna 173 Skyhawk is also briefly visible in the trailers, with GTA Base noting that this is known in the game as the JoBuilt Mammatus. A banner-towing plane also overflies the beach.

The latter of these is a classic aviation scene in Florida (and, indeed, coastal cities in the US more generally). Similarly, a wingwalker can be seen on a biplane that is known in the game as the Western Duster, but seems to be derived from the real-life Stearman Model 75. GTA Base also highlights the Western Mallard (based on the Extra EA-300) and the Mammoth Streamer 216 (based on the DHC-6 Twin Otter).

The lounge also has options for food and beverages.

Alongside the classic blimp, based on the Goodyear Aerospace GZ-20, several helicopters can also be seen in GTA VI's trailers. As seen above, one is reminiscent of an MD 500 or OH-6 'Little Bird.' Elsewhere, Airbus AS350 and Bell 206-type light helicopters are also visible, as well as one that looks like an Airbus EC135 or Bo 105 with twin skids. There are also the classic generic police-style helicopters.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

With earlier video games in the Grand Theft Auto series having also had flyable aircraft, avgeeks and gamers alike certainly have a lot to look forward to on this front. There are likely more to be discovered, as we haven't even scratched the surface on the 27-minute 'Extended Look' video. Either way, as GTA VI goes live on November 19, it's fair to say that, in the skies and on the ground, it promises a lot.

#6087. Surprise: Aer Lingus Unveils First-Ever Premium Economy, Coming To 10 A330s

Aer Lingus is getting on the premium economy hype. The Irish flag carrier has today announced it will introduce the cabin for the first time on 10 of its Airbus A330s, which will also feature new business and economy cabins (the product won’t be coming to the Airbus A321LR/XLR fleet).

This is quite a big change, and one that should give it a leg up in the highly competitive trans-Atlantic market.

The cabin will feature just four rows with 28 seats in a 2-3-2 configuration. That’s about average when compared to other premium economy cabins. The narrow fuselage of the A330 means there’s only room for three seats in the middle section, rather than the four many other airlines offer.

As for the soft product, Aer Lingus promises three-course dining, drinks throughout the flight, a pillow and blanket, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing (not noise-canceling) headphones.

I actually really like the design and color scheme. It’s modern, looks elegant and premium, and most importantly of all for the airline of the Emerald Isle, the colors are quintessentially Irish.

Aer Lingus says premium economy fares will start from 700 Euros one-way, putting a return trip at around 1,400 Euros. That works out to around $1,534, and a few hundred dollars cheaper than United’s nonstop fares from Newark (EWR) to Dublin (DUB).

We’ll have to wait until October 1 next year to try Aer Lingus’ new premium economy out for ourselves. The airline hasn’t yet announced which routes will get the product first, but we should find out in the coming months.

The good news is, they’ll operate on many of the airline’s 18 nonstop routes from Dublin to the United States.

As a small, almost boutique-style airline with just 63 aircraft, Aer Lingus must remain competitive, especially in the saturated transatlantic market in which it predominantly operates. The addition of premium economy bridges the large gap between economy and business, and should open the airline up to a potential new customer base who’ve never flown it before.

I’ll be attending an event in Dublin tonight, so I should be back with more images and extra info soon!

What do you make of Aer Lingus’ new premium economy?

#6086. Barry Goldwater Saw a Way Out of the Wilderness

No matter how federal elections turn out, there’s always work to be done at the state and local levels.

Senator Barry Goldwater addresses supporters in Arizona during his 1964 presidential campaign.

Hulton-Deutsch Collection/Corbis via Getty Images

Barry Goldwater was acquainted with political setbacks. The morning after the 1964 presidential election, he could count the states he had won on two hands. Harder to number were the Americans who had spent that fall knocking on doors for the first time because a senator from Arizona had given voice to something they believed. Goldwater had asked them to help Americans reclaim power from Washington.

After the loss, Goldwater urged his supporters not to give up the fight for free markets, smaller government, and the American family. It was the collective conviction that Americans could build better lives for their families if they could keep more of what they earned and decide for themselves how to raise their children that kept these people invested in American politics.

#6085. Aer Lingus Retrofitting A330s With New Business, Premium Economy, Economy Cabins

It’s not just Aer Lingus’ premium economy stealing the headlines in Ireland today. Expected to fly passengers for the first time on October 1, 2027, the new cabins are part of a comprehensive Airbus A330 tip-to-tail retrofit that will include new business and economy cabins. We covered the premium economy cabin in a separate article story.

The same 10 Airbus A330s that will get the airline’s new premium economy will also get a swanky new business class. The airline’s Airbus A321XLRs aren’t included in this cabin update.

Aer Lingus opted for its take on the ever-popular Collins Elevation suite. There’ll be 28 seats in a 1-2-1 configuration that stretch out to 78 inches long when in lie-flat mode.

The color palette of Irish greens, whites, and light wood gives the seat an elegant yet distinctly non-corporate feel. It’s a thumbs-up from me.

In terms of updated tech, each seat has 4K HD screens (in all cabins) as well as wireless and USB-C charging. While nothing revolutionary, these touches will significantly modernize Aer Lingus A330 cabins.

Aer Lingus is also introducing a self-service bar stocked with snacks and drinks. I wonder if this will include Champagne…

The airline will also serve up a whole new in-flight dining experience featuring dishes inspired by both Irish ingredients and its transatlantic destinations.

It wouldn’t be a full retrofit without sprucing up economy.

Per the renderings, Aer Lingus has done a great job again with the cabin’s look and feel. The emerald green Shamrocks are a lovely touch.

Seats are configured in the A330’s classic 2-4-2 configuration — a favorite for those traveling in pairs.

While the recline looks a bit modest here, the seat’s thickness looks like it’ll provide more support than some of those ultra-thin, rigid seats airlines are sneaking in these days.

The six-way adjustable headrests should also mean less head-wobbling when catching some shut-eye.

The curved design of the seat backs should hopefully mean noticeably more knee space.

Aer Lingus is also upping its food and beverage ante for economy passengers. In addition to a snack bar, a new mid-flight snack will be offered.

A retrofit program like this was essential for Aer Lingus to remain competitive in the transatlantic market. The introduction of premium economy was a great move, especially since the cabin is known to be highly profitable.

Aer Lingus has also done a great job of matching the Irish color scheme and sleek design across all cabins, which is more than can be said for some airlines these days. 😉

What do you make of Aer Lingus’ new A330 cabins?

American citizens do not need a visa to visit Tunisia for stays of 90 days or less, just a valid passport with at least six months’ validity and one blank page.

Tipping is appreciated but not expected, unlike in many neighboring countries such as Egypt. I generally added 10% to restaurant bills and rounded up taxi fares. For my tours, I tipped between 20 and 50 dinars, depending on the length and whether there was a separate driver.

Tunisia is essentially bilingual, with most people speaking Arabic and French fluently. In most tourist destinations and hotels, people spoke English, but the French I remembered from high school did help me in a few situations.

Ride-hailing apps like Uber are not available in Tunisia. Taxis are available, but ask for the fare upfront or confirm the meter is turned on before getting in. I pre-booked airport transfers through my hotels to avoid negotiating prices on the spot.

For my road trip, I found it easy to rent and drive a car throughout Tunisia. There is a major highway with toll booths running north to south through the country. In more rural parts of the south, roads are still well maintained — just watch out for sneaky speed bumps. All my hotels featured easy parking, but keep in mind that hotels inside medinas may not be accessible by car or might require navigating very narrow streets. Driving behavior is more erratic in Tunis, but generally, I found the rest of the country easy to drive in.

To visit mosques, you’ll need to cover your knees and shoulders — as well as hair if you’re a woman — but coverings are provided free of charge at most. To adapt to the heat and sun, wear loose layers of light-colored linen and be sure to bring a hat.

The U.S. Department of State lists Tunisia as a Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution, which contains areas with a higher security risk, the same as Turkey and Egypt. Save for a few curious stares from men and one overzealous self-appointed medina guide who demanded a tip, I felt perfectly safe as a solo female traveler. It is best to avoid wandering around medinas after dark since most shops and restaurants are closed anyway. I felt most comfortable with pre-arranged guides, but more because they knew exactly where to go, and I didn’t have to navigate things solo.

For the most comfortable weather with a low chance of rain, visit Tunisia between March and May or between October and November. If you do decide to visit for the Aug. 2, 2027 solar eclipse, keep in mind it can get up to 120 degrees Fahrenheit in the middle of the day out in the desert. During my visit in August, I also experienced rolling blackouts and bottled water shortages.

Tunisia is about to have a big year. On the morning of Aug. 2, 2027, a total solar eclipse will cut a path across the central part of the North African nation, bringing several minutes of darkness to sites like the ancient Roman amphitheater in El Jem, the Great Mosque of Kairouan and the dramatic Sahara Desert dunes and canyons surrounding Tozeur.

The latter will also draw “Star Wars” fans to many of the Tatooine filming locations to mark the franchise’s 50th anniversary of the movie’s release in 2027. The capital of Tunis isn’t in the path of totality, but any trip in 2027 should also include a stop in the picturesque cliffside village of Sidi Bou Said, which UNESCO recently added to its World Heritage list, joining other culturally significant sites like the Medina of Tunis and the Archaeological Site of Carthage.

This 7-day itinerary covers a tour of Tunisia’s most important cultural and historic landmarks in a road trip from Tunis to Tozeur and back, plus tips for where to be during the 2027 eclipse and how to maximize the perks and benefits of the Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees) along the way.

Currently, there are no nonstop flights between the United States and Tunisia, so you’ll need to plan for at least one layover before connecting to Tunis-Carthage International Airport (TUN), the country’s largest airport.

I flew to TUN on Air France via Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), since I’m loyal to the SkyTeam alliance and it offered the most frequent connections. However, if you’re loyal to another airline alliance, you can also find connections to TUN on Lufthansa via Frankfurt, ITA via Rome, Royal Air Maroc via Casablanca and Turkish Airlines via Istanbul.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: When booking flights, check the Chase Travel℠ portal to see what routes and airlines are available to book using the Points Boost feature. I found several business-class fares offering the maximum Points Boost value of 2 cents per point. I ultimately transferred 142,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Air France-KLM Flying Blue after finding an amazing round-trip business-class fare directly on the Air France website, yielding a value of 5.83 cents per mile.

I landed in Tunis around 5 p.m. after a red-eye flight from New York and a relaxed connection in Paris.

A pre-arranged car transfer whisked me to the Four Seasons Hotel Tunis, a luxury beachfront resort in the suburb of Gammarth, about 30 minutes from the airport. Upon arrival, staff greeted me warmly and took me directly to my upgraded Deluxe Sea-View Room for an in-room check-in. The spacious room had a balcony overlooking the Mediterranean, a walk-in closet and a marble bathroom with a separate tub and a shower.

After a quick rinse, I wandered down to Blu, the hotel’s alfresco poolside restaurant, where I enjoyed a refreshing salad of a soft local cheese, tomatoes, onions and peppers served with a glass of Tunisian rosé. Since it was my first day in the country, the friendly staff made sure I tried some spicy Tunisian harissa, a smoky chili paste drizzled in olive oil that I sopped up with fluffy squares of focaccia.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Book the Four Seasons Hotel Tunis through The Edit to use one of the twice-annual, up-to-$250 credits toward prepaid hotel stays of two or more nights reserved through Chase Travel. By booking through The Edit, I also received other perks like complimentary hotel breakfast for two and up to $100 property credit, which I used for meals but could have used toward spa treatments like the ceremonial hammam experience, which comes out to approximately $100.

Since I only had one full day in Tunis, I headed out bright and early for a private tour of the capital’s major sites, booked through Chase Travel with Didon Tours. My guide, Baligh, and a private driver picked me up for a full 8-hour day that included lunch and fascinating storytelling about the city’s ancient and modern history and politics.

To beat the cruise groups and midday heat, we visited the ancient ruins of Carthage first, taking in the views from Byrsa Hill before heading down to the circular Punic port and the massive seaside complex of the Baths of Antoninus.

From there, we drove to the charming blue-and-white village of Sidi Bou Said, Tunisia’s newest UNESCO World Heritage site, for fresh juice and almond cakes at Cafe des Delices and iconic views of the beach below. While we didn’t have much time to browse the cliffside town’s shops, I did pick up some handmade souvenirs at the ceramic store at 16 Rue Habib Thameur.

For lunch, we stopped in the coastal suburb of Le Goulette at Restaurant La Victoire for a traditional Tunisian meal of brick à l’oeuf, a deep-fried pastry stuffed with egg, tuna and onion and a freshly grilled dorade fish served with rice and carrots.

Next, we turned inland toward the western side of the city to visit the Bardo Museum, set in a former palace and home to the world’s largest collection of Roman mosaics. (Don’t miss the mosaic of the Roman poet Virgil, flanked by the muses of history and tragedy, as it’s considered to be the Mona Lisa of Tunisia.)

Finally, we hit the medina of Tunis, where we visited the courtyard of the Zitouna Mosque and made a quick pass through the souk's meandering lanes before returning to the hotel for a much-deserved swim in the indoor pool and a nap before a quiet room-service dinner.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Earn 8 points per dollar spent on Chase Travel purchases, including activities and tours like the one I booked. Those with more time can add another day in Tunis and split this itinerary into two for a more relaxed pace in each location.

Around midday, I returned to the airport to pick up a rental car from Avis and set the GPS to drive two hours south to Kairouan, a UNESCO-recognized city famous for its picturesque medina and Great Mosque, which dates to the 9th century AD. While Kairouan is considered one of the holy cities of Islam, film buffs may recognize it from “Raiders of the Lost Ark,” where it stood in for 1930s Cairo. It lies along the northern boundary of the 2027 solar eclipse’s path of totality.

La Kasbah Hotel, booked via Chase Travel, provided a soft landing with its private parking lot, pool and strong air conditioning. The shops and sites in the medina tend to close in the late afternoon, so if you arrive after then, plan on a quiet night in the hotel, cooling off in the pool or lounging on woven rugs in its vintage café, drinking mint tea.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Pay for car rentals with Chase Sapphire Reserve to receive primary auto rental coverage (just be sure to decline the agency's collision insurance). Though I didn’t end up needing it, I had peace of mind knowing I was covered for up to $75,000 of theft or collision damage to the rental car.

Having arrived the previous afternoon after the mosque closed, I went first thing the next morning to admire the column-lined courtyard and three-tiered minaret before the tour groups arrived. The ticket to the mosque also included admission to the nearby Sidi Abid el Ghariani Mausoleum, built in the Moorish style with black and white marble arches. A few doors down, I stopped by the former home of the governor of Kairouan, an ornately decorated mansion that now serves as a rug shop. While I wasn’t in the market for a carpet, I enjoyed the architecture and left with a handwoven scarf for 40 dinars ($14).

After checking out, I hit the road again for the 4.5-hour drive south to Tozeur, a city in the heart of the Sahara Desert. Though I drove straight through, making brief stops at gas stations along the way, it’s also possible to break up the drive with stops at either the well-preserved archaeological site of Sbeitla or the Roman baths of Gafsa.

Just be mindful of timing: I wouldn’t recommend driving at night. Though the roads are well-maintained, speed bumps are common and harder to spot after dark.

Once in Tozeur, I checked into Dar Saida Beya, a traditional Tunisian guesthouse, booked through Chase Travel. After a long drive, I had a quiet evening to walk around and explore the nearby old town center.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Though the upscale Mora Sahara Tozeur resort west of town isn’t bookable via Chase Travel currently, it’s still possible to earn 4 points per dollar spent on direct hotel bookings made with the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

The Atlas Mountains meet the salt flats and sands of the Sahara Desert in Tozeur, creating an otherworldly landscape that inspired many film directors. Most notably, the canyons and dunes around Tozeur served as the filming location for the desert planet of Tatooine in the “Star Wars” movies. The epic sci-fi series is celebrating the 50th anniversary of its release in 2027, and fans can experience the eclipse from here, since Tozeur falls along the southern boundary of the path of totality.

I booked a 7-hour tour with Attractive Discoveries via Chase Travel to see everything the area had to offer. Before diving into the area’s cinematic legacy, my driver and guide, Firas, began the day at Chebika Oasis, where a 45-minute hike wound through the ruins of a former Berber village and down to the oasis and its waterfall.

Our next stop was the Grand Canyon of Tunisia, Mides Canyon, roughly a mile from the Algerian border and featured in films like “The English Patient.” During the 30-minute hike along the dry riverbed, I spotted no fewer than six falcons diving in and out of the cliff face while hunting.

To avoid the worst heat of the day, the tour included a break from 1 to 5 p.m., during which we stopped to pick some dates from my guide’s family’s oasis of palm trees. I also tried a makloub sandwich filled with chicken, cheese and harissa and took a short nap.

At 5 p.m. on the dot, Firas picked me up again in his 4x4 to head out into the desert to watch the sunset over the dunes. Along our drive, we spotted a herd of camels, stopped to climb the Ong Jmal or “Camel’s Neck” rock formation and did some adrenaline-inducing 4x4 driving. We arrived at the remaining film sets that served as the desert trading post of Mos Espa in “The Phantom Menace” just before sunset.

To cap off the day, we drank fresh mint tea with almonds — a local treat — and watched the sun set behind the dunes before heading back into town.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Put the card's up to $300 annual credit to work on travel purchases like the tour I booked. The credit is applied automatically to eligible purchases each account anniversary year.

The biggest Star Wars fans may want to stay another day to visit other nearby filming locations, such as Sidi Bouhlel Canyon and the Lars family homestead exterior near the town of Nefta.

Since I had another 4.5-hour drive ahead of me that day, I left around 11 a.m. to drive back north to the city of El Jem via Chott el Djerid. Before heading off across the massive salt lake, I filled up my gas tank and packed snacks for the long drive since there aren’t many places to stop in the first couple of hours.

Built about 1,800 years ago, the Roman amphitheater of El Jem is roughly 70% the size of Rome’s amphitheater but has significantly fewer crowds and offers wide-open access to each level — even the underground level where animals were kept before they fought gladiators.

After checking into Hotel Julius, booked through Chase Travel, I dropped my bags and took the five-minute walk to the amphitheater before it closed. The 20 dinar ($7) ticket includes entrance to both the amphitheater and the nearby El Jem Archaeological Museum on the same day. Since I arrived a little later in the afternoon, I went to the museum first thing the next morning and justified the extra $7 by spending a leisurely morning taking in the incredibly detailed mosaics without being rushed.

El Jem falls within the path of totality for the 2027 solar eclipse, so history buffs may want to make this city their home base for the celestial event.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Tunisia is still a predominantly cash-based society, so it may be hard to find restaurants that accept cards. I couldn’t earn 3 points per dollar spent on dining worldwide with my Chase Sapphire Reserve in El Jem, but the two fricassee (fried dough buns stuffed with egg, tuna, potato and harissa) I ordered at a street food stall on the way back from the amphitheater only cost 7 cents total (yes, really), so I wasn’t worried about missing out on too many points.

After checking out the museum, I loaded up my rental car one last time for the two-hour drive back to Tunis. Those with more time and desire to sit on the beach than I did could easily add a day or two in the coastal town of Hammamet, which sits about two-thirds of the way back to Tunis from El Jem.

Once I handed off my rental car keys at the airport, I met the taxi driver I had prearranged with my final hotel, Dar Ben Gacem, a traditional guesthouse in the Tunis medina. Since my tour of Tunis at the beginning of the trip only included a brief visit to the medina, I was glad to have the rest of the afternoon and evening to poke around the shops and alleys of the historic city center and do some final souvenir shopping before flying home the next day.

Keep in mind that most stalls in the medina are open from around 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., with more closed on Fridays and Sundays, so plan your visit accordingly. (Plus, many restaurants are closed for dinner on Sunday nights as well.)

Though some flights depart in the evening, I opted to take a connecting flight back to Paris in the morning and stay an extra night to avoid a rushed final day.

During my week-long road trip, I explored Tunisia’s ancient ruins, UNESCO-recognized Islamic architecture and otherworldly desert landscapes, many of which lie in the path of totality of the 2027 solar eclipse. Booking through Chase Travel maximized my Ultimate Rewards earnings, while the card benefits helped offset travel expenses along the way, like the $300 annual travel credit on tours, The Edit perks and $250 statement credit at the Four Seasons and primary rental car coverage through Avis. When I returned to New York, I was glad I had enrolled in Global Entry before my trip. The Sapphire Reserve's $120 Global Entry application fee statement credit helped offset the cost, and the program made reentering the U.S. much easier.

#6083. Chase Ink Business Preferred Card Bonus: 100K Points Welcome Offer

The Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card has a phenomenal sign-up bonus of 100,000 points after spending $8,000 within three first three months, and there’s lots of value to this card in the long term, especially thanks to its reasonable $95 annual fee — read my Ink Preferred review here. If you’re eligible for the card, there’s no reason not to apply.

This is part of the Chase Ink Business card portfolio, and it’s arguably Chase’s most rewarding and best value business credit card. In this post I’d like to go over the Ink Business Preferred bonus details, including eligibility requirements.

Link: Learn more about the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card with 100K bonus points

The Chase Ink Preferred Card currently has a welcome offer of 100,000 Ultimate Rewards points after spending $8,000 within the first three months.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Chase Ultimate Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each, meaning the 100,000 points are worth $1,700 to me, which is among the best bonuses out there. There are lots of great uses of Chase points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners.

Chase Ultimate Rewards partners with programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue, British Airways Club, United MileagePlus, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, World of Hyatt, and more. If you want to cash out Chase points (which I wouldn’t recommend), you can get one cent of value per point, meaning the 100,000 points would be worth $1,000.

Just to give some examples of possible uses of the points, you could transfer 34,000 points to Iberia Club for a one-way Iberia business class ticket from Boston to Madrid, or 60,000 points to Flying Blue for a one-way Air France or KLM business class ticket from Miami to Paris. You can stretch your points even further by taking advantage of transfer bonuses.

Let me emphasize that the Chase Ink Preferred 100K bonus is the best publicly available sign-up bonus that’s currently available on the card, and it has been the standard offer since November 2025. How do the previous Chase Ink Preferred offers compare, though?

As you can see, the Ink Business Preferred sign-up bonus on the card has varied from 80,000 points to 120,000 points, and the current bonus of 100,000 points is 10,000 points better than the previous offer, which was for up to 90,000 points.

Everyone has to decide for themselves if it’s worth waiting for the possibility of another welcome bonus of over 100,000 points. Personally I probably wouldn’t wait, since we have no reason to believe such an offer is returning soon. Furthermore, with the card’s useful points categories for spending, there’s potentially quite an opportunity cost to waiting. But still, if you’re in no rush, it could be worth waiting.

When it comes to getting approved for the Chase Ink Preferred Card and earning the welcome bonus, what rules should you be aware of? Well, there are the card specific policies, and then also the more generic Chase policies. When you pull up the application, you’ll see the following terms:

The new cardmember bonus may not be available to you if you have ever had this card. We may also consider factors pertinent to your business in determining your bonus eligibility.

As you can see, officially the welcome bonus may not be available to you if you currently have this card, or if you’ve had it in the past. However, eligibility for the card (including the bonus) is unrelated to whether you have any other Chase business card.

In other words, you’re eligible for this card, including the bonus, if you have other cards from Chase, including cards in the business lineup. Speaking of which, those cards have some amazing bonuses as well, which are worth considering:

Beyond that, there are some general Chase rules to be aware of:

While Chase business cards can be tough to get approved for, they offer such fantastic bonuses and perks, so it’s worth the effort, in my opinion. Furthermore, it’s nice how the eligibility requirements aren’t too strict in terms of qualifying for the bonus.

The Chase Ink Preferred Card has a $95 annual fee (with no cost for additional employee cards), and offers all kinds of amazing perks that make it worth holding onto. Among other things, here’s what makes the card so valuable:

Let me acknowledge that the Ink Preferred isn’t right for everyone. As I see it, the Ink Preferred is all about the rewards structure and the strong purchase and travel protection, while also having a reasonable cost. If you’re looking for airport lounge access or a card with all kinds of premium perks and credits, then consider the Sapphire Reserve Business, which many people will find to be worthwhile for the Chase Sapphire Lounge access, Priority Pass membership, travel credits, and more.

The Chase Ink Preferred Card is one of the best business cards out there, and if you’re eligible for the card, there’s lots of merit to applying.

Not only does the card have a big bonus, but it’s worth holding onto for the great rewards structure, excellent protection benefits, and the ability to maximize other cards in the Chase ecosystem. With the changes we’ve seen to other Chase cards in recent times, this card is arguably even more compelling than in the past.

Do you have the Chase Ink Preferred Card, and if so, what has your experience been?

#6082. Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the issues were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”

Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from new software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin said “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”

Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

“This is an emergency,” he said. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”

The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

Mullin said the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

“We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin said. "Nickel and diming it together does not work."

Thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications."

Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment."

Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

The 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

The committee’s majority said Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a new one was built.

Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications issues.

“Technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell said.

Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and said their committee would “thoroughly review the issues that led to this nationwide ground stop.”

Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

At issue in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have said they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

#6081. Democrats Have the Electoral College in Their Sights

Will the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact soon cross the 270-vote threshold?

Delegates point to an electoral map at the Democratic National Convention in Philadelphia, Pa., in 2016.

The blue wave washed over a slew of state legislative chambers and six new governorships. Next year, a majority of Americans will live in a state with a Democratic governing trifecta. One of the biggest dangers of Democrats’ new political clout is that they will now push to override the Electoral College and effectively force the country into a nationwide presidential popular voting system as early as 2028.

Their vehicle is called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their electoral votes to the winner of the national popular vote, no matter which candidate carries each state. The compact was born after former President George W. Bush’s narrow Electoral College victory in 2000, and it was turbocharged following Donald Trump’s 2016 win despite his losing the popular vote. The District of Columbia and 18 states have joined, accounting for 222 electoral votes.

John Fund is National Review’s national-affairs reporter.
