#6080. World Of Hyatt 2027 Updates: Milestone Rewards From 10 Nights, New Rewards, And More

World of Hyatt members can expect more flexibility and choice from January 1, 2027. Highlights of the update include earning Milestone Rewards sooner, a bunch of new Milestone Rewards, and more flexibility when redeeming rewards and paying for stays. There’s actually no huge catch, and the changes I learned about last night on an intimate call with the Hyatt team are genuinely member-focused.

The update follows the new Hyatt-Delta relationship, which also launched this week.

Starting January 1, 2027, World of Hyatt members will start enjoying Milestone Rewards after 10 nights stayed or 20,000 base points. That’s great news for relatively infrequent Hyatt guests (like myself), who will no longer have to stay 20 nights or earn 35,000 base points to earn their first Milestone Reward.

At 10 nights or 20,000 base points, members will be able to choose from:

Milestone Rewards will be unlocked at every ten nights, up to 150 nights.

Not only is it about to become quicker to earn Milestone Rewards, but there’ll also be new awards to choose from each level. Here are a few examples of the 20+ new rewards:

The downside of free parking becoming a Milestone Reward means that World of Hyatt members who earn Globalist from 2027 onwards will no longer enjoy it as a permanent status perk on award stays. This will be a notable downgrade to Globalists who value their parking perk.

Hyatt has published a handy new infographic with all the details.

There are also two more important Milestone Reward changes to note, both of which aren’t such positive news:

For the first time, World of Hyatt members will be able to stack multiple awards on a single stay. For example, you can use a Suite Upgrade Voucher, a Guest of Honor Award, and claim free parking, all on the same stay.

All awards will also expire after 365 of being issued. That’s great for awards that used to only last 180 days.

I think this could be my favorite update. Hyatt is enhancing its Pay My Way option to allow guests to choose how to pay for each night of a stay. As someone who struggles to rack up Hyatt points (Hyatt isn’t a transfer partner of any cards in the U.K.), this should certainly streamline booking stays for me.

The booking page will display each award applied to each individual night and provide guests with a drop-down menu to select how they’d like to pay for each night.

At a time when we’re plagued with loyalty program devaluations, these changes coming to World of Hyatt appear to be a genuinely positive slew of updates. Even when you consider some of the less favorable updates, like Globalists losing free parking and some award expiration dates being limited to 365 days, the changes will be positive overall for the vast majority of World of Hyatt members.

What do you make of these World of Hyatt changes?

Epic celestial events and ancient landmarks with no galaxy far, far away required.

Caribbean luxury that rewards every dollar you spend.

Best in July through August + December through March

New sightseeing trains and upscale points hotels make Japan’s stunning northern island even more alluring in 2027.

For those who want to experience Hokkaido’s beautiful countryside by train, Hokkaido Railway Company will debut two scenic tourist trains in 2027: the Red Star luxury train in February, when the region is blanketed in Hokkaido’s signature fluffy snow, and the Blue Star premium class train in June, just in time for Hokkaido’s lavender season.

And for skiers and snowboarders who are looking to experience Hokkaido’s incredible winter sports scene, Moxy Niseko will debut in late 2026, just in time for the start of ski season. Other exciting Niseko openings to look forward to in the coming years include Six Senses Niseko and an Aman property. In nearby Sapporo, new and forthcoming points hotels are plentiful, too: 2025 saw the opening of the InterContinental Sapporo, and both Hyatt Centric and Fairmont are planned for 2027 into 2028. -⁠Ellie Nan Storck

World-class dining and hotels to help fans refuel between Women’s World Cup matches.

One of the most accessible host cities of the Women’s World Cup is also among the most captivating. Beyond the pitch, visitors can experience the city’s dining renaissance, the long-awaited Museum of Image and Sound and the one of the oldest national history museums in the Americas, recently reopened after a 2018 fire. Plus, Rio (and nearby Maricá) is the midst of a luxury hotel boom, with exciting points properties opening over the coming years. December will bring the opening of Accor’s Sofitel Rio de Janeiro Ipanema, and over the next few years, Marriott will debut an eco-luxe Ritz Carlton Reserve and an all-inclusive JW Marriott in Maricá. -⁠Rachel Craft

Best in March through May + October through November

A perennial favorite is experiencing a luxury hotel boom.

Mexico’s massive capital never lacked excellent hotel options, but a recent slate of renovations and openings has us more excited than ever to revisit the city. The St. Regis Mexico City completed a multimillion dollar renovation with Frida Kahlo-inspired design elements in Sept. 2026. Hyatt loyalists can look forward to the February opening of the colorful new Standard Hotel in the Tabacalera neighborhood, followed by the April debut of the luxe Park Hyatt in Polanco. Other upcoming projects to look forward to include a Mama Shelter (part of the ALL Accor hotel loyalty program) in the heart of Roma Norte, set to open by the end of 2026, as well as Pendry Mexico City and Rosewood Mexico City, both planned for 2027. -⁠Lyndsey Matthews

The perfect mix of new luxury hotels, a distinct wine scene and endless opportunities to get outside.

In the Texas Hill Country, charming towns steeped in German culture are surrounded by award-winning wineries, idyllic swimming holes and Main Streets packed with restaurants, shops and some of the friendliest people in the Lone Star State. Near Fredericksburg, the epicenter of the Hill Country’s must-visit charm, Waldorf Astoria is opening its first Texas property, while Aman has plans for a secluded ranch retreat of its own. Add mouthwatering barbecue, legendary live music, popular rivers to float and an expanding Austin-Bergstrom International Airport (AUS), and there are more reasons than ever to head for the hills. -⁠Tanner Saunders

Rich in natural beauty, this coastal California town is ready to step into the spotlight.

Wellness travelers, adventure travelers and everyone in between will fall for this sleepy coastal enclave along the northern California coast. Unwind at Marriott Bonvoy’s newest adventure lodge after exploring the recently opened Great Redwood Trail or sampling the latest additions to the town’s renowned sustainable food and wine scene. And thanks to nonstop flights from Alaska Airlines and Southwest and $20 million in roadwork funding, Mendocino is easier than ever to reach. -⁠Rachel Craft

Experience a quieter side of India in one of the world’s lushest biodiversity hotspots

Like many of the best places, it can take a lot of time and effort to get to Coorg, a hill station in India’s verdant, biodiverse Western Ghats. But it is well worth it to see this little-visited region rife with endemic wildlife including elephants, leopards and myriad avian species. Spend your days sampling world-class coffee at the area’s many plantations, hiking the misty mountain trails and recentering yourself with immersive multiday Ayurvedic wellness programs at the stunning new Leela Coorg Forest Sanctuary. -⁠Eric Rosen

In anticipation of hosting the EXPO 2027, the Serbian capital is undergoing a major glow-up

From May 15 to Aug.15, the Serbian capital will host a specialized world exposition with 140-plus countries gathering to showcase innovations in architecture and design. In anticipation of the event, Belgrade is debuting several major projects of its own, including a Nikola Tesla Museum designed by Zaha Hadid Architects. The former main railway station will become the new permanent home of the Historical Museum of Serbia, while the Museum of the City of Belgrade and the Museum of Natural History Belgrade will also open in new facilities. Finally, the Aeronautical Museum of Belgrade will also complete a modernization project in 2027. To accommodate the influx of visitors, the city already opened a St. Regis in 2024, while the InterContinental Belgrade is accepting reservations from next March, with a Ritz-Carlton also anticipated to open, too. -⁠Lyndsey Matthews

Best in May through June, September through October

A pair of new destination-worthy hotels, both bookable with points.

Hyatt and Marriott will both debut luxury properties in Detroit come 2027. Hilton’s new hotel, the NoMad Detroit, will open inside the historic Michigan Grand Central Station, a once-abandoned Beaux-Arts landmark restored by Ford. Later in the year, the Marriott Edition will open as part of a ground-up development, bringing downtown Detroit its first five-star hotel. -⁠Carly Helfand

A new film festival is just one facet of this art-meets-outdoors jewel.

Between hosting its first Sundance Film Festival and celebrating 50 years of the iconic Pearl Street Mall, Colorado’s trendy cultural hub is going all out. Visitors can also look forward to new dining concepts from Michelin-recognized chefs, new interactive art labs and easy access to new Rocky Mountain hiking trails. An hour away, Denver International Airport (DEN) is expanding to accommodate increased traffic from United, Southwest and even Delta. -⁠Rachel Craft

Jungle-covered islands and seas teeming with marine life beckon explorers beyond the bright lights of Bali.

Cruise companies are lining up new expeditions to explore the Indonesian archipelago’s untouched corners, including a seven-day sailing aboard Uniworld’s Aqua Blu that will stop in Komodo National Park and the Spice Islands, Ponant’s team-up with Smithsonian Journeys on a 15-day jaunt around the Maluku islands among other ports of call and specialized dive-focused sailings in wild West Papua, reef-rich Raja Ampat and untamed Borneo from Swan Hellenic and Noble Caledonia. It’s the best way to experience regions of the Indonesian archipelago most folks never see. -⁠Eric Rosen

Australia’s first Michelin Guide, new luxury hotels and experiences, nonstop access from the U.S. and an extraordinary mix of world-class wine, wildlife and wilderness make 2027 South Australia’s moment on the global stage.

Australia’s first Michelin Guide and United’s nonstop San Francisco-Adelaide flight are putting South Australia within easier reach — and on the global culinary map, too. A significant transformation of Adelaide Central Market, Australia’s first Treehouse Hotel and new luxury stays are adding fresh reasons to visit, alongside the Barossa and McLaren Vale wine regions and the wildlife and rugged beauty of Kangaroo Island. -⁠Tanner Saunders

Best in April through June, September through October

Natural wonders and a burgeoning culture scene without the crowds.

Though Kazakhstan first made a name for itself as a nature travel destination, this Eurasian country wants the world to know there’s more to it than its glorious landscapes. Travelers can enjoy a new art museum and immersive ethno-village in the cultural capital of Almaty, check into new hotels in the Burabay resort region or combine natural and cultural wonders at the newly inscribed Mangystau Rock Mosques UNESCO World Heritage Site. With plans to launch the first-ever direct flight from the U.S. in 2027, this hidden gem may not stay hidden for long. -⁠Rachel Craft

Best in May through June, September through October

Two iconic cultural institutions, back and better than ever.

The Pergamon Museum will reopen in June after a multi-year renovation, debuting a fully redesigned Museum of Islamic Art and making the Pergamon Altar accessible for the first time in more than a decade. Later in the year, the Bauhaus Archive will reopen after extensive renovations with a new annex building. With nonstop options from the U.S. on United, Delta and Lufthansa — and strong Hilton and Marriott footprints downtown — early points bookings are a smart play for visiting Berlin in 2027. -⁠Carly Helfand

Best in April through June, September through November

Experience a slower type of journey that has captivated travelers for over 1,000 years.

Special events will be taking place at waystations along this ancient pilgrimage trail throughout the Holy Year of 2027. Among the highlights are braving the wine battle in Haro at the end of June, or attending St. James’s Feast Day on July 25 in Santiago de Compostela, where you can see the famous swinging of the Botafumeiro silver incense burner and attend an awe-inspiring mass in the Praza do Obradoiro. Aside from a full calendar of culinary festivals and lively concerts in Santiago, you can take in quieter stretches of the trail among the forested peaks of Cantabria and the vineyards of Rioja. -⁠Eric Rosen

Astrotourism investments and a highly anticipated points hotel transformation.

Dramatic coastal landscapes, the new Atlantic Canada UNESCO Tourism Corridor and the re-opening of the transformed The Algonquin Resort St. Andrews by-the-Sea, Autograph Collection resort make a compelling case for a 2027 visit to New Brunswick. Specifically, we’re excited to check out the Bay of Fundy Dark Sky Corridor that’s set to open in 2027 — a 137-mile stretch that could be the densest cluster of dark-sky and observatory areas on the planet. A stargazer’s dream come true. -⁠Madison Blancaflor

A burgeoning wine scene, an exciting UNESCO designation and outdoor attractions aplenty give one of BC’s prettiest regions a well deserved moment in the spotlight

With plenty of sunny days and a generally milder climate than the rest of British Columbia, the Okanagan Valley is becoming an increasingly compelling alternative to larger wine regions; oenophiles can look forward to sipping wines from smaller producers (small but mighty; there are over 200) in a community-forward and breathtaking lakeside setting.

Those in search of a city getaway should head to Kelowna, the valley’s largest metropolis set along the breezy shorelines of Okanagan Lake, where a major culinary moment is afoot. Recently designated Canada’s first UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy — a designation that honors not only the city’s agricultural innovation and culinary creativity, but the traditional foodways and land stewardship of the indigenous Syilx people — Kelowna offers a fast-growing restaurant scene (many with a sustainable, farm-to-table focus) and its own array of impressive wineries. -⁠Ellie Nan Storck

Travelers can look forward to fully restored access to Denali Park Road for the first time in six years

With more access now than ever, thanks to both recently expanded Alaska Airlines routes to nearby Fairbanks International Airport (FAI) and the very exciting full reopening of Denali Park Road for the summer season, 2027 is the year to plan an epic trip to Denali National Park. And the fun doesn’t stop there — Holland America, celebrating 80 years of Alaskan exploration, will complete a massive transformation of Holland America Denali Lodge, debuting 72 new guest rooms, updated public spaces and refreshed dining programs. Beyond the park, the Alaska Railroad will celebrate its centennial in 2027, and travelers can experience a legendary scenic trip between Anchorage, Talkeetna, Denali and Fairbanks. -⁠Ellie Nan Storck

Expanded access from the U.S. and newly awarded Michelin key hotel recognition.

Delta is adding a new nonstop route from L.A. to Manila and Philippine Airlines is joining the oneworld alliance, making a trip to the gorgeous islands of The Philippines easier than ever in 2027. Head to the islands early in the year for milder temperatures, vibrant festivals and the chance to ethically swim with majestic whale sharks in Donsol, Sorsogon. Nature lovers and beach loungers can also enjoy luxury properties like the Raffles Makati and the forthcoming Mandarin Oriental Makati, Manila (opening in December) or use points to book the brand new AC Hotel by Marriott Manila. -⁠Madison Blancaflor

Best in June through September, January through March

These lush African islands are ready for their moment in the sun.

Thanks to its pristine tropical forests and rare wildlife species, in 2025 São Tomé and Principe became the first country in the world whose entire territory, both land and sea, was designated as a UNESCO biosphere reserve. This past year, the country scored a second UNESCO designation for its historical roças, or colonial agricultural estates, making São Tomé and Principe ripe for discovery. Even better — you can use your Star Alliance points and miles to fly direct from Lisbon on TAP and Hilton points can set you up for a beachy stay at the luxurious Sundy Praia – Principe Collection. -⁠Eric Rosen

Best in April through May, September through October

For travelers ready to venture beyond familiar South American tourism destinations and experience a different side of the continent.

Travelers who have already visited Peru, Brazil, Argentina and other South American hot spots can find something different in the continent’s less-visited interior. Don’t go expecting a long list of world-famous sights or extensive tourism infrastructure. Instead, go for a quieter, slower-paced trip shaped by Indigenous Guaraní culture and landscapes ranging from the vast Chaco lowlands to the biodiverse remnants of the Atlantic Forest along the Paraná River. New attractions are adding reasons to visit: MUVA Museo Viedma, a museum exploring Paraguay’s Guaraní-Jesuit heritage through murals by artist Manuel Viedma, opened in Misiones in May 2026, and Asunción’s Museo de Ciencias plans to open a planetarium in 2028. -⁠Mackenzie Roche

#6078. Lufthansa’s A380 Business Class Seat Retrofit Nearly Done, But It Isn’t Allegris

In January 2026, Lufthansa formally announced plans to retrofit its Airbus A380s with new business class seats. The first plane with new cabins entered service in April 2026, and Lufthansa had committed to retrofitting all the planes by the middle of 2027.

There’s now a positive update, as it looks like Lufthansa is running way ahead on that schedule, and all A380s should be retrofitted within the coming weeks…

Lufthansa is introducing a new business class product on its entire fleet of eight Airbus A380s. Rather interestingly, it’s only business class that’s getting new seats, while first class, premium economy, and economy, remain the same, aside from some minor upgrades (like improved inflight entertainment).

The first A380 with new interiors entered service in April 2026, and AeroRoutes flags how as of December 18, 2026, Lufthansa is exclusively showing the new business class configuration on all routes. So starting in the coming weeks, you can expect the entire A380 network to feature the new cabins.

Lufthansa A380s are based in Munich (MUC), and currently fly to Bangkok (BKK), Delhi (DEL), Los Angeles (LAX), Mumbai (BOM), San Francisco (SFO), and Washington (IAD). As you’d expect, there’s seasonal variation in the routes, though.

What’s interesting is that Lufthansa isn’t introducing its new Allegris business class on these planes, but instead, is introducing another “off the shelf” product. Specifically, the airline has opted for the Thompson Aero Vantage XL product, which is in a staggered configuration.

Each seat has direct aisle access, seat width of 58cm, and a bed length of at least two meters. Seats feature bluetooth connectivity and flexible partitions. Lufthansa is calling this “Premium XXL,” which… I’m not sure if that’s supposed to describe the seat, or if Lufthansa is taking some liberties on a new Grindr profile, somehow turning Vantage XL into Premium XXL.

As A380s are reconfigured, the business class cabin is shrinking in size by 10 seats, going from 78 seats to 68 seats. First class continues to have eight seats, premium economy continues to have 52 seats, and economy continues to have 371 seats.

It’s pretty cool to note how Lufthansa has reversed course on the A380. At the beginning of the pandemic, Lufthansa grounded its fleet of Airbus A380s, and the intent was that these planes would be retired, and would only reenter service “in the event of an unexpectedly rapid market recovery.”

With the strong recovery we’ve seen in transatlantic leisure demand, the airline made the decision to start bringing back Airbus A380s as of the summer of 2023, and eight of the initial 14 are now back in service (six of them were sold). At first, the return of the A380s was mostly described as a temporary measure, in light of delayed Boeing 777-9 deliveries. The airline didn’t commit to keeping these planes around in the long run, though that changed over time.

In recent years it has become clear that the A380 will have a long term place in Lufthansa’s fleet. Clearly this investment in the business class product reflects that.

Lufthansa of course has its new Allegris cabins, including the new Allegris business class and new Allegris first class. These cabins debuted on newly delivered Airbus A350-900s, and we’re also seeing them on newly delivered Boeing 787-9s (though without first class).

So why is Lufthansa not installing its new Allegris seats on the A380s? Well, I’d assume it comes down to a couple of factors. The biggest reason is quite straightforward — Lufthansa has had a really tough time getting its new Allegris seats certified, and these seats need to be certified on each individual aircraft. The idea is that by picking an “off the shelf” product, these seats are already certified, and therefore the airline could actually rely on getting them into service immediately.

Second of all, I imagine that given the narrower fuselage of the A380 upper deck, it might’ve required even more complicated customization to fit the new Allegris seats up there.

For once, I’d say Lufthansa made a wise decision by just picking a generic product for its A380s. I think the big mystery is why Lufthansa just didn’t do this for its other planes, to avoid this entire mess. Separately, Lufthansa is reconfiguring its Boeing 747-8s, in a complicated two-part process. Initially, we’ll see the new Allegris business class seats on the lower deck, while the same business class seats will remain on the upper deck.

Lufthansa is wrapping up the process of introducing a new business class product on its Airbus A380s. The first plane with new cabins entered service in April 2026. While the initial plan was for all planes to be reconfigured as of the middle of 2027, it looks like that project will instead wrap up by December 2026, which is amazing.

Rather than installing the new Allegris business class seats, the airline is instead installing a more generic product, the Thompson Aero Vantage XL seat, which is a significant improvement over the product you’ll otherwise find on these jets. As planes are reconfigured, business class capacity is being reduced by 10 seats, from 78 to 68.

Lufthansa sure is all over the place when it comes to modernizing its cabins. Either way, this change is good to see.

What do you make of Lufthansa’s new A380 business class?

Lufthansa has more segmentation than a literal orange. Not sure that makes them particularly ‘supreme’ though. (Tried this "joke" over at LALF yesterday, eh, seems just as applicable today.)

If only they had done this 10 years ago...

Lufthansa's A380 are now seeing a 3rd type of business class. 1st type was the one they were introduced in the fleet with which was an outdated product in 2-2-2 2nd type is the current one which is being replaced. 3rd type is this new one which is much better. When airlines were introducing their A380s with state of the art products back in 2007-2012, Lufthansa, Air France and British Airways introduced their A380s with the most outdated seats at that time. Air France retired all their A380s earlier. BA is still flying them with those outdated business class seats which will be replaced soon. But Lufthansa missed the opportunity to go 4 abreast when they reconfigured their A380s with the current 6-abreast business class seats. At that time their CEO (not sure whether it was Franz or Spohr) was asked why he did not choose a product which was 4 abreast and he responded that "Germans enjoy/like talking to each other while flying and that they like seating next to someone". That was a dumb excuse to not go 4-abreast earlier. It seems that Germans no longer like to talk to each other while flying.

In pictures, it looks so much more spacious than Allegris. I would be perfectly happy with this product. In a perfect world, LX would scrap the seats for the 330 refurbishment and install these seats. Install a generic 4-seat first class as well...

#6077. American Airlines Replaces Its Rebooking Cards—Agents Now Must Do More Than Hand Them To Stranded Passengers

American Airlines is replacing the cards it hands passengers when their flights fall apart. The new Travel Assistance Card points customers to rebooking, baggage tracking, eligible vouchers and other help. And employees are being told to do more than hand over the card and send passengers away. An internal memo set this week as the start date at domestic airports. Use the Travel Assistance Card as a guided customer support tool, not simply as a handout. That’s a small change in what American hands customers, with a much bigger expectation for what employees are supposed to do. What Replaces The RICAP Card I’ve written about American’s RICAP cards and the special phone number printed on them. The name stands for Reservations Irregular Ops Customer Assistance Program. Airport agents gave them to customers affected by delays and cancellations, providing a way to get rebooked when airport lines were long. American periodically changed the number. They didn’t want it becoming everyone’s everyday reservations shortcut, and employees had to throw away old cards so they weren’t sending stranded passengers to a disconnected line. The old cards already had QR codes. The change here is a broader set of resources and instructions for how employees should use the card. The new version provides web addresses and QR codes for: Rebooking and baggage tracking. Eligible vouchers and refund information. Answers to common questions, chat support, the American Airlines app and additional travel assistance. Employees are told to offer it during cancellations, significant delays, missed connections, weather events and other operational disruptions. They’re supposed to explain how to scan the code or use the web address, then help the passenger identify which resources address their problem. Domestic mainline and regional stations are instructed to switch once their new cards arrive and discontinue all previous RICAP cards. International stations keep using RICAP. American Has Been Building More Ways To Recover From A Disruption This fits a series of changes at American: January’s disruption screens brought clearer status banners alongside rebooking, bag tracking and digital vouchers in the app and on the website. Agents gained the ability to issue meal vouchers to an entire eligible flight, rather than processing everyone individually. In June, automatic meal vouchers expanded beyond elite members to all AAdvantage members. Earlier this month, American added standby inside its disruption rebooking tool. Passsengers can try for an earlier nonstop while keeping their confirmed replacement flight until standby clears. The latest hotel and transportation update described automatic offers for qualifying overnight delays and an Uber Central rollout allowing authorized agents to arrange rides without passengers downloading Uber. American’s January app screens show the resources this card is meant to help passengers find: This Is Part Of Becoming An Airline People Will Pay More To Fly American has been adding better seats, lounges and food. Their premium push also depends on what happens to passengers whose flights don’t run on time. Robert Isom included disruption recovery technology in his plan to reclaim American’s premium reputation. And Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden has put the value of a one point improvement in net promoter score at $50 million to $100 million in revenue. A passenger who gets rebooked quickly and into a hotel can still be willing to buy American again. Spending hours in a line, then discovering that nobody can help, undermines the rest of the money they’re spending on the product. They’ve also been trying to reduce the disruptions themselves. American spread Dallas–Fort Worth’s schedule across 13 smaller connecting banks instead of nine. Management reported missed connections down 50% in the early April results. American’s overall reliability still doesn’t outperform though. In the September performance figures I covered, American arrived on time 77.11% of the time, compared with 78.65% for United and 82.52% for Delta. And American has been working against itself in how it handles passengers. I covered the loss of routinely staffed customer service counters at Washington National, where passengers were directed to digital tools and phones, with live help brought out during major disruptions. The new instruction to guide passengers through the card makes sense. Someone who can’t get the app to offer a workable itinerary still needs an employee’s help. At a gate with one employee, though, boarding the next departure and walking several stranded customers through their options compete for the same person’s time. This memo gives that employee another task. It doesn’t add anyone else to help. This fits a series of changes at American:

Agents gained the ability to issue meal vouchers to an entire eligible flight, rather than processing everyone individually. In June, automatic meal vouchers expanded beyond elite members to all AAdvantage members.

Earlier this month, American added standby inside its disruption rebooking tool. Passsengers can try for an earlier nonstop while keeping their confirmed replacement flight until standby clears.

The latest hotel and transportation update described automatic offers for qualifying overnight delays and an Uber Central rollout allowing authorized agents to arrange rides without passengers downloading Uber.

American’s January app screens show the resources this card is meant to help passengers find:

American has been adding better seats, lounges and food. Their premium push also depends on what happens to passengers whose flights don’t run on time. Robert Isom included disruption recovery technology in his plan to reclaim American’s premium reputation. And Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden has put the value of a one point improvement in net promoter score at $50 million to $100 million in revenue. A passenger who gets rebooked quickly and into a hotel can still be willing to buy American again. Spending hours in a line, then discovering that nobody can help, undermines the rest of the money they’re spending on the product. They’ve also been trying to reduce the disruptions themselves. American spread Dallas–Fort Worth’s schedule across 13 smaller connecting banks instead of nine. Management reported missed connections down 50% in the early April results. American’s overall reliability still doesn’t outperform though. In the September performance figures I covered, American arrived on time 77.11% of the time, compared with 78.65% for United and 82.52% for Delta. And American has been working against itself in how it handles passengers. I covered the loss of routinely staffed customer service counters at Washington National, where passengers were directed to digital tools and phones, with live help brought out during major disruptions. The new instruction to guide passengers through the card makes sense. Someone who can’t get the app to offer a workable itinerary still needs an employee’s help. At a gate with one employee, though, boarding the next departure and walking several stranded customers through their options compete for the same person’s time. This memo gives that employee another task. It doesn’t add anyone else to help. #6076. A Trump–Xi–Putin Summit Could Remake the World Order

Can a triangle of the U.S., China, and Russia create a sustainable equilibrium of power, rules, and values?

From left: Russian President Vladimir Putin, President Donald Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping

NR illustration; Alexander Kazakov, Kevin Lamarque, Tingshu Wang/Reuters

The proposed Trump–Xi–Putin meeting in Shenzhen this month could become one of the most consequential diplomatic encounters since the Cold War. Whatever the three leaders might negotiate concerning Ukraine, Taiwan, trade, nuclear weapons, or artificial intelligence, its larger significance would be unmistakable: The three powers most capable of shaping the international order would be gathering not primarily to defend it but to renegotiate their positions within, or against, it.

The irony is extraordinary. Russia seeks to overturn an order from which it believes itself excluded. China seeks to reshape an order from which it has benefited enormously. The United States, which created and sustained that order, increasingly regards its maintenance as an excessive burden. The revolutionary, the reformer, and the reluctant guardian have become, in different ways, revisionists.

From left: Russian President Vladimir Putin, President Donald Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping

NR illustration; Alexander Kazakov, Kevin Lamarque, Tingshu Wang/Reuters

#6074. Delta CEO’s Cope: Ed Bastian Says Doesn’t Need Starlink, Current Wi-Fi Good Enough

Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian says “customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.” That’s a remarkable claim from an airline that’s spent years promoting free internet as a reason to choose its premium experience. Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, Bastian defended passing on Starlink and waiting for Amazon Leo which is still unproven and whose timetable is now in question. He downplayed competitors’ progress, argued Delta’s current Viasat service comes close enough, and expressed confidence that Amazon would match or beat Starlink. It was pure cope. Delta doesn’t plan to begin installing Amazon until 2028 and that’s if the service works and delivers on schedule. United and Southwest both plan to finish their Starlink installations in 2027, and American is adding the service as well (so are Alaska and even Frontier). Delta’s Wifi Was Fine When Fewer People Used It Delta’s Viasat internet was fine when a few people on each flight were paying to use it. Make it free, get a much larger share of the plane online, and the experience can become unusable. I wrote about this last December after flying Delta to Las Vegas. The system repeatedly bogged down until nothing would load. I’d rather pay for internet that works than get free internet that doesn’t. Bandwidth has to be shared. Removing the price doesn’t create more capacity, but it gives a lot more people a reason to connect. A connection that works well with light use just isn’t the same thing – and Starlink’s low earth orbit satellites simply give the signal less distance to travel, delivering almost no latency. Bastian points to two new Viasat satellites. ViaSat-3 F3 entered service in August, and F2 entered service in September. But Delta’s own current wifi explanation acknowledges that performance varies with customer demand and satellite capacity, with less consistent service in high-demand or capacity-constrained areas. The airline knows this problem exists, which is why they’re touting Amazon’s service as a future improvement. United And Southwest Are Already Flying Starlink Bastian suggests most airlines promoting Starlink haven’t started yet. He doesn’t identify which airlines he’s counting. Here’s what the competitors actually say: United Airlines: More than half its daily flights already have Starlink. It expects nearly 64% by year-end and completion of installations by the end of 2027. Southwest Airlines: Its latest quarterly filing confirms equipped aircraft are already in service, with the full fleet expected to be finished in fall 2027. Last week it publicized gaming and livestreaming aboard a flight from Austin to San Diego. Alaska and Hawaiian: The group’s October 26 installation update shows all 93 Embraer 175s, Hawaiian’s 18 Airbus A321neos and 24 Airbus A330s equipped, along with 16 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft. Even Southwest expects to have Starlink throughout its fleet before Delta starts putting Amazon on its first 500 aircraft. That’s an awkward comparison for the airline charging a premium when it’ll be universal on the only U.S. airline without first class even. Wifi Doesn’t Have To Decide Every Ticket To Cost Delta Money I explained last month that I’ve avoided United and Southwest when I couldn’t count on functional internet. Starlink changes that calculation. I’ll pay more to work onboard because losing several productive hours costs more than the airfare savings. Recon Analytics finds wifi ranks among the top five business-trip airline selection factors for 32.6% of flyers, and first for 6.5%. Even among leisure travelers, 3.8% rank it first. Delta doesn’t need to lose everyone. It can lose a few expensive trips from customers who fly often, buy premium seats and carry airline credit cards. That’s precisely the business it wants. United is already using wifi to recruit those customers. It says its wifi-focused status match campaign produced a tenfold increase in daily applications. Amazon Still Has To Deliver. Bastian says that when Delta gets Amazon Leo, “we’ll be at least as good as Starlink if not better.” He hasn’t demonstrated that. Amazon needs enough satellites in the right orbits, working aircraft equipment, certification, and an airline installation program. It then has to deliver consistently with actual passengers using it. Delta’s own materials make the 2028 start subject to technical, certification and deployment milestones. And 2028 is the start of installations on an initial 500 aircraft. As I covered yesterday, Sunday’s failed Vulcan launch lost 40 Amazon satellites. We don’t yet know whether that pushes back Delta’s rollout. But the risk extends beyond replacing those satellites: Amazon contracted for 38 Vulcan missions to launch more than 1,500 of them. Amazon’s prelaunch photo shows the satellites stacked for that mission. Bastian’s account of testing Starlink is consistent with reporting from 2022. Delta had an early look at the product. It chose different commercial terms. I’ve covered the dispute over Delta’s branded portal. And last month Bastian said the branding disagreement out loud: “(Elon) thought it should be called Starlink on the planes. I said ‘No, it’s gotta be Delta.’” Amazon could offer a broader deal involving cloud computing and entertainment. Delta also gets to keep directing passengers through its own platform, where it promotes partners and sells them things. But a cheaper contract has to save enough to cover the business lost while passengers wait. If someone moves expensive flights to United, earns status there and starts spending on a United credit card, Delta may have to buy that loyalty back long after Amazon finally arrives. What customers consider to be “premium” is an ever changing thing. What exactly is so premium about Delta as compared to others? On time performance? It’s surely not the food. FAs are as much of a mixed bag as at UA/AA.

Even if DL wifi is usable, it’s certainly not thought of as premium. Starlink is simply excellent and is thought of as premium. We’ve just witnessed one of the most significant air travel disruptions in recent memory.

The recent Federal Aviation Administration outage led to more than 18,000 flight cancellations over three days and left millions of passengers scrambling to deal with the fallout.

And that's just the latest air travel meltdown to hit the U.S.

In recent years, we’ve seen major travel woes triggered by bad weather, government shutdowns and tech glitches.

Our TPG reporters have covered all of these issues, and occasionally even gotten stranded at airports themselves.

In the wake of this latest major disruption, we’ve put our heads together to share some of our best tips for dealing with airport chaos.

When I fly, I am constantly checking my airline’s app for any sign of trouble. I monitor my incoming flight, and often spot delays or cancellations as soon as they pop up.

This allows me to immediately rebook myself on another flight.

When flight woes are brewing, it can sometimes make sense to book yourself a backup flight with miles, says Becky Blaine, TPG’s managing editor of newsletters.

“Don’t wait for the airline to rebook you,” she says.

Just remember to cancel it if you end up not needing it.

Most U.S. carriers will return your miles if you decide to cancel — just be sure you avoid booking basic economy on these three airlines.

Also, be careful about booking a backup ticket on your original airline. Some carriers will cancel one of your reservations if the system detects possible duplicate bookings.

Whatever direction you take, be decisive, TPG’s senior director of content Summer Hull suggests.

“Either be proactive, or be willing to accept that you might be stuck for a while,” she says.

If you’re going to book a backup flight with points, lock it in. If the airline offers you a flight option you like, take it.

During travel chaos, seats will disappear rapidly as other flyers pivot. And the longer you wait, the fewer options you’ll have.

“That will sometimes mean you might have wasted some money or points being proactive,” Hull adds. “But if you wait until you know for sure ... your options will decrease.”

Sometimes, it also pays to know when to call it quits and get a room for the night.

If the flight board is a mess, planes aren't taking off, and your chances of getting out are slim, throwing in the towel and getting a hotel room can be the smarter move.

This is another case where being decisive matters.

“Book your hotel as soon as possible if you think you’ll get stuck overnight,” TPG’s Eric Rosen says.

When there’s mass flight trouble, empty rooms near the airport can disappear fast.

These days, your airline’s app is often your best bet for rebooking yourself.

But if that’s not cutting it, you could be looking at a long customer service line or an even longer wait by phone.

TPG lead writer Katie Genter recommends a different option: Try contacting the airline via social media.

Some carriers will assist customers with reservations via direct messages.

Just be sure to have your confirmation number handy, because that’s the first thing the airline agent will ask for.

Most airline lounges have customer assistance desks, too.

If you have access to your airline's lounge, the wait may be far shorter there than down on the airport concourse.

Keep in mind, representatives in credit card-affiliated lounges are typically not able to help you with your reservation, since they don’t actually work for the airline.

When dealing with airline customer service, you can help your cause by doing your own homework, says Ben Mutzabaugh, managing editor of aviation.

He recommends looking up available flights and presenting the agent with options.

When on the phone with an airline agent, a flyer who has done their homework is able to come up with quicker solutions by saying things like: “What about the 7:30 flight instead of the 5:30?" or "I can fly into Newark instead of JFK" or, "I see this other airline has a flight to my city that’s not canceled. Any chance I can get on that?"

If all else fails, go back to the basics, recommends Carly Helfand, TPG director of content.

Her strategy if she’s not getting the answer she needs: "Be very nice, ask for exactly what you want, and hang up and call again. Eventually, you’ll find an agent who will give it to you."

Be just as persistent when searching for a replacement flight.

Often, the airline will offer you rebooking options when your flight is delayed or canceled. Sometimes, the ideal flight isn’t available, but that doesn’t mean it’s a lost cause.

“Keep checking,” TPG’s Clint Henderson says. “Often during irregular options, seats open up as people abandon flights.”

What is your top strategy for navigating flight trouble? Let us know in the comments below!

#6072. FAA’s Flight Shutdown Fuels A $30 Billion Funding Push—Most Of The Money Isn’t Even For Air Traffic Control

After the FAA communications breakdown brought departures across the country to a halt on Friday, the travel industry has its answer: give air traffic control another $30 billion. Most of the money in the bill they’re pushing wouldn’t even go to air traffic control. The U.S. Travel Association says Friday’s ground stop demonstrates that the FAA “lacks the resources necessary to modernize America’s aging aviation infrastructure.” It wants Congress to pass the Modern Skies Act sponsored by Senator Eric Schmitt (R-MO) before the end of this Congress. That legislation would provide $30.1 billion, including $15 billion for airport terminals. It would leave the FAA running air traffic control under essentially the same institutional structure that’s spent decades failing to deliver promised improvements. We need modern equipment. We also need to modernize the organization buying and operating it. Using this failure to sell airport terminal subsidies does neither particularly well. A Local Equipment Change Disrupted Most Of The National Network The nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m. Eastern Friday and lasted until 8:15 p.m. The airline recovery took much longer. There were over 18,000 cancellations from Friday through Sunday. Planes and crews wound up in the wrong places. Crew duty limits and missed connections kept the disruption going after communications stabilized. The FAA identifies two sites: a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, where contractor L3Harris was installing a router, and a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas. Excessive connection attempts flooded their ancient private network, disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds at 17 of 22 en route centers and spreading into approach control facilities. Blocking the two sites stabilized the network. Officials also disabled the broadcasting function on about 60 similar routers. Some radio frequencies and radar feeds kept working, allowing aircraft already airborne to land. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford describes the work as routine maintenance, separate from the new $12.5 billion modernization program. That makes the question about managing the system day to day even more pressing if it can destabilize the whole system with only the third nationwide ground stop in U.S. history. Most Of The $30 Billion Would Go To Airports John Kefaliotis at Reason Foundation breaks down the spending. The introduced bill, S. 5572: Purpose Funding Terminal rebuilding pilot for up to three airports $10 billion Other airport terminal grants $5 billion Discretionary airport improvement grants $3 billion Common automation platform and controller workstation $7.2 billion Cloud computing and associated telecommunications $2 billion Air traffic control facilities, including digital towers $2 billion Air traffic flow management technology $600 million Consolidating terminal air traffic control facilities $300 million That’s $12.1 billion for air traffic control systems and facilities, versus $18 billion for airports. About 40% goes to air traffic control. The administration’s announcement includes building airports, but the sales pitch after Friday’s failure is that Congress needs to fund the air traffic control fix. The $10 billion terminal pilot is particularly brazen. It would cover up to 90% of costs at no more than three medium hub airports. Eligibility requires a principal terminal built before 1990 that hasn’t undergone comprehensive redevelopment since then, plus a project with environmental review complete and final design underway. The Transportation Secretary picks the recipients. The bill’s sponsor is a Missouri senator. At St. Louis airport last month, Duffy was asked whether the program appeared tailor made for the airport’s single terminal project. His answer: “That’s a fair assessment.” It’s not even clear whether other airports even qualify given the Rube Goldbergesque rules in the bill. It’s pure pork barrel spending. The same local report notes that Southwest Airlines, which operates more than half of Lambert’s flights, would otherwise bear the largest share of the terminal project’s cost. Moving that bill to federal taxpayers is a windfall for Southwest. The separate $3 billion airport grant pot also bypasses normal allocation formulas and minimum shares. Politicians get more discretion over where the money goes. Bundling that with air traffic control improvements makes it easier to portray objections to the airport spending as opposition to aviation safety. The FAA Has Already Been Spending Billions Congress provided roughly $12.5 billion in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year, also from taxpayers rather than airlines and passengers. That came on top of billions in earlier modernization spending largely lit on fire. The Transportation Department’s inspector general reports that the FAA spent more than $15 billion on NextGen through the end of 2024. The effort began in 2003, with completion originally envisioned for 2025. Major capabilities slipped to 2030 or later, costs rose, and the agency reduced what it would deliver. There are improvements underway. Duffy says 69% of copper communications have been replaced and electronic flight strips are installed at 25 towers. But he also acknowledged the FAA’s history during Saturday’s briefing: “They haven’t spent the money well.” Secretary Sean Duffy’s November 14 briefing on the ground stop and modernization funding The FAA set out a plan in 1983 “to equip 150 to 250 airport control towers by 2000.” They went way over budget and didn’t accomplish much. Meanwhile, all of Nav Canada facilities went electronic 15 years ago (and all control towers and TRACONs even earlier). Their solution is used in Australia, Italy, the U.K. and Dubai. We could license the Canadian solution, or other commercial ones, but instead the FAA has been contracting for their own solution since three years before the Beastie Boys were fighting for your right to party. Wait until you explain paper flight strips!https://t.co/fyU7aSILWr pic.twitter.com/gOBIHME3oK — gary leff (@garyleff) July 2, 2023 Modernize The Organization That Runs Air Traffic Control When I reviewed the administration’s plan in May 2025, my concern was that the same institution that had failed to deliver for decades would be asked to execute another enormous upgrade, faster, without fixing its underlying incentives. And there wasn’t a plan to make real changes there. I’ve laid out the Canadian alternative. NAV CANADA has operated since 1996 as a private nonprofit without equity shareholders. It funds operations and capital investment through customer charges and issuing bonds for long-term investments. Transport Canada regulates its safety. Commercial airlines elect four of its 15 directors. Government, employees, general aviation and independent directors also have roles. There’s no need to hand the system to an airline monopoly to get it out of congressional budgeting. The FAA, by contrast, regulates itself – which is a recipe for unaccountability. An outside regulator would have a clearer job: demand safe performance from an operator whose failures it isn’t also responsible for defending. Commercial airlines elect four of its 15 directors. Government, employees, general aviation and independent directors also have roles. There’s no need to hand the system to an airline monopoly to get it out of congressional budgeting.

The FAA, by contrast, regulates itself – which is a recipe for unaccountability. An outside regulator would have a clearer job: demand safe performance from an operator whose failures it isn’t also responsible for defending.

#6071. This week: Permitting bill hits Senate floor amid aviation funding fight

The lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are currently scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen said Sunday on CNN.

​Van Hollen has also said he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A new issue is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Fox News Sunday.

Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

"We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy said in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel."

Meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

On the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

New member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

That includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is currently the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.

Marriott’s website and app briefly blocked loyalty member log-ins Tuesday. The company says the outage wasn’t a cyberattack. United Airlines and many non-travel companies have suffered various tech disruptions in recent days.

Members of Marriott's loyalty program had trouble signing in Tuesday, with problems affecting access through its website and mobile app.

Marriott Bonvoy members couldn't sign in to Marriott.com or the Bonvoy app for several hours Tuesday, cutting off the login-dependent features that run a modern hotel stay — mobile check-in, digital room keys, messaging with hotel staff, and room-service ordering. Downdetector began logging complaints around 9:15 a.m. ET, reports climbed into the hundreds, and the pace slowed after 1 p.m.; by 2 p.m. Skift's tests found sign-in working again. A Marriott spokesperson said the company resolved a technical issue affecting sign-in on both the website and the app, said teams worked with its technology partners to restore functionality, and said its review found no indication the disruption was cybersecurity-related. The outage landed on a day when Downdetector also showed problems at Gmail, iCloud, and Apple payment services, and CNN reported a National Security Agency communications network went offline; United Airlines, Microsoft, and Chase had tech disruptions over the past week. Marriott is in the middle of a multi-year overhaul of its property-management, central-reservations, and loyalty technology.

#6069. James Talarico’s ‘Incarnational Politics’

The new senator from Texas has bad ideas about Christianity and democracy, but the press seems okay with that.

The day after the Democrats trounced the Republicans in the midterm elections, Ezra Klein of the New York Times tweeted, “One of the more exciting parts of this election — among many — is the return of a religious left.” Accompanying the enthusiastic remark was a clip from his interview earlier this year with James Talarico, the Democrat who won the Texas senatorial race. In the clip, Talarico — a Presbyterian seminarian — advocates a political attitude in which Americans recognize each other as being made in God’s image and treat each other accordingly. He calls this “an incarnational politics.”

Incarnational politics — hoo boy. The term, a nearly paradoxical union of the sacred and the profane, sounds just enough like intersectional politics to catch the attention of progressives. It also sounds like an edgy indie band that never quite made it. (“I saw Incarnational Politics open for Bad Religion in ’91.”)

#6068. You Can Transfer British Airways Avios To Someone Else For $11 Using The Finnair Loophole

British Airways charges most members £50 per transaction to give Avios to someone else, and each transfer tops out at 60,000 points. Move the same points through Finnair and you can give someone 100,000 Avios for a single €10 fee. You can move British Airways Avios into a Finnair account, and Finnair charges €10 to transfer Avios to another member. I’ve written about moving Avios between airline programs to get the best redemption deal. The same flexibility lets you choose which program’s rules to use when giving points to another person. For two people with British Airways balances, the process is: Each person links their own British Airways and Finnair accounts. Names and email addresses need to match within each person’s accounts, and both programs need two-factor authentication enabled. The person giving the points moves their Avios into their own Finnair account. That transfer is free and 1:1. They use Finnair Shop’s transfer function to send the Avios to the other person’s Finnair account, paying €10. The recipient can use the points through Finnair or move them into their own linked British Airways account, again free at 1:1. Under the British Airways transfer terms, sending 100,000 Avios takes two transactions at £50 apiece, or the equivalent charged in your home currency (Gold members are exempt from that fee). Senders and recipients are each limited to 200,000 Avios per calendar year. Finnair doesn’t cap the amount or frequency of member transfers beyond your available balance. However, moving the points between airlines has its own limits. Open the accounts in advance. Finnair requires an account to be at least 30 days old to link with another Avios program. The sender must have been a member for at least 90 days to transfer to another person online. Finnair allows newer members to transfer via customer care at a higher €20 transfer fee. This route is for adults. Linking requires members to be at least 18, and you can’t transfer Avios into a Finnair Plus Junior account. Transfer ceiling. Finnair allows 1–999,999 Avios per cross-program transaction. Basic members have a shared 1 million Avios limit over 12 months, counting all linked programs and both directions. Higher tiers don’t have that 12-month cap. You may not need to pay anything. British Airways’ free household account pools balances for redemptions, and you can often simply book an award for someone else. But this lets you do it without restricting redemptions from your account to members of your household account. Don’t leave the points sitting in a dormant Finnair account. Transfers don’t restart their 18-month expiration clock. One Reddit member reported losing newly transferred Avios less than two weeks later because the Finnair account was already inactive. They subsequently reported getting the points back after contacting the airline. Topics on this pageAviosBritish AirwaysFinnairLoyalty programReddit+1 more More From View from the Wing

There shouldn’t need to be loopholes for this. Transferring points you already own should be free. We ought to properly regulate these corporate pseudocurrencies to include basic consumer protections—like free transfers, advance notice for program changes, and stabilized values—so these stealth devaluations stop. You’d think the banks underwriting these multi-billion-dollar currencies would want stability, too, before constant devaluations burn out the consumers fueling their credit card portfolios.

Wasn’t there an old Court case involving UA and a customer over the “meaning” of lifetime membership in their Club? If memory serves, the court sided with airline saying lifetime is what the airline says. What you describes a similar case.

The 30-day account age rule is the part I’d flag for anyone trying this in a hurry — you really do need to set the Finnair accounts up well ahead of time. The expiry warning matters too: moving points doesn’t restart that 18-month clock, so it’s worth checking the receiving account is active before sending a large balance across. For smaller gifts, the household account route Gary mentions is probably simpler, but for a one-off larger transfer this €10 path is hard to beat.

@alanZ — H’yup. Lagen v. United Continental Holdings. Flyer spent years working towards United’s million-miler program, which promised ‘premier executive’ status. But, when United merged with Continental, and slashed those perks, he sued for breach of contract. 7th Circuit sided with airline, citing MileagePlus rules, which gave United the unilateral right to modify, devalue, or terminate program benefits “on a whim” with or without notice. I prefer Judge Hamilton’s dissent, which notes an airline’s definition of ‘lifetime’ means: “Lifetime, unless we change our mind.” So, like I’ve been saying, we can close this regulatory vacuum, if we wanted, but we haven’t in the US at least for now.

The Chase Ultimate Rewards program just added Cathay Pacific Asia Miles and Qantas Frequent Flyer as transfer partners. Eligible Chase cardmembers can now transfer Ultimate Rewards points to both of these programs at a 1:1 ratio.

TPG's Nov. 2026 valuations peg Chase Ultimate Rewards points at 2.05 cents each, compared with 1.3 cents each for Asia Miles and Qantas Frequent Flyer points. However, that doesn't mean you can't get excellent value by transferring Chase points to either program for an award flight; transferable rewards are generally worth more because of their flexibility.

Cathay Pacific and Qantas are part of the Oneworld alliance. This means that, in addition to Cathay Pacific and Qantas flights, you may also find award availability through these airlines on flights operated by other Oneworld alliance airlines, including American Airlines and Alaska Airlines.

Chase already partners with several Avios programs, which provide access to many Oneworld award flights. However, the addition of Asia Miles and Qantas Frequent Flyer gives cardmembers more ways to compare award pricing and availability across the alliance. Of course, not all award flights are bookable through every partner program, so you'll want to check award pricing and availability with each program before transferring Chase Ultimate Rewards points.

These two new transfer partners also provide additional ways to book award flights across the Pacific. While Cathay Pacific premium-cabin award space can be extremely limited through other Oneworld programs, Asia Miles may offer access to additional award availability.

Business and first availability between North America and Hong Kong is currently sparse even through Asia Miles, but you can fly in premium economy on some dates for as little as 52,000 Asia Miles one-way.

And if you have your eye on an around-the-world award, Qantas has a special Oneworld Classic Flight Reward that can cover up to 35,000 miles of travel on a single itinerary for 152,200 points in economy or 365,800 points in business. You'll need to fly at least two Oneworld airlines other than Qantas to qualify for this award.

You can also transfer points from several other transferable rewards programs to Qantas Frequent Flyer and Cathay Pacific Asia Miles. Now, Chase Ultimate Rewards points provide another way to top off your account when you're short of the miles needed for an award.

#6066. New Hyatt Credit Card Offer: Earn 4 Free Nights—Why I Spend On The Card Towards Elite Status

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The World Of Hyatt Credit Card (See rates and fees) has a new initial bonus: earn 4 free nights at any Category 1-4 Hyatt hotel or resort after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. That’s an improved offer from a card whose bonuses have usually been more modest than competing travel cards.

I have this card, and I put actual spending on it. Hyatt points are still valuable, but what gets me to use the card is the credit toward elite status and the rewards earned along the way. Hyatt status does more to improve my hotel stays than status with other major chains.

These are four separate certificates, so you can use them for one trip or spread them across different stays. You’ll need standard room award availability, and the certificates expire 12 months after they’re issued. The terms require checkout before the expiration date. Under Hyatt’s current award chart, a Category 4 standard room can cost as much as 25,000 points per night. Four certificates could therefore cover nights that would otherwise require 100,000 points. Their category restrictions and expiration date make them less flexible than having those points in your account. The card has a $95 annual fee. Chase excludes current holders of this card and previous cardmembers who received its initial bonus within the past 24 months. The usual Chase restriction on applicants who’ve opened five or more personal cards in the past 24 months also generally applies. Why I Keep The Card And Spend On It The annual Category 1-4 free night after each cardmember anniversary makes the $95 fee easy to justify. There’s also a second Category 1-4 night after $15,000 in purchases during a calendar year which makes that spending more rewarding. And these nights are transferable to another World of Hyatt member. If I won’t use one, I can give it to someone who will. For spending, the card earns 4 Hyatt points per dollar on qualifying Hyatt purchases; 2 on restaurants, airline tickets bought directly from airlines, local transit and commuting, and fitness club and gym memberships; and 1 on other purchases. More significantly, it comes with 5 qualifying nights each year, plus 2 more qualifying nights for every $5,000 spent. Those nights count toward both status and Milestone Rewards. Put $15,000 of otherwise unbonused spending on the card during a calendar year and you earn: 15,000 Hyatt points. An additional Category 1-4 free night certificate. 6 qualifying nights from spending, giving you 11 including the card’s annual 5. That means 49 qualifying nights actually spent in hotels, plus the card’s 5 annual nights and 6 from spending, gets you to the 60 needed for Globalist. And the $5,000 spent earning the initial bonus counts toward the $15,000 free-night threshold in the calendar year when you spend it. Milestone Rewards start at 20 qualifying nights and continue every 10 nights through 150. Some of the rewards on the way to Globalist are: Qualifying Nights Notable Rewards 30 A Category 1-4 free night, plus a choice of additional reward. 40 A Guest of Honor Award, plus a choice that includes a Suite Upgrade Award. 50 A choice that includes 2 Suite Upgrade Awards. 60 Globalist status, a Category 1-7 free night, 2 Suite Upgrade Awards, 2 Guest of Honor Awards, and My Hyatt Concierge. The value of another $5,000 in spending depends on where those two nights get me. Crossing a threshold for suite upgrades or Globalist can be worth giving up a higher earning rate on another card. Hyatt Status Is Stronger Than At Other Major Chains The card itself comes with Discoverist status. That’s better than a hole in the head as my grandfather used to say. But reaching Globalist has real value – as well as the milestone choices along the way. The biggest benefit is confirming a suite at the time of booking with a Suite Upgrade Award for up to seven nights when an eligible standard suite is available for the stay. That’s a huge value on family trips. I also value having a My Hyatt Concierge I can email requests to, actual delivery of 4 p.m. late checkout at eligible properties, and a more generous breakfast benefit than I get from other chains. At participating hotels without an available club lounge, Globalist breakfast generally covers a full breakfast for up to two adults and two children registered in the room, including tax and gratuity. Late checkout has exceptions, including availability limits at resorts, but I’m usually proactively offered late checkout everywhere else (and personally find it honored more often than not at resorts). The Free Night Certificates Should Be More Flexible The current version of this card launched in 2018. Its annual certificate is still capped at Category 4, while category creep has taken away many of the hotels where I’d most want to use it. Just this year, 14 hotels moved from Category 4 to Category 5, including Hyatt Regency Seattle, Hyatt Regency Grand Cypress and Hyatt Regency Jersey City. Five moved the other way, bringing options like Hyatt Centric Congress Avenue Austin and Dream Nashville within reach, but the certificate lost more hotels than it gained. I’d like Hyatt to at least let members add points to a certificate to book a higher category. The certificate works at a Category 4 hotel charging 25,000 points, but won’t work at a Category 5 hotel when it’s charging 15,000 points. And I wish Hyatt would let us combine these free nights with Suite Upgrade Awards or Guest of Honor Awards. I value them most traveling with my family when I’m paying for rooms out of pocket. That’s always when I want to use my suite upgrades! I don’t need a suite on a business stay (paid by someone else, when it’s just me) or to use the free night award. These are four separate certificates, so you can use them for one trip or spread them across different stays. You’ll need standard room award availability, and the certificates expire 12 months after they’re issued. The terms require checkout before the expiration date.

Under Hyatt’s current award chart, a Category 4 standard room can cost as much as 25,000 points per night. Four certificates could therefore cover nights that would otherwise require 100,000 points. Their category restrictions and expiration date make them less flexible than having those points in your account.

The card has a $95 annual fee. Chase excludes current holders of this card and previous cardmembers who received its initial bonus within the past 24 months. The usual Chase restriction on applicants who’ve opened five or more personal cards in the past 24 months also generally applies.

The annual Category 1-4 free night after each cardmember anniversary makes the $95 fee easy to justify. There’s also a second Category 1-4 night after $15,000 in purchases during a calendar year which makes that spending more rewarding. And these nights are transferable to another World of Hyatt member. If I won’t use one, I can give it to someone who will. For spending, the card earns 4 Hyatt points per dollar on qualifying Hyatt purchases; 2 on restaurants, airline tickets bought directly from airlines, local transit and commuting, and fitness club and gym memberships; and 1 on other purchases. More significantly, it comes with 5 qualifying nights each year, plus 2 more qualifying nights for every $5,000 spent. Those nights count toward both status and Milestone Rewards. Put $15,000 of otherwise unbonused spending on the card during a calendar year and you earn: 15,000 Hyatt points. An additional Category 1-4 free night certificate. 6 qualifying nights from spending, giving you 11 including the card’s annual 5. That means 49 qualifying nights actually spent in hotels, plus the card’s 5 annual nights and 6 from spending, gets you to the 60 needed for Globalist. And the $5,000 spent earning the initial bonus counts toward the $15,000 free-night threshold in the calendar year when you spend it. Milestone Rewards start at 20 qualifying nights and continue every 10 nights through 150. Some of the rewards on the way to Globalist are: Qualifying Nights Notable Rewards 30 A Category 1-4 free night, plus a choice of additional reward. 40 A Guest of Honor Award, plus a choice that includes a Suite Upgrade Award. 50 A choice that includes 2 Suite Upgrade Awards. 60 Globalist status, a Category 1-7 free night, 2 Suite Upgrade Awards, 2 Guest of Honor Awards, and My Hyatt Concierge. The value of another $5,000 in spending depends on where those two nights get me. Crossing a threshold for suite upgrades or Globalist can be worth giving up a higher earning rate on another card. Hyatt Status Is Stronger Than At Other Major Chains The card itself comes with Discoverist status. That’s better than a hole in the head as my grandfather used to say. But reaching Globalist has real value – as well as the milestone choices along the way. The biggest benefit is confirming a suite at the time of booking with a Suite Upgrade Award for up to seven nights when an eligible standard suite is available for the stay. That’s a huge value on family trips. I also value having a My Hyatt Concierge I can email requests to, actual delivery of 4 p.m. late checkout at eligible properties, and a more generous breakfast benefit than I get from other chains. At participating hotels without an available club lounge, Globalist breakfast generally covers a full breakfast for up to two adults and two children registered in the room, including tax and gratuity. Late checkout has exceptions, including availability limits at resorts, but I’m usually proactively offered late checkout everywhere else (and personally find it honored more often than not at resorts). The Free Night Certificates Should Be More Flexible The current version of this card launched in 2018. Its annual certificate is still capped at Category 4, while category creep has taken away many of the hotels where I’d most want to use it. Just this year, 14 hotels moved from Category 4 to Category 5, including Hyatt Regency Seattle, Hyatt Regency Grand Cypress and Hyatt Regency Jersey City. Five moved the other way, bringing options like Hyatt Centric Congress Avenue Austin and Dream Nashville within reach, but the certificate lost more hotels than it gained.
