#6065. Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

In conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s new book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major issues of our time.

It’s often said that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

The sheer length of his new book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

Supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single issue in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most important foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”

Recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

“We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he says. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”

One of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

“I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

“The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling showed only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

Describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he says there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”

“I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden says. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

“I had it on good authority that several big names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

Biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

#6064. Accor’s $1.8 Billion Ennismore Buyout Tops 4 Rival Lifestyle Deals Combined

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Roswyn a Morgans Originals Hotel, Mumbai, set to open in March 2026. Ennismore

Hotel groups have spent years buying lifestyle brands. Accor just committed $1.8 billion to buyout the minority investors in its Ennismore joint venture. A comparison with past deals adds some enlightening context.

Accor's buyout of its partners in its Ennismore joint venture, announced Tuesday, is the largest amount a hotel group has paid for a lifestyle brand company to date.

The Paris-based group will pay about €1.6 billion (nearly $1.8 billion) in a multi-stage deal that values the lifestyle venture's equity at about €3.7 billion ($4.1 billion).

It's the latest in a string of lifestyle-brand purchases by major hotel groups. Marriott bought the citizenM brand for $355 million. Hilton got Graduate for $210 million. Hyatt paid $150 million upfront for The Standard, in a deal that eventually totaled about $335 million. IHG picked up Ruby for about $116 million.

Accor's buyout will be more than the four deals above, combined. A look at the deal and recent comparisons helps cast some light on the lifestyle trend and what Accor is betting on.

Tags: accor, citizenm, ennismore, graduate hotels, hilton, hotel brands, hyatt, marriott, skift intelligence, two roads hospitality

Skift provides the insights. You make the decisions.

Decision intelligence for travel leaders.

Accor will pay about €1.6 billion (nearly $1.8 billion) to buy out the minority holders of its Ennismore lifestyle joint venture, a multi-stage deal that values Ennismore's equity at about €3.7 billion ($4.1 billion) — the largest sum a hotel group has paid for a lifestyle brand company to date, and more than Marriott's citizenM, Hilton's Graduate, Hyatt's Standard International, and IHG's Ruby deals combined. What Accor is buying differs from those transactions: where Marriott and Hilton acquired trademarks and a fee stream, Ennismore brings brand teams, management contracts for nearly 200 hotels, a design studio, and more than 800 restaurants and bars, including Paris Society's venue collection. Ennismore accounts for about 20% of Accor's recurring EBITDA and generated €205 million in EBITDA in 2025, putting the deal at roughly 18 times earnings on both Accor's 2027 projection and Skift's calculation against 2025 results. That's the same multiple Accor used in 2022 when it sold a 10.8% stake to Qatari investors, and Ennismore's annual EBITDA has roughly doubled since. By comparison, Hyatt paid 12 to 13 times projected EBITDA for Two Roads Hospitality in 2018, and the recent brand-only deals ranged from about 9 to 15 times expected fees.

#6063. We Need a Better GOP

President Donald Trump attends the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, September 9, 2026.

The old Republican establishment could be out of touch, unimaginative, and too comfortable with revolving-door practices that enriched former officeholders and staffers, among other failings.

Beginning in 2016, Donald Trump burned this establishment to the ground and created a new one that has its own myriad deficiencies, some of which echo the failings of yore; the extremely online elements of today’s establishment, for instance, have found a whole new way to be out of touch.

We say this not to pine for yesterday’s establishment — parties never go back, only forward — but to make the point that every party elite reaches its point of exhaustion, and that’s where the Trump establishment is now.

There is a robust intramural argument on the right over how to interpret the historic loss in the midterms. We have our own views, but the most elemental need is a better GOP — one that is not beholden to the will of one man, doesn’t tolerate corruption, insists on strict adherence to the rule of law, encourages Congress to take up its allotted role in our constitutional system, rewards policy entrepreneurship on the part of officeholders, and focuses on results rather than performative provocations.

It’s possible to imagine any number of people leading such a national party, and it could have different ideological colorations depending on that leader and underlying circumstances. All that is TBD and should be a matter of fierce debate and competition. But unless the party moves beyond today’s establishment and renews itself, it risks subsequent devastating votes of no confidence from the American public.

Consider the issue of corruption, which was one of the biggest concerns of voters in the midterms. It is one thing for a party to suffer politically in the course of making progress on an important priority — say, stepped-up immigration enforcement. It is another to suffer from the perception — and, sadly, the reality — that politically connected people are engaged in untoward schemes for their own enrichment. The former is an inevitable political trade-off; the latter is a party’s elite feasting on its power and connections with no heed to the consequences for the larger cause.

President Trump, who has an overawing dominance over the party, is the source of many of the GOP’s current discontents. His influence is not going to drastically diminish anytime soon, and we know that many good Republicans have considered him better than the alternative, or have thrilled to his no-holds-barred assaults on the left. However one evaluates the Trump phenomenon, though, attempts to rely on the tropes that fueled his rise beginning in 2016, or ape his political style, will almost certainly fail — for the simple reasons that times change and Trump’s persona is not replicable.

The GOP could do much worse than look to the states, where Republican governors and legislators have cut taxes, restrained spending, pared back regulations, protected unborn children, and pursued reforms of schooling and housing. One reason that Florida constituted high ground beyond the reach of the blue wave is that it has been so well governed for so long, and it has had a series of reformist Republican governors focused on results.

At the national level, the GOP obviously needs a cost-of-living agenda that addresses high costs in health care, medicine, and education, and there’s much work that’s been done on these issues at the state level and among conservative policy thinkers. But arriving at a coherent agenda will require a seriousness of purpose and substantive focus that have been lacking for years now. That doesn’t mean the party should be dull and conventional — much can be learned from Trump’s zest for combat and vivid political branding — but it needs to recover a sense of institutional self-respect.

The new establishment, via President Trump, has worked its way back around to what were widely considered weaknesses of the old one. Republicans were once determined to make another push for amnesty after every election loss, and now, the president has floated that idea in response to the Democratic midterm victory; Republicans were once too soft on China, and Trump has been notably conciliatory in his second term; the GOP once talked a good game on deficit spending but didn’t do nearly enough to curtail it, while we are now adding to the debt hand over fist during a time of economic expansion and relative peace; the Tom DeLay–led Republican House was much too cozy with lobbyists, but prior GOP ethical lapses have been eclipsed over the past two years.

The old establishment had reached its expiration date and, regardless, isn’t coming back, while the current establishment is harmful to the party’s image and interests and an obstacle to change.

As Lincoln said, it is a time to think anew and act anew. The GOP desperately needs something fresh and different, with ideas and policies designed to meet the challenges of the day.

#6062. Klook’s AI Agent Handles the Admin, but Operators Want Help Selling

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Caption: The set of a Bollywood movie at Madame Tussauds Singapore. Travelers can buy tickets to this attraction and have their reservations instantly confirmed via Klook, an online travel agency that specializes in experiences. Madame Tussauds Singapore source Merlin Entertainments

Klook’s K.ai doesn’t just advise small operators. It makes the changes for them, and an early user says it is already saving time. The bigger payoff, for operators and for Klook, could come from the tools still in development, such as pricing advice that helps them sell more.

Every morning, staff at MyProGuide used to check inventory by hand, spending at least 30 minutes on each product. The tour-guide and day-tour supplier, which has sold on Klook for more than a decade, now hands much of that work to a recently released AI agent built into Klook’s merchant portal.

Founder Jo Wong said the agent, K.ai, already helps his 35 staff review bookings, spot products nearing capacity and pull together complex data more quickly. What he wants next is harder to deliver: pricing recommendations, market price comparisons and booking-trend analysis, the tools that could help him sell more. For now, he is using K.ai to run daily operations rather than to drive bookings.

K.ai is aimed at the small operators that make up most of the experience sector. It takes instructions in plain language. Ask for last week’s bookings and it pulls a report. Tell it

Klook has released K.ai, an AI agent built into its merchant portal that takes plain-language instructions from tour and activity operators — pulling booking reports, previewing and applying price changes, drafting product listings, and flagging shifts in performance using review and sales data. Co-founder and CTO Bernie Xiong said Klook is rolling it out in phases worldwide ahead of the year-end travel season and aims to reach all merchants by the end of the year, free for now, because many experiences merchants don't have dedicated teams for technology or back-office work. Klook said early users completed individual pricing and inventory updates 95% faster, and that merchants using K.ai recorded 3.4 times as many monthly bookings as those who didn't — a comparison drawn from a randomly selected early-rollout group in which merchants chose whether to use the tool, so it may partly reflect differences between the merchants themselves. The pitch lands in the least digitized part of travel: Klook, citing Euromonitor, said about 34% of experiences bookings are made online, against 66% for accommodation and 81% for flights, and small and midsize operators make up about 95% of the sector. MyProGuide founder Jo Wong, who used to spend at least 30 minutes a day checking inventory by hand for each product, said the agent now handles daily operations for his 35 staff. What he wants next — pricing recommendations, market price comparisons, and booking-trend analysis — is still being developed.

Some pretty significant changes are coming for Hyatt loyalists in 2027.

After introducing a five-tier award chart and annual category changes this May, we weren't sure what to expect with this announcement — but the good news is that the updates are largely positive, save for a few changes that might frustrate higher-tier members.

"We’re shaping the future of World of Hyatt around what our members value most. After a year of listening, one thing is clear: members want more distinctive benefits, more freedom to use their awards, and the opportunity to choose awards that matter most to them,” said Laurie Blair, senior vice president, global marketing and loyalty, Hyatt. “We’re continuing to deliver more of what members want, with the ability to combine valuable awards, earn Tier Qualifying Nights faster, and choose more of the experiences they love. Together, these new options make every milestone a chance to personalize the journey ahead."

From a newly minted Delta partnership (with exciting double-dipping benefits) and more flexibility with awards and earnings, here is what we know about the changes, which will go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Related: Complete guide to the World of Hyatt loyalty program

For years, Hyatt has allowed members to redeem one award per stay. If you wanted to use a Category 1-7 certificate, you couldn't also use a Suite Upgrade Award. If you gifted Category 1-4 certificates to friends or family members, they couldn't also use Guest of Honor awards to receive your Globalist benefits.

Starting Jan. 1, members will be able to stack Free Night Awards, Suite Upgrade Awards, Guest of Honor Awards and Free Parking Awards (more on this in a bit) on the same reservation. This is a fantastic improvement that addresses a key frustration for many loyal members, who currently must carefully pick which award makes the most sense on a given stay.

In addition, all awards will now be available for 365 days from the date of issuance.

This is great news for the free-night certificates you earn through Hyatt's Milestone Rewards, which were previously valid for only six months. Next year, you'll have twice as much time to use them.

However, this will negatively impact Suite Upgrade Awards.

Today, you can select these upgrades starting at 40 nights, and when you do, they're valid through the end of the year plus an additional 14 months. Now, they'll have a shorter window of validity — potentially much shorter.

For example, if you reached 40 nights on Aug. 1, 2026, and immediately picked a Suite Upgrade Award, it'll expire Feb. 28, 2028 — giving you 19 months to use it. If you hit that same threshold on July 15, 2027, and again picked an upgrade immediately, it'll only be valid through July 14, 2028.

You'll still have up to 90 days to select each milestone reward, so come 2027, you may want to wait until the end of that window to commit to an upgrade award if you don't have an immediate use for it.

Related: How to redeem Hyatt points for free nights and more

One of the biggest changes within this update to the World of Hyatt program is the flexibility of Milestone Rewards — and the rewards themselves. Starting in January, Milestone Rewards will now begin at 10 qualifying nights or 20,000 Base Points, with additional milestones every 10 qualifying nights, up to 150 nights per calendar year.

Additionally, the company has added a handful of new awards, including the following:

Here is a full breakdown of your choices starting Jan. 1, 2027:

In addition to the new options, you'll have additional flexibility at certain milestones.

For example, the 30-night milestone is currently a Category 1-4 certificate plus a choice of other options. Now, you can choose between that award or 10,000 bonus points, plus a second choice among five options. And at 60 nights, rather than the one-size-fits-all approach, with the same four rewards for every member, you now get to pick three of the four.

Unfortunately, there are three (potentially) negative changes to flag here:

Losing free parking on award stays is a notable loss, as is the reduction in Suite Upgrade Awards. That said, just how impactful these are will depend on your individual stay habits.

In September, Delta and Hyatt announced an upcoming partnership, and we've finally learned about the details — and yes, elite SkyMiles and World of Hyatt members will be able to "double-dip" with their hotel stay and flight earnings.

As noted by TPG writer Sean Cudahy, there are two primary things to keep in mind about the Delta-Hyatt partnership:

When Delta SkyMiles and World of Hyatt members link their accounts, they'll be able to access the new Delta Milestone Rewards detailed above starting in 2027. These rewards start at 20 qualifying nights or 35,000 Base Points and include eCertificates, Delta Sky Club passes and even opportunities to earn Medallion Status.

Finally, World of Hyatt will also debut an updated booking flow through its app and website that will make it easier to tailor your trip to your needs and rewards. Right now, the "Pay My Way" options are fairly limited — essentially just cash or points. The new flow will give much more flexibility.

"Members can select, gift and redeem eligible awards online or in the World of Hyatt app, while an enhanced Pay My Way experience will let members tailor payment for each night using awards, points, cash or Points + Cash," the company shared in the press release.

Overall, we're calling these changes a net positive. The ability to combine awards on a single stay is the standout here, and it's great to have the extra time to use many awards that currently have a very limited window. The new Delta-Hyatt tie-up is also exciting, with reciprocal earning opportunities for elite members of each program. Finally, it's great to see an expanded list of Milestone Rewards and additional flexibility in customizing them.

That said, there are some notable drawbacks here, especially the loss of free parking on award stays for Globalists — though it's nice to have a transition period through February 2028 before that takes effect for existing Globalists.

As a reminder, these new perks won't launch until Jan. 1, 2027, so it's status quo until then.

The World of Hyatt program is making several changes that'll impact its most frequent guests starting in 2027. Between the long-awaited benefit of being able to combine awards, a slew of new Milestone Rewards and some shiny new partner perks with Delta, Hyatt is adding a lot of new potential value for members. Of course, it's not all positive — but many of us here at TPG are excited about what's to come.

What do you think about these program updates? Feel free to sound off in the comments section below!

#6060. 3 Women Stranded By FAA Nationwide Ground Stop Bought A $48,000 Ford Bronco—Then Drove 27 Hours Home

Three women stranded in Charlotte after Friday’s nationwide flight grounding bought a $48,000 Ford Bronco and drove 27 hours home to North Dakota. They’d gone away for work training. They came home with a new car. Tara Harding (I first read this as Tonya Harding) and two employees needed to get back to their families in Bismarck, and had patients to see Monday morning. Tara Harding and her employees were at the airport trying to get home from a work trip when a nationwide ground stop left them stranded in Charlotte, North Carolina — roughly 1,600 miles from home in Bismarck, North Dakota. She found a $48,000 solution in the form of a new Ford Bronco. https://t.co/xpP9fmCsm8 — NBC News (@NBCNews) November 16, 2026 They couldn’t find a rental car within four hours of Charlotte. They tried other ways home, including a train, bus and U-Haul. None worked. Delta Air Lines left them stranded. Harding’s mother-in-law suggested buying a car. They bought the Bronco with no money down. Harding initially planned to sell it to a dealership once they reached home. The women took turns driving and sleeping. While flights resumed at 8:15 p.m. Eastern on Friday, over 18,000 trips were cancelled and there simply weren’t seats to accommodate all passengers on later flights and it took several days to clear everyone out. There’s a calculation in buying the car, deducting depreciation, taxes and fees, financing costs and operating expenses, and selling it on the other end. There’s a very close precedent. During Southwest Airlines’ Christmas 2022 meltdown, a couple bought a $500 used car to get home, and Southwest reimbursed them. This incident wasn’t any airline’s fault. In the end, Harding abandoned the plan to resell the car. Tara Harding (I first read this as Tonya Harding) and two employees needed to get back to their families in Bismarck, and had patients to see Monday morning.

Tara Harding and her employees were at the airport trying to get home from a work trip when a nationwide ground stop left them stranded in Charlotte, North Carolina — roughly 1,600 miles from home in Bismarck, North Dakota.

She found a $48,000 solution in the form of a new Ford Bronco. https://t.co/xpP9fmCsm8

They couldn’t find a rental car within four hours of Charlotte. They tried other ways home, including a train, bus and U-Haul. None worked. Delta Air Lines left them stranded. Harding’s mother-in-law suggested buying a car.

They bought the Bronco with no money down. Harding initially planned to sell it to a dealership once they reached home. The women took turns driving and sleeping.

While flights resumed at 8:15 p.m. Eastern on Friday, over 18,000 trips were cancelled and there simply weren’t seats to accommodate all passengers on later flights and it took several days to clear everyone out.

There’s a calculation in buying the car, deducting depreciation, taxes and fees, financing costs and operating expenses, and selling it on the other end. There’s a very close precedent. During Southwest Airlines’ Christmas 2022 meltdown, a couple bought a $500 used car to get home, and Southwest reimbursed them. This incident wasn’t any airline’s fault. In the end, Harding abandoned the plan to resell the car.

Traveling nurses can make more than doctors. Google AI says that a doctor specializing in pediatric infectious diseases can, in an entire lifetime if they have a lot of student loans, never reach the lifetime earnings of a nurse and be $2.5 million behind by age 65.

Also contributing is that nurses pay increases but doctors pay gets cut by Congress every year in the form of reduction in Medicare payments, which private insurance copies. Both BidenAndTrump have done this. Doctors are banned by federal law from unionizing to negotiate with Medicare or private insurance. Hospitals are allowed to buy doctor’s practices and bill Medicare for a facility fee added to every office visit but doctors are banned from charging a facility fee because hospitals and insurance companies have powerful lobbies but doctors do not (The AMA routinely does not lobby much for doctors pay but does lobby for its CPT code licensing system for billing).

Source: several doctors that I’ve talked with on flights.

Overall it probably was something she planned to do anyway and just worked out she could buy it in Charlotte and drive home.

Oh yeah @1990 – you keep going on about protections like EU261. That wouldn’t apply, even in the EU, if the air traffic control system went down. If you can’t deal with uncertainty in life you are over extended or inflexible. Get over it – stuff happens.

(Matt and I were having fun. No one expects a free $48K Jeep after their flight gets cancelled. Duty of care, rebooking, basic compensation if its the airlines fault, yeah, all that is reasonable, and would make for a better system, here, too.)

EU 261 would not give any cash payout in this situation, since outside the control of the airline. However, you’d be entitled to refund or rebooking, and if taking rebooking, duty of care remains. That pretty much only pays accommodations, meals and incidentals. I remember this well from being in Germany at the time of the Icelandic volcano eruption in 2010. Even then, the LCCs fought the duty of care in the courts and I’m not sure many passengers outside the major carriers were able to collect. Remember, it is not as easy to sue in the EU as in the US.

Indian arrivals to Vietnam are growing more than twice as fast as the overall market, and Vietnamese carriers are chasing that demand into cities like Ahmedabad. Seats alone won’t lock it in, though. Vietnam still needs the food, guides, and wedding and events products Indian travelers expect.

Vietnam’s airlines are adding flights to India as arrivals from one of the country’s fastest-growing source markets show no sign of slowing.

Sun PhuQuoc Airways will launch Ahmedabad-Phu Quoc flights on Dec. 3, and Vietnam Airlines will take its Delhi and Bengaluru services to daily from Dec. 14. That comes weeks after Vietnam Airlines opened its own Ahmedabad route.

Low-cost carrier VietJet today runs the most extensive network between the two countries, connecting Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang with six Indian cities.

Vietnam welcomed 746,000 Indian visitors in 2025, making India its sixth-largest international source market. Arrivals rose from 138,000 in 2022 to 507,000 in 2024. In the first nine months of 2026, the country received 670,972 Indian visitors, according to Vietnam’s National Statistics Office.

Vietnam's carriers are adding capacity to India as Indian arrivals keep climbing. Sun PhuQuoc Airways launches Ahmedabad–Phu Quoc on Dec. 3 with five weekly flights, going daily from early February 2027, and Vietnam Airlines takes its Delhi–Hanoi and Bengaluru–Hanoi services to daily from Dec. 14, weeks after opening Ahmedabad–Hanoi on Nov. 3. VietJet currently operates the most extensive network between the two countries, linking Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City, and Da Nang with six Indian cities. Vietnam received 746,000 Indian visitors in 2025, its sixth-largest source market, up from 138,000 in 2022. In the first nine months of 2026, Indian arrivals reached 670,972 and grew 33% year over year, more than twice Vietnam's overall international arrivals growth of 14.5%. Booking.com data shared with Skift ranked Vietnam among the top three most-searched international destinations for Indian travelers this year, and Ixigo said bookings to Vietnam have doubled year on year. Demand extends beyond leisure into weddings, corporate travel, and events, with provincial authorities in Khanh Hoa and Quang Ninh now building India into their tourism plans. Vietnam's tourism industry has called for more India-focused products, including wedding packages, Indian food options at hotels, culturally familiar guides, and Hindi-language marketing.

#6057. How Marriott Members Can Sometimes Earn Points Twice On The Same Spending

A Marriott Bonvoy member reports earning qualifying spend or extra points by charging gift card purchases to the room bill even though Marriott expressly excludes gift card purchases from the spending requirement for Ambassador status. Ambassador takes 100 qualifying nights and $23,000 in annual qualifying spend. Someone staying at inexpensive and even moderately-priced hotels can clear the nights while falling well short on dollars. If a gift card counts when you buy it, you could move future hotel spending into the current qualification year. And if the purchase and the eventual hotel stay both earn points, you’ve earned twice on the same money. An April 4 report on US Card Forum laid out some properties where this worked, and where it didn’t. Property   Reported result Ritz-Carlton Waikiki spa   Gift cards charged to the room counted toward qualifying spend. St. Regis Longboat Key   Two $1,500 cards purchased, then used at checkout; the member reports an extra round of points. Tampa EDITION   Allowed the gift-card room charge; no separate points or spending total supplied. JW Marriott Clearwater   Refused to put the purchase on the room bill. Unnamed hotel, separate commenter   A charge labeled “gc” reached the folio but earned no points. Marriott’s terms (section 4.2.b.v) exclude Marriott Gift Card purchases from Annual Qualifying Spend. The Ambassador help page says the same thing. This comes down to how the hotel records the charge and sends it to Marriott. If a gift card sale goes through as an eligible incidental, the loyalty system credits the amount without recognizing what was actually sold. A properly identified gift card entry gets excluded. There are two places this can fail: the hotel can refuse the room charge, or accept it but keep it out of the amount eligible for points and status. An employee saying “yes, we can charge that to your room” doesn’t tell you whether it will post as eligible spend. I’ve covered another example of hotel level accounting producing more Ambassador credit than you’d expect. In 2024, the Renaissance Dallas advertised a rate with 30% additional qualifying spend for $20 extra per night. That suggested how the property’s handling of a charge can affect the way Marriott credits it. If you’re a Marriott person, who’s going to spend money with them anyway (clearly an Ambassador member does) this is an interesting thing to experiment with but I also wouldn’t hit it too hard with an Ambassador account that I valued. Me, I haven’t been an Ambassador since the end of the Starwood days. #6056. Climate Change Could Squeeze a Third of Tourist Destinations by 2050

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Climate change won’t just bring more extreme weather. It will shorten the seasons and change the activities many destinations are built on. Operators should be planning now for shoulder seasons and cooler-hour itineraries, not waiting for the next heat wave.

Climate change is coming for the tourist season.

More than a third of destinations could see conditions for sightseeing, swimming and hiking worsen by 2050, according to a new report, and some of travel’s biggest beach regions could lose months of good weather.

The report, by NGO Travel Forward, risk modeling firm Risklayer, and the Dutch public-private partnership Centre of Expertise Leisure, Tourism and Hospitality (CELTH), models climate hazards and conditions for common tourist activities across 2,588 destinations in 263 countries and territories.

Called Destination Climate RiskScan, it found that 36% of destinations would be “squeezed” by 2050 under a moderate emissions scenario, facing more extreme weather and a climate less suited to common tourism activities. That  percentage soars to 62% by 2050 under a high emission scenario.

Decision intelligence for travel leaders.

A new report modeling climate conditions across 2,588 destinations in 263 countries finds that 36% of them could be "squeezed" by 2050 under a moderate emissions scenario — facing more climate hazards alongside worse conditions for sightseeing, swimming, hiking, and camping — with that figure rising to 62% under high emissions. The Destination Climate RiskScan, produced by NGO Travel Forward, risk modeling firm Risklayer, and Dutch partnership CELTH, scores hazard exposure and activity suitability on a 0–100 index. The steepest declines land in the hottest regions: Caribbean hiking and camping could fall 53 points by 2080 under high emissions, Southeast Asian swimming 48 points, and Mediterranean hiking and camping 48 points. Southeast Asia's typical beach and swimming season could shrink from eight months in 2010 to three by 2080, and the Caribbean's from 10 to six. Northern Europe and the Nordics are projected to become more comfortable for every activity assessed except skiing, though the ski model excluded artificial snowmaking. The authors stress these are measures of climatic suitability, not forecasts of visitor demand or commercial viability. The report lands as policymakers meet at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, where tourism is a thematic focus.

#6055. She Lived to the Sound of God’s Music

Remembering God’s gift to New York City girls and beyond.

From left: Sr. Christine Cosgrove, O.P., the author, Sr. Martha Kunesh, O.P., and speaker Kristen Hanson, an advocate against assisted suicide, at a National Review Institute/Sheen Center event on the virtue of hope.

Could anything sound more exotic today? This opening line comes from a 16th-century prayer by the Carmelite reformer St. Teresa of Avila. She carried it in the breviary she used for daily prayer. It also captures the quiet steadiness of Sister Martha Kunesh, O.P. (the initials stand for “Order of Preachers”), who entered a Dominican convent just before the opening of the Second Vatican Council. She took the religious name Sister Teresa Avila (“the ‘of’ was silent,” it was said). She eventually returned to her birth name, but she never lost the contemplative spirit of her first patron.

Kathryn Jean Lopez is a senior fellow at the National Review Institute and the religion editor of National Review. Sign up for her weekly newsletter here. She is the author of A Year with the Mystics: Visionary Wisdom for Daily Living.

National Review Institute is a non-profit, 501(c)(3), journalistic think tank that preserves and promotes William F. Buckley Jr.’s legacy, supports the National Review mission, and advances the principles of a free society through educational and outreach programs. All contributions to it are deductible for income, gift, and estate tax purposes. EIN# 13-3649537

#6054. Hyatt And Delta Launch Extra Points On Flights And Hotel Stays—But Standard Coach Tickets Don’t Qualify

Hyatt and Delta have launched extra points on flights and hotel stays, with airline status, lounge passes and hotel free night awards coming next year. But there’s a big restriction: even a Hyatt Globalist buying a regular Delta coach ticket earns no Hyatt points. That’s not ‘basic economy doesn’t count’ – it’s listerally standard main cabin coach that earns nothing. The companies announced their partnership in September. Now we know how the benefits actually work. This brings back some of what Hyatt members lost when American Airlines stopped reciprocal points earning at the end of 2024. But Delta excludes regular coach, gives Hyatt’s lowest elite tier half as many points, and pays hotel guests in a less valuable airline currency (SkyMiles). Who Earns Extra Points And Miles Start by linking your World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles accounts. Ongoing extra earning depends on your status: Your Status   Additional Earnings Delta Silver, Gold, Platinum or Diamond Medallion   1 SkyMile per eligible dollar spent with Hyatt, on top of Hyatt points Hyatt Discoverist   1 Hyatt point per $2 of eligible Delta premium cabin spending, on top of SkyMiles Hyatt Explorist, Globalist or Lifetime Globalist   1 Hyatt point per eligible dollar of Delta premium cabin spending, on top of SkyMiles Hyatt status qualifies you for Hyatt points on eligible Delta flights. Delta status qualifies you for SkyMiles on eligible Hyatt spending. For flights, Delta Comfort, Premium Select, First Class and Delta One qualify. Basic, Classic and Extra fare versions qualify when they’re sold in one of those cabins. So basic extra legroom coach qualifies, full fair regular coach doesn’t. . The flight earning rules also require: A Delta marketed and operated flight, with a Delta-issued ticket beginning 006. Your SkyMiles number attached before departure and Hyatt elite status when the flight is completed. A qualifying paid ticket. Eligible spending includes the base fare and airline imposed surcharges, but excludes government taxes, airport fees and amounts paid with miles. These are Hyatt bonus points. They don’t count as base points toward Hyatt status or lifetime Globalist. For hotel spending, eligible room charges, incidentals and qualifying purchases without an overnight stay can earn SkyMiles. Mr & Mrs Smith and The Venetian qualify when booked through Hyatt. Homes & Hideaways and FIND experiences are excluded. Hyatt Nights Can Earn Delta Credits, Lounge Visits And Status Beginning January 1, 2027, linked Hyatt members will have Delta options among their Milestone Rewards. These are choices, so you’ll need to compare them with the other rewards available at the same threshold. The specific awards are: Hyatt Qualification   Delta Reward Choice 20 qualifying nights or 35,000 base points   $25 Delta eCertificate 40 qualifying nights or 65,000 base points   $75 Delta eCertificate 60 qualifying nights or 100,000 base points   $100 Delta eCertificate 70, 80 or 90 qualifying nights   Two single visit Delta Sky Club passes 100 qualifying nights   Delta Gold Medallion status 150 qualifying nights   Delta Platinum Medallion status, without Choice Benefits The flight certificates and lounge passes expire one year after issuance. Each lounge pass covers one person for one visit with a qualifying same-day boarding pass (basic economy passengers excluded). The status awards are for your own account. They don’t provide anything extra if you already hold that tier or higher, and selecting the same status again doesn’t extend it. Platinum at 150 nights is potentially attractive, albeith without the Choice Benefits that normally come with that status (e.g. four Regional Upgrade Certificates). Delta Elites Can Choose Hyatt Free Nights Starting February 1, 2027, for the 2028 Medallion Year, Delta is adding: A Hyatt Category 1–4 free night as a Platinum Choice Benefit. A Hyatt Category 1–7 free night as a Diamond Choice Benefit. These aren’t extra certificates automatically handed to every Platinum and Diamond. You select one instead of another Choice Benefit. No new option to redeem SkyMiles directly for Hyatt free night certificates was announced, like we’d seen with the American partnership. Perhaps the biggest loss is Hyatt redemptions for American Airlines status for a day. Launch Bonuses Don’t Require Elite Status All linked members can participate in the launch offers: November 17–December 31, 2026: Register separately and complete a qualifying Hyatt stay to earn one additional qualifying night credit. That’s one bonus night total, not double nights for the entire stay. January 4–February 15, 2027: Complete your first eligible paid Delta Comfort-or-higher flight to earn 1,000 bonus Hyatt points. January 4–February 15, 2027: Complete your first qualifying Hyatt stay to earn 1,000 bonus SkyMiles. Paid and award stays qualify for the hotel promotions. Mr & Mrs Smith and The Venetian bookings through Hyatt qualify, while Homes & Hideaways doesn’t. The year-end stay must finish after registration and by December 31. For the January hotel offer, checkout must be by February 15. There’s also an Alila Mayakoba trip sweepstakes through November 23. Hyatt says reciprocal status challenges are coming. Is This Better Than Hyatt’s American Airlines Partnership? There are two different American partnerships to compare against. The original version, which ran through 2024, was better for everyday earning. Hyatt Discoverists earned the same one point per dollar on American airfare as Globalists, and regular coach counted. American elites earned a mile per eligible Hyatt dollar, and those miles also counted as Loyalty Points once that status system was introduced. Delta’s hotel earning has the same nominal mileage rate, but American miles are worth more. And there’s no status credit from those points. American’s final double earning terms also covered eligible FIND and Homes & Hideaways spending, both excluded here. On the flight side you’re earning Hyatt points either way, so the problem isn’t SkyMiles valuation. It’s the cabins that don’t qualify and the halved Discoverist rate. The 2025 American redesign removed double dipping and largely made members pay for partner benefits with their own points or by giving up another reward. Delta restores some actual additional earnings. The milestone comparison is mixed: Flight credits can be more useful than seat coupons. American offered two Preferred Seat coupons at 20 and 30 nights, then two Main Cabin Extra coupons at 40 and 50. Delta status starts later. American Gold was a choice at 70, 80 and 90 Hyatt nights. Delta offers lounge passes there, with its first announced status award at 100 nights. At 150 nights, Delta offers a higher tier. American’s offer topped out at Platinum. Delta Platinum is its third tier, although withholding Choice Benefits takes away a valuable part of the package. American also gave ConciergeKey members Hyatt Globalist and offered Hyatt status choices to other AAdvantage members. We’ll see what reciprocal status offers look like. It’s worth linking accounts and registering for the extra Hyatt night if there’s a stay coming up. #6053. Gabe Evans announces 2028 comeback bid from Boebert’s district

Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.

His announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

As part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he said.

The district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

Evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

“Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign said in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”

A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and currently sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

Laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign said she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie said in a statement.

#6052. Air India Express Names Finance Chief as CEO to Turn Growth Into Profit

Photo Caption: Air India Express aircraft Air India Express

Air India and Air India Express now both have new CEOs, and the group’s transformation looks steadier for it. The harder test is whether the new leaders can cut losses that are still running in the billions.

Air India Express on Wednesday announced the appointment of its chief financial officer Deepak Rajawat as CEO, effective Dec. 1, placing a finance and commercial executive at the helm as the airline enters a more demanding phase of its growth under Tata Group, which controls the Air India Group.

Rajawat succeeds Aloke Singh, who left in March to join rival IndiGo as chief strategy officer. Singh oversaw the fleet growing from 26 planes to more than 100, and its merger with AirAsia India also took place on his watch.

The new CEO brings more than two decades of aviation experience, including a stint as chief commercial officer at Vistara, the Tata-Singapore Airlines joint venture that merged into Air India

Air India Express has named its chief financial officer, Deepak Rajawat, as CEO effective December 1, putting a finance and commercial executive in charge as the Tata Group's low-cost carrier moves from rapid fleet expansion to improving efficiency and financial performance. Rajawat succeeds Aloke Singh, who left in March for IndiGo, where he is now chief strategy officer; Singh oversaw growth from 26 planes to more than 100 and the AirAsia India merger. The appointment lands against heavy group losses: Air India Group reported a combined net loss of about $2.3 billion in fiscal 2026, more than double the prior year, and Singapore Airlines, which owns 25.1% of Air India, booked $281.5 million as its share of those losses for the six months to September 30. Air India Express itself was hit by foreign exchange losses and operational disruptions in fiscal 2026, and management has said it will prioritize cost rationalization, network optimization, and revenue enhancement. New Air India CEO Tewolde Gebremariam has been exploring shared corporate functions and cost reductions across the two airlines, even as they pursue different growth strategies. Rajawat inherits about 585 daily flights, 48 domestic and 17 international destinations, a fleet of more than 100 Boeing 737s and Airbus A320s, and a group plan to allocate 190 of the 470 aircraft ordered to Air India Express.

#6051. Chase Adds Qantas And Cathay Pacific Transfers—More Access To Premium Award Seats

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Chase is adding Qantas and Cathay Pacific as 1:1 transfer partners on November 18. For me, the biggest value is access to business and first class award seats that these airlines don’t make available to members of other frequent flyer programs.

These are Chase’s first new airline transfer partners in more than five years. And they’re an unambiguously positive addition, even if neither becomes the program most cardmembers use most often.

Eligible cards include Chase Sapphire Reserve, Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve for Business, Ink Business Preferred and J.P. Morgan Reserve. Both new partners transfer at 1:1. Hyatt transfers are now less generous for Sapphire Preferred and Ink Business Preferred: 4 Chase points become 3 Hyatt points, while the Reserve cards retain 1:1. That distinction doesn’t apply to these new airline partners. Chase Sapphire Reserve® (See rates and fees) is a strong card for actual spending, with 4 points per dollar on flights and hotels booked directly and 3 points per dollar on dining. Adding more transfer partners makes the value of those points even greater. Why I Want Qantas Points Chase already had ways to book oneworld flights through programs like British Airways and Iberia. But being able to book an airline doesn’t mean having access to all of its award seats. Airlines increasingly keep more of their premium cabin availability for their own members. As I explained when Rove added Qantas transfers, Qantas offers its members award space that American AAdvantage, Alaska and British Airways members can’t book. I have family in Australia and have had real success finding Qantas business class awards when there’s flexibility over the U.S. gateway and travel date. I’ll set alerts across several flights rather than insist on one. Some flight between Australia and the U.S. will inevitably open up with a couple of business class awards, usually around 60 days out. Qantas can also be useful for Emirates redemptions. I’d generally rather book the same available Emirates business class seat through Copa ConnectMiles, though. Copa charges 80,000 miles one way between the U.S. and Dubai in business class without fuel surcharges. And Qantas is no longer an unrestricted way around Emirates’ first class award limits. Booking Emirates first class with Qantas points requires Qantas Silver status or higher, and passengers must be at least nine years old. Cathay Offers More Award Space And Lower British Airways Surcharges Cathay Pacific is similar. Its own members get access to far more premium cabin award space than members of partner programs. Asia Miles prices can be high, though. I also like Asia Miles for reducing fuel surcharges on British Airways awards, particularly compared with booking through American AAdvantage. It’s also notable that Chase’s Cathay transfer rate is better than American Express’s. American Express transfers 1,000 Membership Rewards points to just 800 Asia Miles. An award requiring 100,000 Asia Miles takes 100,000 Chase points versus 125,000 Amex points (without transfer bonus). American Express, Citi, Capital One and Rove already partner with both Qantas and Cathay. Chase is catching up with these. I wouldn’t transfer points just because these options have been added. Chase Is Finally Adding Airline Partners Again Chase’s last new transfer partner was Wyndham Rewards in February 2026. Its last new airline partner was Air Canada Aeroplan on August 3, 2021. I welcomed Wyndham because it showed Chase was building out Ultimate Rewards, even though I had little interest in transferring points there. Qantas and Cathay are programs I can see myself using. They bring Chase to 12 airline transfer programs and four hotel programs. I also wonder whether these relationships could lead to more Points Boost opportunities. With Points Boost, Chase can use discounts it negotiates on paid tickets to offer more value per point through its travel portal. More airline relationships could help them offer more flights, more dates, or better redemption values. Qantas has already appeared in Points Boost, and American Airlines has participated without being a Chase transfer partner. But I’d love to see deeper relationships produce more opportunities to redeem at 2 cents per point for premium cabin tickets in the future. #6050. Abu Dhabi Holds Its F1 Hotel Rates as Doha Cuts

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Yas Marina Circuit that hosts the F1 in Abu Dhabi. DCT Abu Dhabi

Abu Dhabi is defending its F1 rate premium on a thinner base of bookings, while Doha has already cut. Late, local-heavy demand will decide whether that holds or forces last-minute discounting.

Abu Dhabi hotels are pricing this year’s Formula 1 weekend at last year’s level despite the U.S.-Iran war, while Doha’s race-weekend rates have fallen 29%.

Abu Dhabi hotels are advertising race-weekend rooms (Dec. 3-5) at an average of AED 2,692 ($733) a night, up 2.4% on last year, according to hospitality analytics firm Lighthouse. That is 184% above the weekend before (AED 948) and 116% more than the weekend after (AED 1,244).

In Doha, asking hotel rates for the Nov. 26-28 race weekend average QAR 1,206 ($331), down 29% from 2025. The rates are 67% above the weekend before (QAR 720) and 78% above the weekend after (QAR 677).

Gulf hotels are heading into the final two races of the 2026 Formula 1 season with sharply different pricing. Abu Dhabi hotels are advertising race-weekend rooms for Dec. 3-5 at an average of AED 2,692 ($733) a night, up 2.4% on last year and 184% above the weekend before, according to Lighthouse. Doha's asking rates for the Nov. 26-28 race weekend average QAR 1,206 ($331), down 29% year over year, though still 67% above the preceding weekend. Short-term rentals show the same split: race-weekend ADR on the books is up 44.7% in Abu Dhabi and down 8.6% in Doha, while demand nights on the books are down about a third in both cities, according to AirDNA data as of Nov. 10. Search patterns have changed too. Lighthouse's Blake Reiter said last year's steady October and November search build-up has not happened this year and weekly searches have stayed flat, with people booking later in the cycle. Local residents account for a larger share of hotel searches in both cities since the second week of September, U.S. search volume for Abu Dhabi is down 67%, and the U.S. share of Doha searches has fallen to 1.4% from 4.8%. Formula 1 said on Nov. 10 that it had stood down Imola as a backup venue and that the Qatar and Abu Dhabi Grands Prix would go ahead as planned, after the cancellation of races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia in April.

JSX, the boutique semi-private flight operator, is launching a new daily route between New York City and Dallas, the company announced this week.

The new service will fly to Dallas Love Field (DAL) starting on Feb. 17, with one daily flight in each direction.

JSX did not immediately disclose which airport in New York it plans to fly from. JSX typically flies to New York’s Teterboro Airport (TEB) and Westchester County Airport (HPN), although various restrictions set by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey mean that JSX cannot publicly promote TEB as a destination.

Those restrictions limit JSX to only selling those New York flights to members of its free Club JSX program, which offers rewards and has no minimum spending or flying requirements. When logged into that platform, the new route is currently bookable from TEB.

Club JSX: Earn rewards and fly in comfort with JSX’s new loyalty program

The carrier will use its Embraer E145 aircraft on the route, which can seat up to 30 passengers in a 1-1 configuration. Introductory fares start at $799 one-way.

"New York City and Dallas are two of America's most influential business and cultural centers, and we believe traveling between them should be as seamless as the opportunities that connect them,” Alex Wilcox, CEO of JSX, said in a statement. "With this new daily service, we're bringing the simplicity, comfort, and convenience of JSX to one of the country's most important travel corridors."

The new flight to Dallas is JSX second New York City expansion in as many weeks; the carrier announced new flights between New York and Boston earlier this month. The Dallas route is the company's fifth route from New York — aside from Boston, JSX flies from New York to Fort Lauderdale Executive Airport (FXE); Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport (OPF); Naples Airport (APF); and President Donald J. Trump International Airport (DJT), formerly known as Palm Beach International, all in Florida.

JSX operates out of 30 airports across the U.S. and Mexico and functions as a public charter service, rather than a formal "airline." This lets the carrier's flights work more like private ones — although anyone can buy a ticket, the flights use posh private Fixed-Base Operators (FBOs) instead of public airport terminals. That allows passengers to venture from curb to seat in just 20 minutes.

More: JSX eyes more turboprops and new mountain routes after strong passenger response

The flight experience itself is equally luxurious with no middle seats, lots of legroom, Starlink Wi-Fi, complimentary snacks and drinks and checked luggage that’s returned right at the side of the plane. The carrier has a fleet of 56 ERJ-family jets and 4 ATR 42-600 turboprop aircraft. Overall, the service pitches the idea of private jet convenience for a fraction of the cost.

JSX passengers used to bypass security screening, like passengers on most private flights. In 2025, the carrier implemented its own in-house screening process to address security concerns.

#6048. World Of Hyatt Status Revamps For 2027—Award Stacking And New Benefit Choices, But Cuts Come Also

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Hyatt will finally let members combine a free night certificate with a confirmed suite upgrade starting January 1, 2027. I’ve wanted that for years. They’re also extending milestone free night certificates from 180 days to a year, and adding rewards after just 10 qualifying nights.

This isn’t an across the board improvement. Suite upgrades will expire sooner. The suite upgrade choice at 50 nights gets cut in half. And My Hyatt Concierge becomes something you select alongside other rewards, rather than something everyone automatically receives at 60 nights. Free parking will no longer be an automatic benefit on award stays for Globalists.

When I covered Hyatt’s last major status benefit refresh in November 2023, I liked it overall. They made awards transferable, added choices, and let members try Globalist benefits before earning Globalist. Guest of Honor became limited, but the Milestone Rewards themselves mostly got better.

This time there are new and better options. I genuinely like a lot of the choices, but there are real tradeoffs. Hyatt is pitching the changes as more choice and flexibility, based on listening to members. That’s actually fair for much of this, though I don’t think members told them what they really wanted was for suite upgrade to expire up to a year earlier.

Hyatt will allow members to combine eligible awards on the same reservation, including Suite Upgrade Awards, Guest of Honor Awards and the new Free Parking Awards. This fixes one of the problems I’ve been complaining about for years. A free night certificate is something you often want to use on a special leisure stay. That’s also when a suite may matter most, especially traveling with family. When I didn’t want to use a free night certificate was a work trip by myself. Free night awards had a lot less value to me because I had to give up a confirmed suite to use them. But being able to use the two awards together makes both more valuable. Combining Guest of Honor with a suite upgrade is useful, too. You can give someone Globalist treatment and confirm their suite ahead of time, rather than leaving the room upgrade to availability when they arrive. Hyatt also promises an enhanced Pay My Way experience, letting members mix awards, points, cash and Points + Cash by night. Online selection, gifting and redemption will be available for eligible awards. Pay My Way and stacking, by the way, really do all work together. Hyatt offers me this illustration, Let’s say a member is making a three night booking. Assuming both the Standard Suite was available for the duration, and there is award inventory available on the selected dates (just like today) – yes, a member could apply a Suite Upgrade Award to the whole stay, a Free Parking award to the whole stay, a Guest of Honor Award to the whole stay, and then pay for the reservation using points on one night, a promotional Free Night Award on another night, and cash on the third night.

Let’s say a member is making a three night booking. Assuming both the Standard Suite was available for the duration, and there is award inventory available on the selected dates (just like today) – yes, a member could apply a Suite Upgrade Award to the whole stay, a Free Parking award to the whole stay, a Guest of Honor Award to the whole stay, and then pay for the reservation using points on one night, a promotional Free Night Award on another night, and cash on the third night.

Milestone Rewards currently begin at 20 qualifying nights. Next year they’ll start at 10 nights or 20,000 base points. Here’s the new chart through 50 nights. Qualifying nights / base points   What you receive 10 / 20,000   Choose one: 1 qualifying night credit, $25 FIND experience credit, or $30 Inclusive Collection spa credit. 20 / 35,000   Choose one: 2 qualifying night credits, $30 spa credit, $25 Delta certificate, 2K Next Stay Award, or 2 Club Access Awards. 30 / 50,000   Choose 10,000 bonus points or a Category 1–4 free night. Also choose one: 2 qualifying night credits, $30 spa credit, $25 Delta certificate, 2K Next Stay Award, or 2 Club Access Awards. 40 / 65,000   Receive 1 Guest of Honor Award. Also choose one: 5 qualifying night credits, $200 Thompson Hotels credit, $75 Delta certificate, 5,000 points, or 1 Suite Upgrade Award. 50 / 80,000   Choose one: $200 Thompson Hotels credit, $75 Delta certificate, 5,000 points, or 1 Suite Upgrade Award. The qualifying night choices add up to 10 nights: one at the first milestone, two at the next, two at 30 nights and five at 40 nights. These count toward both status and Milestone Rewards. That creates a path to Globalist with 50 qualifying nights from other sources, if you select all four night rewards. The requirement remains 60, but 10 can come from these choices. And you earn qualifying nights with the The World Of Hyatt Credit Card (See rates and fees) too – 5 qualifying night credits every year and 2 qualifying night every time you spend $5,000 on the card. The 30 night option to take 10,000 points instead of a Category 1–4 certificate is useful for someone who struggles to use the certificate. A good Category 4 redemption can be worth more, and the certificate will become easier to use with the longer expiration and ability to add a suite upgrade. One Fewer Suite Upgrade, And A Choice About Your Concierge The reduction at 50 nights is easy to miss. The current choice is two Suite Upgrade Awards. The new chart offers one. At 60 nights or 100,000 base points, members will receive: 2 Guest of Honor Awards. A choice of free nights: 2 Category 1–4 awards or 1 Category 1–7 award. Two selections from this menu: 7,500 bonus points, a Free Parking Award, a $100 Delta certificate, 2 Suite Upgrade Awards, or My Hyatt Concierge. You can still select the two suite upgrades and concierge access, keeping the existing 60 night package. But if you want points or parking, something else has to go. And you can’t make the same two choices at 60 nights – you can’t have four upgrades, 15,000 points or two parking awards. You don’t have o select all of your awards at once, though you do have to make these two selections at the same time. Hyatt explains to me that you’ll still have 90 days to make your choices, and: In milestones where there are separate choices, such as 30 nights, the member can make those choices at different points within the 90 day selection window (e.g., could choose the Free Night Award one day, and the HIC Spa credit on a different day.) At 60 nights, the member can choose their free night award choice on a different day from the other selection, but the two selections within “Choose Two” must be made together at the same time. I do plan to keep the concierge benefit, even though mine has never been very responsive. I won’t give up the ability to email someone to address issues. I just wish I would hear back more quickly, and didn’t need to follow up so often. Maybe that’s actually coming? Hyatt tells me they do plan greater investment in the concierge program: [B]y shifting to a choice, we will be able to further invest in My Hyatt Concierge and deliver even more proactive and personalized care. We will share more when available.

And you can’t make the same two choices at 60 nights – you can’t have four upgrades, 15,000 points or two parking awards. You don’t have o select all of your awards at once, though you do have to make these two selections at the same time. Hyatt explains to me that you’ll still have 90 days to make your choices, and:

In milestones where there are separate choices, such as 30 nights, the member can make those choices at different points within the 90 day selection window (e.g., could choose the Free Night Award one day, and the HIC Spa credit on a different day.) At 60 nights, the member can choose their free night award choice on a different day from the other selection, but the two selections within “Choose Two” must be made together at the same time.

I do plan to keep the concierge benefit, even though mine has never been very responsive. I won’t give up the ability to email someone to address issues. I just wish I would hear back more quickly, and didn’t need to follow up so often. Maybe that’s actually coming? Hyatt tells me they do plan greater investment in the concierge program:

[B]y shifting to a choice, we will be able to further invest in My Hyatt Concierge and deliver even more proactive and personalized care. We will share more when available.

As before, lifetime Globalists retain their concierge without having to stay 60 nights.

The new parking award covers a qualifying paid or award stay of up to seven nights, and can be gifted. It appears among the choices at 60, 70, 80 and 90 nights. However it’s no longer simply a benefit for Globalists redeeming points for free nights. I wrote in that Hyatt was surveying turning automatic benefits into awards you could choose and they’ve done that with this one. The benefit is no longer unlimited It comes with a tradeoff – the benefit is instead of something else And you have to plan ahead, one more thing to track and manage, rather than something that’s just ‘taken care of’ in recognition of your loyalty. Hyatt explains the decision to me as, [T]his decision was made as 70% of Globalists did not use the free parking benefit in 2025; 95% used it 4 times or less, and moving this to a choice allowed the program to retain it for members who value it and introduce other exciting new awards like the $200 Thompson Hotels Credit and the $500 Premium Suite Credit. If the benefit wasn’t being used, it actually wasn’t that expensive to offer! And not using it regularly doesn’t mean the option isn’t valued. It may not have been the most valuable benefit of Globalist for most people, but I wouldn’t personally make the tradeoff (in fairness, I’m someone that did use and get value from it). Of course, a parking award will be eligible for use a paid stay while it previously was only available on points. However, at 70, 80 or 90 nights where you can claim it you’re passing up 10,000 points or a suite upgrade to select it. A Year To Use Every Award Is Both An Improvement And A Cut Hyatt’s release presents the new expiration policy as giving members extra time. That’s true for some awards, but the effect runs in both directions. Hyatt tells me, For all awards issued on January 1, 2027 or later, expiration dates will be 365 days from the date of issuance. Milestone free night awards that currently expire after 180 days will get substantially more time. But suite upgrades, ordinary Milestone Guest of Honor awards and club access awards currently have much longer lives, generally through the end of the year earned plus another 14 months under Hyatt’s existing rules. A suite upgrade selected January 1, 2026 remained valid through February 2028. Under a 365 day rule, the same issuance date would produce a January 1, 2027 expiration. That’s more than a year of usefulness gone. Shortening the window makes it harder to hold upgrades for a major trip, to book far ahead, or to save awards from a heavy travel year for a quieter one. More Free Night Choices And Delta Status At Higher Milestones Here’s the rest of the 2027 chart: Qualifying nights   What you receive 70, 80 and 90, at each milestone   1 Guest of Honor Award, plus choose one: a Free Parking Award, 2 single visit Delta Sky Club passes, 10,000 points, or 1 Suite Upgrade Award. 100   Choose 1 Category 1–7 night, 2 Category 1–4 nights, or a $500 premium suite credit. Also choose one: Delta Gold Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. 110, 120, 130 and 140, at each milestone   1 Guest of Honor Award, plus choose one: Delta Gold Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. 150   Choose 2 Category 1–7 nights or an Ultimate Free Night Award. Also choose one: Delta Platinum Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. The Ultimate Free Night at 150 nights isn’t going away. The two Category 1–7 nights are an alternative. Someone who wants two nights at less expensive hotels can choose those, while someone planning one especially expensive night can retain the Ultimate award, which covers participating Category 1–8 hotels, Category A–F all-inclusives and Miraval. The new hotel credits are more restrictive than points: $30 Inclusive Collection spa credit: for spa treatments at participating all-inclusive resorts. $200 Thompson Hotels credit: toward an eligible paid stay. $500 premium suite credit: toward an eligible paid premium suite stay of at least two nights. I’ve wanted a way to use two suite upgrades to confirm a premium suite. A discount on buying a premium suite isn’t as attractive to me. But there are times I might use it. Delta Gold starting at 100 nights and Platinum at 150 nights are interesting choices for someone who flies Delta without status. I still preferred the American partnership. The ability to redeem Hyatt points for American status for a trip was useful for people who didn’t have American status. And the earlier version earned American miles on Hyatt stays. I’d rather earn those than Delta miles. FIND credits are being pared back sharply. The $25 choices at 20 and 30 nights disappear, as do $150 choices at 40 and 50 nights and $300 choices at 70, 80 and 90. A $25 FIND choice appears at the new 10 night milestone. What Hyatt Gets From These Changes The strongest improvements are award stacking, more time to use free night certificates, an earlier first reward, and choices that let members avoid awards they won’t use. A member who doesn’t value concierge access can get something else, while someone who prefers two less expensive hotel nights can choose them. I expect members approaching Globalist will like the qualifying night choices. People who lose free night certificates to expiration should come out ahead, too. Existing Globalists who use all their suite upgrades, plan trips far ahead, or regularly choose FIND experiences have more to lose. Hyatt also gets more ways to influence where members spend. A Thompson credit encourages a paid Thompson stay. A spa credit encourages a treatment that may cost much more than the credit. The premium suite credit encourages someone to buy a room they might otherwise try to upgrade into. Shorter suite award validity should leave fewer outstanding upgrades available for future use. Making concierge elective lets members reveal whether they value the service more than points or another reward. And offering status credits makes the next milestone feel closer, encouraging someone with a modest number of Hyatt nights to keep going. For me, being able to confirm a suite on a free night certificate is the biggest improvement. I care much more about that than a spa coupon. There really is more choice and the ability to earn status faster with these changes. Stacking and combining rewards is great. So is longer expiration of free night awards, though sadly at the cost of shorter expiration for suite upgrade awards. The most consequential change for me might be something that isn’t really being announced. If changing My Hyatt Concierge to a choice benefit really does entail greater investment in the program, it would make the experience far more premium and secure even greater loyalty.
